Time to rise? Ranking European football's sleeping giants
- Published
Deportivo, Parma, Hamburg. Not just a football hipster's holiday hit-list, but a sample of erstwhile headline acts who have returned to their respective top flights in recent years.
You can throw Leeds United, Nottingham Forest, Schalke and Malaga into the mix too.
But with such footballing royalty back in the big time, where can you find Europe's current sleeping giants? Which one-mighty sides are still snoozing?
We first need to establish some criteria - history, heritage, fanbase, stadium. Clubs with huge potential who currently exist outside the top flight.
Calling a big city home helps, but it is not a deal-maker - sorry to fans of Bristol City and second-tier Russian outfit FC Ufa, where the local population tops one million.
Likewise, some clubs with good-sized stadiums have not made the cut. Bari, whose Stadio San Nicola is the third-largest in Italy and was built for Italia '90, stands out, though some of their calcio colleagues outside Serie A also have grounds of more than 30,000 - Hellas Verona, Messina and Palermo among them.
There's a plethora of ex-Premier League teams with top-flight worthy arenas and storied pasts, while Germany is stacked full of historic clubs with huge homes who arguably deserve a spot - Fortuna Dusseldorf, Wolfsburg, Hannover 96 - but we can't include them all.
A sleeping giant must have experienced some element of former glory and Pro Vercelli are the obvious candidate there, winning seven Italian titles by 1922. But, despite being under new ownership, the third-tier side boast neither the ground nor local population to awaken that historic status any time soon.
The other nuance is, that success cannot have come too recently. West Ham, for example, won a European competition three years ago, Wolves are recent top-flight regulars; likewise Stade de Reims, twice European Cup runners-up, and eight-time French champions Nantes.
Leaving out Steaua Bucharest was another big call. European Cup winners 40 years ago and Romania's most dominant club, they now play in Liga II. But, following a deeply divisive split, many of the traditional fanbase follow top-flight FCSB. So who really owns that legacy?
And there was a case for Boavista, title winners in 2001 but whose existence now hangs by a thread. Facing financial ruin, despite fans' best efforts, they have been ejected from Portugal's professional leagues.
Anyway, let's get on with this. Piped through the matrix above, here are my top 10 European sleeping giants - you can have your say in the comments, too.
10. Bursaspor
League titles: One (2009-10). Domestic cups: One (1985-86). Division: 1.Lig, second tier. Stadium: Centennial Ataturk Stadium (43,361)
Historically dominated by Istanbul's elite teams, Bursaspor snapped that long-running streak by becoming only the second club from outside of the capital - and first since Trabzonspor almost three decades earlier - to clinch the Turkish title in 2010.
That meant Champions League nights against Manchester United and Rangers, but in 2024 the Green Crocodiles dropped into the fourth tier for the first time in their history.
Based in a city of about 2.5m people - Bursa sits in the north west, south of Istanbul, near Mount Uludag - and with a unique crocodile-shaped stadium that can house 43,361 fans, Bursaspor have soared up the pyramid since and are looking to return to the Super Lig for the first time since 2019.
9. Dynamo Dresden
League titles: Eight (most recent East German DDR-Oberliga 1989-90). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 89-90). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion (32,085).
Without wanting to turn this into a 2.Bundesliga table, this is the first of four German entries. But Dynamo Dresden, bearing a complex history and situated in the underrepresented east, feel a little different.
Initially enjoying the support of the security forces before their best players were relocated to Berlin, Dynamo became European regulars and lost to Liverpool in the Uefa Cup in 1976 and European Cup two seasons later.
One of East Germany's most dominant clubs, they won eight titles and seven cups and joined the Bundesliga in 1991 following reunification, but they dropped into the third tier four years later amid relegation and mounting debts.
Dynamo, with alumni including Matthias Sammer, have bounced around the regional and lower leagues for many years but now sit in 2.Bundesliga.
Based in a city of more than half a million people, their potential is underpinned by a large, passionate fanbase who averaged over 30,000 for home games in the second tier last term.
8. Kaiserslautern
League titles: Four (most recent 1997-98). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 95-96). Division: 2.Bundesliga. Stadium: Fritz-Walter-Stadion (49,327)
With their 1997-98 success, Kaiserslautern remain the only side to win the Bundesliga immediately after promotion, albeit following a surprise relegation having also been champions in 1991 and enjoyed cup triumphs in 1990 and 1996.
European regulars in the 1990s and early 2000s, it is now almost 15 years since they competed in the Bundesliga, spending four seasons in the third tier before a promotion in 2022.
Despite modest league finishes, the club continue to record average crowds of more than 46,000 and almost pulled off another shock in 2024 when they reached the German Cup final, losing to Xabi Alonso's Leverkusen.
7. Sheffield Wednesday
League titles: Four (most recent 1929-30). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 90-91). Division: League One, third tier. Stadium: Hillsborough (39,732)
Sheffield United fans may argue that they, not city rivals Sheffield Wednesday, should make this list. But the Owls edge it on history and heritage - even if the most recent of their four league titles came almost 100 years ago.
Wednesday were League Cup winners in 1991, and in living memory for many gave us magical moments from the likes of David Hirst, Chris Waddle and Paolo di Canio. Yet they now sit in the third tier after entering administration and enduring relegation last season, before a US consortium bought the club in May.
The Owls, boasting England's 12th biggest club stadium, were relegated from the top flight in 2000, but fans are fuelled with fresh optimism that a reawakening is possible.
6. Hertha BSC
Leagues: Two (most recent 1931). Domestic cups: Two (most recent 2002). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Olympiastadion (74,475).
I'm convinced Hertha have huge potential, if not the history to match some of their counterparts. Their only titles, for example, precede the Bundesliga era.
But the Old Lady once reached a Uefa Cup semi-final and beat Chelsea in the Champions League in 1999.
This season is their fourth consecutive campaign outside the top tier, but Hertha continue to play at Berlin's Olympiastadion and regularly attract more than 50,000 fans. A new ground on the Olympic Park site, housing up to 52,000, is being considered.
Currently top of 2.Bundesliga, Hertha can tap into a deep talent pool on their doorstep - highly rated youngsters Ibrahim Maza and Kennet Eichhorn have joined Leverkusen, goalkeeper Tjark Ernst went to Feyenoord - and look equipped to return to the Bundesliga in fine shape.
5. Bordeaux
Leagues: Six (most recent 2008-09). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 12-13). Division: Regional 1, sixth tier. Stadium: Stade Atlantique (42,115)
Bordeaux's recent troubles have been well documented. Relegated from Ligue 1 in 2022 before administration meant they tumbled into the fourth tier, this summer they were again demoted to the regional sixth tier because of financial issues.
Having seemingly hit the bottom, the 2009 French champions now at least have something to build on after being bought by US investment fund Park Bench for one euro.
Les Girondins are dripping in history. Once home to former greats Jean Tigana and Zinedine Zidane, as well as current France internationals Aurelien Tchouameni and Jules Kounde, their decade-old home hosted a Euro 2016 quarter-final - albeit Bordeaux are not playing there at present as they try to shape their future.
4. FC Nuremberg
League titles: Nine (most recent 1967-68). Domestic cups: Four (most recent 06-07). Division: 2.Bundesliga, second tier. Stadium: Max-Morlock-Stadion (50,000).
Perhaps it's not overly imaginative to be opting for the current top two in Germany's second tier but FC Nuremberg meet all the selection criteria laid out above.
They have the history - nine titles, with the latest of four cup triumphs coming in 2007; a 50,000-seater home; large local fanbase in a one-club city - and the heritage.
They're nicknamed 'Der Club' because of their status in early German football.
Oh, and World Cup winner and Germany's all-time top goalscorer Miroslav Klose is their boss.
3. Real Zaragoza
Domestic cups: Six (most recent 2003-04). European: Cup Winners' Cup (1994-95). Division: Primera Federacion, third tier. Stadium: La Romareda (under reconstruction but projected 43,000).
David Seaman, look away now. Arsenal fans of a certain vintage will remember former Spurs boy Nayim's long, looping winner beating the moustachioed stopper in the final minute of extra time to give Real Zaragoza the Cup Winners' Cup.
There have been two Copa del Rey triumphs, European journeys and star names since - Pablo Aimar, Diego Milito and David Villa among them - but three decades later, Los Manos find themselves in Spain's third tier.
Ander Herrera, aged 37, is back at his boyhood club, who are in the process of developing a new 43,114-capacity stadium for the 2030 World Cup, in an attempt to help the fallen giants return to former glories.
"Real Zaragoza belong to Europe, they belong to compete for trophies, to be fighting with the biggest clubs in Spain and in Europe," said Herrera.
2. Saint-Etienne
League titles: 10 (most recent 1980–81). Domestic cups: Seven (most recent 2012–13). Continental: European Cup runners-up (1975–76). Division: Ligue 2, second division. Stadium: Stade Geoffroy-Guichard (41,965)
Saint-Etienne were, until Paris St-Germain overtook them in the past decade, the most-decorated club in France with 10 league titles in 25 seasons from 1956-57 to 1980-81.
Les Verts reached the European Cup final in 1976, losing to a vintage Bayern Munich side, while their last silverware came in the now-defunct Coupe de la Ligue 13 years ago with a team spearheaded by Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang.
They are presently spending their fourth season in five in the second tier, but they continue to produce top prospects. Star defenders William Saliba and Wesley Fofana came off the production line, while 18-year-old attacking talent Djylian N'Guessan will join Liverpool in January.
Then there is their 41,965-capacity Stade Geoffroy-Guichard home, nicknamed the 'cauldron', which was a whisker from seeing Ligue 1 football again this term - Les Verts lost to Nice in the promotion/relegation play-off, meaning the wait to rejoin France's elite continues.
1. Sampdoria
League titles: 1990-91. Domestic cups: Four (most recent 93–94). Continental: Cup Winners' Cup (89–90), European Cup runners-up (91-92). Division: Serie B, second tier. Stadium: Stadio Luigi Ferraris (33,205)
Sampdoria were once continental big-hitters, not merely domestic champions during a golden era of Italian football.
Buoyed by Paolo Mantovani's investment, the Genoa outfit won the Coppa Italia four times between 1985 and 1994, clinched the Scudetto in 1991 and reached three European finals, winning the Cup Winners' Cup in 1990 a year after losing to Barcelona in the final.
In 1992, the team of Gianluca Vialli, Roberto Mancini and Gianluca Pagliuca were again beaten by Barcelona in extra time of the European Cup final at Wembley.
More big names followed in the period between Sven-Goran Eriksson's side winning the club's last major trophy in 1994 and a first relegation five years later - Clarence Seedorf, Juan Sebastian Veron and Ariel Ortega included.
Samp had spells back in Europe before finishing bottom of Serie A in 2023 amid serious financial problems and almost dropped into the third tier.
Under new ownership, though, fans hope the club's future is more stable - and the architecturally iconic Stadio Luigi Ferraris home they share with rivals Genoa is set to undergo an expensive redevelopment before Italy host Euro 2032.

Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
- Published
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.
Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.
On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.
But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.
So how did we get here? And what happens next?
What happened in the Afcon final?
In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.
Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.
With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.
The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.
Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.
Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.
Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.
Or so they thought.
- 'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph 
  - Published19 January
- Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes 
  - Published24 February
Why was the Afcon final result overturned?
Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.
Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".
In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.
While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.
The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.
- Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe 
  - Published13 May
- Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member 
  - Published19 March
What is the Court of Arbitration for Sport?
Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.
For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.
More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.
The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.
In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.
If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.
- How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it? 
  - Published28 September
When will we get a verdict?
While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.
In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".
Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.
The good news is that it can be quicker.
In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.
The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.
What could the long-term fallout be?
Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.
Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.
The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at a referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.
"This new rule will also apply to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.
Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.
Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.
The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.
The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.
Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.
With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.
But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Man City's statement win has feeling of irrelevance with season in limbo

Manchester City made what they will regard as a powerful statement in the most hostile territory against Liverpool at Anfield - but is it a statement that carries any weight during a Premier League season in limbo?
City's attention turned to on-field matters in their first game since being found guilty of 114 charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.
The fates, and fixture list, decreed it would be at Liverpool, whose fans nurse the most burning sense of injustice after finishing second to City in 2013-14, 2018-19 and 2021-22.
Their argument centres on the belief those titles could have been theirs had City not possessed the high finance of their Abu Dhabi-based owners, using it in the manner that led to them being investigated.
With this as the backdrop, City strode into this fevered Anfield atmosphere, with Liverpool fans high on adrenaline and determined to make their contempt for their rivals obvious - then outclassed Andoni Iraola's side in a 3-0 win.
On another day, in other circumstances, the manner of City's victory would have fed the narrative that this was a performance of champions, a winning marker laid down to their rivals as they hold a three-point lead at the top of the table.
Not here. Not in the Premier League's dysfunctional state.
Instead, once the predictable sound and fury had been diluted by City's composure and the swift realisation they were not unnerved by Anfield or the storm raging around the club, this was a surreal experience.
After the feast of excitement delivered when Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp presided over the greatest domestic rivalry of recent years, this was an occasion - remarkable as it seems - that seemed robbed of a sense of jeopardy by the circumstances surrounding it.
Yes, it was a statement display and City celebrated wildly at the final whistle, but will it count for anything given they await potential sanctions suggested including Premier League relegation or a record points deduction?
As Erling Haaland looked close to tears in front of Manchester City's fans, including his father Alf-Inge, and head coach Enzo Maresca pumped his fists in jubilation, Anfield's DJ slipped Fleetwood Mac's 'Little Lies' on to the loudspeakers in a final message of defiance.
Maresca said: "We knew there was going to be noise but we need to make our own noise by winning games. We need to learn to deal with the noise but the message is to win games.
"For me it's quite easy. I try to focus on things I can control. There are things that are not in my hands so I don't stress about them.
"I cannot control things outside football, so why stress? I stress about gameplan, day-by-day training sessions, but the rest it's not in my hands."
Haaland added: "For every single person part of Manchester City, every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time. It was tough. It was hard, but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone.
"It's always tough to come here. If you look at the record it's tough. With the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp era it was tough for both teams, always has been. It was important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do something about. The thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do."
City have appealed against the verdict, but until the dust settles and final decisions are made, this Premier League season is in a holding pattern.
When City come to Anfield and win, especially as convincingly as they did here, it should be a win without qualification or questions.
This does not apply amid the current uncertainty.
Every victory, every league table, will come with a metaphorical asterisk until clarity and finality comes. No-one knows when this will be.
City's players did their jobs to perfection, victory secured by second-half goals from Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki. It is all they can do.
There can be no escape, however, from the cloud hanging over Manchester City because every win will carry the same rider - producing a state of inertia that is not good for the Premier League.
In the end, a day that promised huge discomfort for City ended in a stroll.
City navigated the hostile reception awaiting them at Anfield by arriving through the staff and contractors' entrance - while an inevitable febrile environment awaited them.
Even the derided half-and-half scarves were doing a roaring trade, until it was noticed the sky blue half read: 'Shamchester City - The Cheats'.
The announcement of City's line-up was drowned out by deafening jeers, while banners around Anfield carried a variety of messages.
They including 'A Generation Of Supporters Cheated', 'And After All You Really Robbed Us All' and - in a nod to the Oasis song Stop Crying Your Heart Out, written by Noel Gallagher who was at Anfield, 'All Of Your Stars Are Fading Away'.
This was all watched by an impassive City chief executive Ferran Soriano, but any notion their fans would turn on the owners was dispelled by a flag reading: 'In Khaldoon We Trust. We've Won It All', a gesture of support for the embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.
City's fans also waved hundreds of inflatable bananas, an old habit when they spent time in the lower leagues in reduced circumstances. There remains the possibility they will get the chance to wave them down the tiers once more in the near future.
The first half did much to pour cold water on what started as a red-hot atmosphere, further diluted by City's second-half domination, although Liverpool's fans rammed home their disgust until the final whistle, chanting "cheat" every time their opponents passed in a lengthy period of possession.
Former Liverpool and England defender Stephen Warnock told BBC Radio 5 Live: "This needs rectifying as quickly as possible, but this isn't an easy thing to come to a conclusion. It's never-ending. It's so difficult and it's going to take so long to sort out."
He added: "The hard part is that this is a brilliant Manchester City team, but you have to caveat it and say they have done it illegally and they bought their way. You're caught in what you're thinking about this City team.
"I admire them because they're so good individually and so great, but the way it has been done and put together has not been put together correctly."
While ex-Man Utd striker Wayne Rooney, added: "I know what it is like from managing Derby County when they had a points deduction. The mindset and message to the players was simple – just try to win the next game.
"All the noise around the club, from the media and other fans, will make them even hungrier to succeed."
As City walked off, they were accompanied by the taunt of "You're going down" from the Kop.
City's fans answered with the trademark: "We're not really here."
This, in essence, is what makes this Premier League campaign one that might yet be rendered void. City might win the title - but who knows if they will be here next season?
As Maresca's side move into top gear and threaten to accelerate away from the chasing pack with wins such as this, no-one has a clue what their final destination will be.

Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) MP Nishikant Dubey on Sunday hit back at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk over Starlink's proposed entry into India's satellite communications market, asking him to first provide affordable internet connections to poor people in the United States. Dubey also raised concerns over the security implications of the satellite internet service, asserting that India would not change its security policy under pressure. In a post on X, Dubey said a Parliamentary Committee had examined the challenges that Starlink could pose to India's security agencies. He added that the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Home Affairs and investigative agencies had raised concerns over the potential threats. "As the Chairman of the Parliamentary Committee, our committee has understood the challenges facing the country's security agencies through @elonmusk's Starlink. The Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Home Affairs, and our investigation agencies are being affected by the dangerous games of these threats," Dubey wrote. Quick answers to key questions Dubey said Starlink could pose challenges to India's security agencies and argued that national security should take precedence over commercial interests. He said India would not change its security policy under pressure. According to Dubey, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Home Affairs and investigative agencies raised concerns about potential security threats. He also said similar concerns had been flagged in 2013–14. The government said security assessments of all three licensed satellite communications providers are underway. Once an assessment is complete, a provider may seek spectrum assignment; the ministry said the three entities are at broadly the same regulatory stage. Musk says Starlink would increase competition and give Indian consumers more broadband choices. He has also argued that the service would need affordable pricing to attract customers in India. Musk argues that another provider could give consumers more choices and benefit the average citizen. He has acknowledged that competition could reduce existing companies’ profits, while saying it would not necessarily put them out of business. Referring to the previous UPA government, the BJP MP said the concerns surrounding such threats were not new and had been flagged more than a decade ago. "In 2013-14, the government of Manmohan Singh ji had informed @TRAI about these threats," he said. Dubey maintained that national security would take precedence over commercial considerations, noting that India would not compromise its policies to facilitate the entry of a foreign company. "First, provide connections to the poor in your own country, America, at affordable rates, and then level accusations; India is a healthy democratic, sovereign nation; it does not change its security policy under pressure or social media," he added. He further stated that if commercial interests were the deciding factor, the government could have welcomed Starlink despite objections from security agencies. “If our policy were driven by money, we would have rolled out the red-carpet welcome for you despite opposition from the security agencies. Don't you provide even more support to political parties from America to Britain?” he further added. Dubey's remarks came amid an ongoing debate over Starlink's proposed commercial launch in India, with Musk arguing that the company's entry would increase competition and give consumers more choices in the broadband market. On Saturday (local time), Musk criticised arguments against Starlink's entry, alleging that India's broadband business was dominated by a monopoly and that some online users were defending existing market players. "The ridiculous arguments by Ambani’s army of In ternet shills make no sense. On the one hand, they say Starlink couldn’t possibly compete with the amazing low prices offered by Ambani’s de facto monopoly in India and then, in the same breath, they essentially claim that Starlink would be too strong of a competitor! This is absurd hypocrisy and hyperbole," Musk wrote on X. He acknowledged that the arrival of another service provider could affect the profits of existing companies but argued that this would not necessarily undermine their businesses. “Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he added. The latest remarks followed an earlier post in which Musk sarcastically targeted arguments against Starlink's proposed entry while seeking permission to operate in India. Meanwhile, the Ministry of Communications has rejected suggestions that India's regulatory framework for satellite communication services favours certain companies over others. "The Government has put in place a fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework for all telecommunication services, including satellite communication services. Under this, telecom licences have been granted to three Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite services based on non-geosynchronous satellite orbit-based satellite communications, as part of its commitment to enable provision of satellite communication services in India," the ministry said in a statement issued on October 8. It clarified that security assessments of all three licensees were currently under way. "As and when this process is completed for a licensed entity, it may proceed to the next step of seeking assignment of spectrum. South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

Priya (name changed), 32, from Kerala, had been struggling with recurring episodes of depression that affected her ability to carry out everyday activities. This non-invasive procedure uses magnetic pulses to stimulate specific areas of the brain.
Priya’s experience reveals a challenge in managing depression, say experts. While antidepressants help many people, some continue to experience symptoms despite treatment, requiring doctors to reassess the diagnosis and consider other interventions.

Detentions continue in Delhi despite Supreme Court order, 100 held from Connaught Place
About 100 protesters were packed into two buses and removed from the area.
Delhi Police on Sunday continued to detain protesters, including CPI(M) leader John Brittas, around Connaught Place as groups returned to renew their demonstrations against chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, even as the Supreme Court ordered that peaceful, unarmed protesters cannot be detained except through the “procedure established by law”.
About 100 protesters were packed into two buses and removed from the area. A man was pulled out of a burger joint on suspicion of being a protester. The man later said he was just standing alone when the police dragged him before letting him go.
A special bench of justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the directions after an urgent hearing on petitions alleging mass detentions, restrictions on movement, suspension of internet services and non-compliance with the court’s October 9 order on transport curbs ahead of Saturday’s protest against Kumar.
Deep Dive
The court also directed that metro and railway services in Delhi operate normally, internet connectivity remain undisturbed and free movement of people be restored. It ordered authorities to remove a notice imposing prohibitory restrictions around the Supreme Court and other court complexes to ensure unhindered “access to justice”.
Brittas told reporters the police’s conduct was a flagrant violation of the basic rules. “Brute force has been used against people who were protesting peacefully. No matter how hard they try to break this agitation, it will only grow by leaps and bounds, and we will continue to protest peacefully. This will only push the protest to greater heights. Just think about the police rushing into an aircraft to take Abhijit Dipke and others into custody. What was the hurry to board an aircraft? Are those people hijackers? This is a violation of basic rules of civil aviation,” he said.
One of the detained persons, who sought anonymity, told HT that he was peacefully standing in the area. “I would have also been beaten if I was alone. I was just standing there near the protest. Even if they are protesting, it is their right. Why are they being detained and beaten up,” the person said.
Delhi Police have registered more than 20 first information reports (FIRs) over attempts to hold a protest in the Capital on Saturday despite restrictions imposed by the force, senior officers said. More than 20 FIRs have also been registered over alleged attacks on police personnel during the demonstrations, with police citing attempts to disrupt law and order and obstruct government officials from performing their duties, an officer said.
Ratna Singh, legal affairs head of CJP, said the “fact that this even has to be brought before the Supreme Court is telling. After what happened yesterday, we must ask why the state machinery is being directed to infringe fundamental rights left, right and centre.”
Delhi Police’s response was awaited.

A large randomised controlled trial among heart failure patients in India led by the Sree Chitra Tirunal Institute for Medical Sciences and Technology (SCTIMST) in Kerala, has found that hospitalisation episodes and all-cause mortality among heart failure patients can be significantly reduced if patients are systematically followed-up by a nurse, with the help of a mobile health application.
The two-year Telemonitoring and Integrated Multidisciplinary care for Heart Failure (TIME-HF) trial found that heart failure patients with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) who received nurse-led collaborative care had a 22% lower risk of death than those receiving usual care. They were also more likely to remain alive without hospitalisation during the two-year follow-up.
The trial results were published in the American Heart Association’s Journal, Circulation, on August 30, 2026.
What makes the trial relevant is that it addresses critical gaps in heart failure care: in Keralam, heart failure registries have reported high mortality post-discharge — 82.7% mortality over 10 years, alongside the fact fact that only 25.4% of the patients with heart failure receive guideline-based therapies. It also holds lessons for the rest of the country: with nearly 27% of all deaths in India being due to heart disease, and 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease occurring between the ages of 40 and 69 years, there is an urgent need for quality, post-discharge care.
What the trial did
The TIME-HF trial involved 1,507 adults at 22 government and private hospitals in Keralam and neighbouring States, with 755 patients assigned to the intervention and 752 to usual care. The mean age was 61.9 years; 77.6% were men, 57.3% lived in rural areas and 70% had relatively low educational attainment. Ischaemic heart disease was the predominant cause of heart failure, accounting for 77.4% of cases.
Results indicated that nurse-led intervention substantially improved prescription of the four major components of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure — renin-angiotensin system inhibition/ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
“Our heart failure patients receive sub-optimal care, as most of them do not adhere to therapies or follow up with the doctor on time. There is also the issue of physician inertia. HF Registry evidence indicates that the median survival after diagnosis of heart failure is just 3.7 years. This collaborative care model is proof that survival and quality of life of these patients can be improved if we systematically address the gaps in care so that proven therapies for heart failure become part of routine care,” said lead researcher and additional professor at SCTIMST P. Jeemon.
Centring nursing care
The model put a trained nurse at the centre of the care pathway, who would closely monitor heart failure patients after discharge, educate the patient and family about heart-failure self-care, lifestyle modification and encourage medication adherence.
Nurses reviewed the patients’ medication regimen at discharge to ensure that there was no deviation from the guideline-mediated therapies. This was again reviewed at every follow-up visit with the help of a mobile-health app. The m-health app helped the nurses monitor all physical parameters of the patient real time and to identify warning signs of worsening disease, communicate and connect with patients and physicians so that timely hospitalisation was possible.
All participants underwent scheduled follow-up visits every three months for two years. Adherence to all four guideline-directed medical therapies was only 22.1% in the usual-care group, while it was 37.3% in the intervention group at two years.
“The health system engaging with the patient regularly was the key here. The m-health app gave the patient updates in real time to the nurse. Oxygen saturation levels, weight gain, weight loss, drop in blood pressure or respiratory rate comes as alerts, and then were escalated to the physician,” Dr. Jeemon points out.
The TIME-HF trial thus helped address one of the health system’s persistent weaknesses: that of proper follow-up care of patients with chronic diseases. The model is suited for strengthening chronic disease management and reducing the burden of hospitalisation and mortality in resource-limited settings across the country, experts said.

An Australian trekker who was last seen on a remote South American hiking trail has been found dead, his family have said.
Jordan Yap, 30, last made contact with friends and family on 14 September ahead of a planned 10-day solo trek along Peru’s Huayhuash mountain range, 400km north-east of Lima.
In a social media post on Saturday, his friends and family said “with a heavy heart we are sorry to tell you Jordan has been found, and he did not survive”.
“We want to thank everyone who has helped; friends and family, the contributors, the search teams, the police, the many groups we engaged with who gave their time and effort, everyone who helped to share on social media. We are appreciative of all of you.
“Please remember Jordan as the vibrant man he was, and for the immense joy he brought to so many people’s lives.
“Rest in peace Jordan – from your friends and family.”
The Melbourne man was last seen near the beginning of his trek across the Cordillera Huayhuash circuit, which is regarded as a challenging, high-altitude trek through the remote Andes mountains. His friends and family regarded him as a very experienced hiker.
His friends and family became concerned after he failed to make contact on his estimated return date, failed to check back into the Krusty hostel in Huaraz and missed a scheduled flight from Lima to Cusco.
The avid trekker misplaced a satellite beacon he was travelling with days before he set off on the 120km hike, raising further concerns.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has been contacted for comment.

What is the oldest Samsung device that still gets software updates in 2026?
Knowing how long your phone will get updates is important for deciding when to upgrade.
Android 17 brought several productivity-focused improvements to smartphones this year. Naturally, the latest devices will support future updates for at least a couple of years. But if you have a Samsung device that's inching toward its proverbial "end of life," you may want to know if your phone will keep getting updates. Samsung has already shipped Android 17-based One UI 9 on devices like the Galaxy Fold 8 series and the Flip 8.
While security updates are commonly sent to phones well past their prime, software updates that bring meaningful changes aren't as common. That goes double for Samsung's affordable A series. Longer support periods from smartphone makers are a relatively new trend, meaning older-generation phones don't share that kind of longevity and may already be out of support.
Keeping track of how long a phone will be supported is essential when you're deciding to hold on to an existing phone or purchase a new one. Here's what you need to know about which phones Samsung hasn't abandoned just yet, from flagships to budget phones.
What Samsung phones still get updates in 2026?
How long a Samsung smartphone receives Android updates depends on the device's tier. Flagships enjoy up to 7 years of support while mid-range devices get about 5-6 years. Budget models get up to 4 years of support.
Here are the Samsung phones that still get Android updates in 2026:
- The Samsung Galaxy S23, S23+ and S23 Ultra's Android updates end in February 2027. The S22 lineup and the S21 FE 5G lost support earlier this year.
- The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Z Flip 4's Android updates ended in August 2026. The Fold 5, Flip 5 and up continue to receive updates.
- Samsung's Galaxy A06 4G lost Android updates in August 2026, but its 5G variant will get Android updates until February 2031.
- The Samsung Galaxy A15 will receive updates until December 2027, and the A24 gets them until May 2027.
- Samsung's Galaxy A34 gets these updates until March 2027. The A54 5G will get Android updates until March 2027, while the A73 no longer gets them as of April 2026.
And here are the Samsung tablets that continue to get Android updates in 2026:
- The Galaxy Tab S9, Galaxy Tab S9+ and Tab S9 Ultra will get Android software updates until August 2027. The Tab S9 FE+ and FE get them until October 2027.
- The Samsung Galaxy Tab A9+ and A9 get Android updates until October 2026. They only get 2 generations of OS updates.
- The Galaxy Tab Active 5 receives Android updates until January 2028, while the Active 5 Pro gets them until 2033.
These Samsung wearables will continue to get updates this year:
- The Galaxy Watch 5 and Watch 5 Pro from 2022 will get Wear OS updates until December 2026
What happens if your Samsung phone is no longer supported?
Manufacturers don't warn you before cutting you off from software and security updates. You'll have to look up your smartphone model online to verify. Samsung has a handy security update list you can check. If you go into your Settings app and find that your phone hasn't been updated in several months or years, chances are that your phone isn't supported anymore.
That bargain on a refurbished model you spotted online might be moot if it loses access to updates within the year. Lose security patches, and your phone becomes vulnerable to all sorts of new threats from hackers.
As your phone misses out on more updates, apps slowly become incompatible if they're designed with the latest OS versions in mind. Worse, strange popups and apps that appear without warning and guzzle your internet data might mean your device has been hacked. These are clear signs that you're due for a new phone.

Twenty people have been arrested after thousands gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.
The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.
The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after climbing on to the Battle of Britain memorial, having Palestine Action placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests.
Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
A ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.
Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organisers said 250,000 people were at the march.
The Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.
The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.
“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.
“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”
The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.
At Labour party conference last month, Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”
Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”
Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.
“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.
The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.
A counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.
The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.
Last Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in central London was held.
The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.
The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) held a protest at Shivaji Park Maidan in Mumbai on 02 October 2026, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation. The protesters raised concerns over the alleged exclusion of voters during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demanded greater transparency in the election process. Although Mumbai Police had denied permission for the meeting, hundreds of people took part in the protest and raised slogans. Police later registered an FIR against the organisers and 400–500 unidentified participants for violating the restrictions.
Against this backdrop, a video circulating on social media (here, here) claims to show footage of the CJP protest at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of CJP’s protest demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar at Shivaji Park ground in Mumbai on 02 October 2026.
Fact: The viral video is unrelated to the CJP protest in Mumbai. It is an old video showing a public meeting organised by AIMIM leader Asaduddin Owaisi at the Central Library Ground in Bhopal on 15 September, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to the same footage (here and here) from 18 September 2026, nearly two weeks before the CJP protest in Mumbai.
We found that the video was uploaded on Facebook and Instagram by a Bhopal-based content creator, Amin Siddiqui, on 18 September 2026. We also found several other videos showing the same scenes on his Instagram page (here, here, and here). These videos indicate that the footage is from a public meeting addressed by AIMIM president Asaduddin Owaisi in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh.
News reports (here and here) also confirm that Owaisi addressed a public meeting at the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal on 15 September 2026, opposing the Uniform Civil Code Bill passed by the Madhya Pradesh Assembly.
When we compared the visuals from the viral video with the location on Google Street View, we found that the surroundings match the Central Library Grounds in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh, confirming that the video is related to the Bhopal meeting.
To sum up, an old Bhopal public meeting video is being falsely shared as a CJP protest video in Mumbai.

Choreographer and filmmaker Ganesh Acharya has unveiled the trailer of his upcoming directorial, Ganesh Dust To Stardust. Starring Shivanshu Soni, Alok Shaw, Sukanya Kalan and Sakshi Pawaskar, the film centres on the challenges people face while pursuing their ambitions and the determination required to overcome difficult circumstances. It is scheduled to release in theatres on December 11, 2026.
Ganesh Acharya unveils trailer of Ganesh Dust To Stardust; film to release in theatres on December 11

With Ganesh Dust To Stardust, Acharya brings his experience as a choreographer to a story that connects dance with the pursuit of success. The film explores the idea that ambition alone may not be enough, with perseverance, hard work and sacrifice also playing a role in turning aspirations into reality.
Speaking about the trailer, Ganesh Acharya shared, “I have always believed that everyone has the right to dream, but dreams don’t come true just by dreaming. This film is very close to my heart, and I hope that everyone who watches it finds a little bit of their own dreams, struggles and aspirations in it.”

The ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 is a practical, performance-driven business laptop featuring a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, an exceptional keyboard, excellent port selection, and easy RAM/storage upgradability. However, its main drawbacks are mediocre battery life, a dim display limited to 45% NTSC, and an underwhelming webcam.
ASUS offers the ExpertBook series in many configurations. If you want the best business laptop Asus offers, consider the ASUS ExpertBook Ultra. If you are a business owner who wants a premium design without compromising essential business features, the ASUS ExpertBook B Series is worth considering. Finally, the ASUS ExpertBook P Series is for those looking for an affordable business laptop without paying a premium.
In that regard, the ASUS ExpertBook P3 is a sweet spot for people looking for an affordable business laptop. It doesn’t try to compete with the flashy, ultra-thin consumer aesthetics of the Apple MacBook Air or Dell XPS line; instead, it positions itself as an aggressive challenger to the Lenovo ThinkPad and HP EliteBook ecosystems, as well as other business laptop ranges.
I have been using the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 version (2026) for the past several days. Overall, it has been a solid business laptop. The model I am testing comes with a powerful Intel Core Ultra 7 255H and delivers excellent performance, a reliable port selection, the best keyboard in its class, and plenty of business-focused features.
ASUS has also expanded the ASUS ExpertBook P3 G2 series, now offering more choices than before with both Intel and AMD configurations across different sizes, while also addressing some of the shortcomings we noticed with the earlier ExpertBook P series.
In this full, detailed review, I will share my experience with the ASUS P3 G1, compare it to the original P3 launched in 2025, and see how it stacks up against the recently announced ASUS P3 G2 series. By the end, you should have a better idea of whether the Asus P3 G1 still makes sense or is worth going for the latest generations instead.
Table of Contents
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review
Design and Build: Practical Over Premium
Asus ExpertBook laptops are easy to spot from miles away. Most models across the lineup look the same and follow a very similar design language, with an understated gray finish and a clean, minimal look.
Asus ExpertBook P3 G1 also follows the same design. It may not impress you with flashy looks or an ultra-slim profile, which is something the ExpertBook P3 isn’t trying to do anyway. This is a practical, business-first laptop.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 comes in two chassis variants. The 1A variant has a plastic chassis, and the 2A variant has a metal chassis for those who want an even sturdier, more premium build.
My unit comes with a plastic body, but it doesn’t feel cheap by any means. In fact, it is a step up from some of the older ExpertBook laptops I have reviewed in the past.
Although the chassis is plastic, the matte, grainy finish hides it and gives it a much more premium feel. I love minimal laptop designs, and the ASUS ExpertBook takes that approach even further with nothing but the ASUS logo on the lid. The matte, grainy finish is also fingerprint-resistant; as a result, smudges don’t show up, and it stays clean.
The same treatment continues when you open the lid. The hinge is now slightly stronger. The display is stiffer than ideal to position, but it still wobbles a bit when you type and change its angle.
The lid opens up to 180 degrees, allowing the display to lie completely flat on the surface. It can come in handy if you want to share your screen with someone across the table. One limitation, though: since this variant doesn’t have a touchscreen, you cannot really use the display while it is lying flat.
Build quality is stronger than last generation, but it still has noticeable flex, especially in the center of the keyboard and between the touchpad and the keyboard. Thankfully, I didn’t notice it while typing. The deck doesn’t bend much under normal use unless you press harder.
The rounded corners also make the laptop more comfortable to hold during longer carrying periods.
One thing Asus continues to get right is port selection. In a world where fewer ports have become the norm for a premium experience, Asus ExpertBook P3 supports all major ports, including one Thunderbolt 4 USB-C, one USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, two USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-A ports, a full-size RJ45 Gigabit Ethernet port, HDMI 2.1 TMDS, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a Kensington Nano lock. You get pretty much every port you expect from a business laptop. That also means you can connect most everyday accessories directly to the laptop without carrying a separate dongle.
The chassis is also MIL-STD 810H tested across 24 procedures. The laptop should handle everyday wear and tear. Note that the laptop is not water-resistant.
The keyboard supports backlighting. This makes it easy to see and type in low-light conditions. The backlight also doesn’t leak when you’re looking straight at the laptop. It also has durable keys, and ASUS claims the keyboard is tested for up to 10 million keystrokes to withstand wear and tear over time.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 is available in both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes. My review unit is the 14-inch variant with a WUXGA 16:10 display. The side bezels are fairly noticeable, and there is a rather large chin at the bottom that also houses the Asus ExpertBook logo. Above the display is a physical privacy shutter, which I truly appreciate for business-centric users who want better privacy.
Display: Good for Work, Not for Creative Use
The 14-inch display is a sweet spot if you want something compact without giving up too much screen space.
ASUS ExpertBook doesn’t get the kind of high-end OLED displays Asus offers on some of its high-end laptops or even more affordable VivoBook models. It is a 14-inch IPS-level display with WUXGA 1920 × 1200 resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, a 60Hz refresh rate, up to 300 nits of brightness, and 45% NTSC color coverage.
The display quality is decent and gets the job done, especially if you’re buying the ExpertBook primarily for office work. It is perfectly fine for browsing and using office apps like spreadsheets and documents, but if you work on photos or video editing, you will probably want something with better color coverage.
The display also has an anti-glare coating, which does a good job of cutting down reflections and makes it easier to use in bright environments. However, the trade-off is that a matte finish coating removes some of the visual punch you get from glossy panels. Colors aren’t as vibrant, although the text remains sharp.
Watching videos and content on this WUXGA IPS-level panel isn’t a pleasant experience, but as I said, for everyday tasks such as browsing, spreadsheets, and other office applications, it feels comfortable to use, and the text looks sharp enough to read clearly.
Performance: More Power Than Most Office Users Need
Performance is easily one of the ExpertBook P3’s strongest aspects. Asus offers it with either a Core Ultra 5 225H or Core Ultra 7 255H. My unit came with an Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, paired with 16GB DDR5 RAM and a 512GB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD.
At the heart of the configuration is the Intel Core Ultra 7 255H, a high-performance processor with 16 cores, 16 threads, a maximum clock speed of 5.1GHz, and integrated Intel Graphics. In everyday use, this combination handles almost any task without breaking a sweat. Whether you’re using multiple graphics-heavy applications, running dozens of browser tabs, or switching between office apps all day.
Another advantage is upgradability. Asus ExpertBook P3 comes with two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots, and the existing RAM isn’t soldered to the motherboard, so you can upgrade later if you want to, and it won’t cost you a bomb upfront, which is the case with most modern laptops.
It also has two storage slots: one M.2 2280 PCIe 4.0 slot and one M.2 2230 PCIe 4.0 slot, giving you more room to expand the storage later.
One thing I did notice is that the laptop gets quite warm at the bottom even during something as basic as browsing the web. You can definitely feel the heat when using it in your lap. It is not entirely surprising, though, considering the Core Ultra 7 255H is an H-series processor designed for higher performance.
Keyboard and Trackpad: The Keyboard Is the Star
The keyboard is easily one of my favorite things about the Asus ExpertBook P3. It offers one of the best typing experiences I have had on a laptop after Mac. A lot of that comes down to the 1.5mm key travel, which delivers a great typing experience. The keys are also large and well spaced, giving your fingers plenty of room to move around. It didn’t take me long to get comfortable with this keyboard.
The trackpad is also large enough for daily use. The large surface area makes it easy to move the cursor and also use gestures.
I have no issues with the keyboard and trackpad, though some users may find the fingerprint sensor placement inconvenient because it is integrated into the power button. To prevent accidental presses, ASUS made the power button slightly firmer.
Battery Life: The Biggest Compromise
This kind of performance is always welcome, especially if you regularly handle high-demand tasks. The trade-off, though, is battery life. My configuration comes with a 50Wh, 3-cell battery, and the ExpertBook P3 takes a noticeable hit here.
Even for basic use, I was getting only about 8-9 hours. On medium to heavy gaming, the battery life dropped to 4 to 5 hours, which isn’t the performance you want if you plan to use it on battery power all day.
ASUS bundles a 65W USB-C charger in the box, and it can take your laptop from 0 to 100 in less than 2 hours. That’s fairly quick, but I really wish Windows laptop makers offered more travel-friendly options instead of big, bulky charging bricks and three-pin plugs.
Sound: Decent, but Nothing Special
The speakers are decently loud, but they don’t get particularly loud. ASUS uses two built-in speakers with Dirac audio support. Thankfully, Asus includes a built-in 3.5mm headphone jack, so you can plug in wired headphones or earphones directly without relying on the built-in speakers.
Windows 11 Home: Still Too Cluttered
I have never been a fan of Windows’ cluttered experience. If you’ve used Windows for years, you probably won’t mind much, but if you are coming from a Mac or Linux, you’ll have to deal with Windows’ cluttered experience first.
It took me more than three hours to set up the device, including the unwanted Windows updates I had to install during setup. Plus, the Windows update prompts never stop. Even Microsoft has promised to improve the Windows laptop experience by eliminating these unwanted distractions.
Since this is an ExpertBook, ASUS includes business-centric features, including AI ExpertMeet for meetings. However, this configuration lacks some useful Copilot+ AI features for those who care about privacy and want to run AI features locally on the device. The Core Ultra 7 255H delivers up to 13 TOPS of NPU performance, well short of the 40+ TOPS required for a Copilot+ PC. You may need to rely on cloud processing for more demanding AI features.
Camera: Still Needs Work
ASUS has been pretty good at improving the little things in everyday use, but the camera is still one area that needs work. My configuration comes with a 1080p FHD IR camera with Windows Hello support and a physical privacy shutter. Even on the maxed-out ExpertBook Ultra, the camera quality is rather underwhelming, especially on business laptops like this, where it matters a lot.
Even in good lighting, the camera adds plenty of noise, and in low light, it gets worse. However, you can always connect an external camera if camera quality matters to you. But this is something Asus needs to improve.
ASUS ExpertBook P3 G1 Review Verdict: Powerful and Practical, but Battery Holds It Back
Overall, if performance is high on your priority list, then the ASUS ExpertBook P3 might be a better choice. Everyday tasks feel quick and responsive, plus it also has plenty of power for more demanding tasks. The excellent keyboard, with 1.5mm key travel, makes typing sessions comfortable, and the full selection of ports lets you connect any peripherals without constantly reaching for or using a dongle. The biggest advantage of the Asus ExpertBook P3 is plenty of room to upgrade later. It offers dual SO-DIMM slots for memory and dual M.2 slots for additional PCIe storage.
Among the pros are also some compromises. Battery life takes a noticeable hit when you push the processor harder, and while the laptop can handle some AI workloads locally, it cannot run the full set of Copilot+ PC features.

Pat Cummins claimed three for 54 as Australia took a 139-run lead against South Africa at Stumps on day three of the first Test.
A collective bowling effort from Australia saw South Africa bowled out for 284 on Sunday in its first innings – Mitchell Starc (two for 63), Josh Hazlewood (two for 54) and Nathan Lyon (two for 58) took a brace each.
Australia had scored 390 runs in its first innings with Matt Renshaw hitting a career-best 190 to help the visiting side recover from a precarious 124 for six.
In its second innings, Australia was 33-0 at stumps in 5.4 overs when play was called off early again due to bad light, with nearly 13 overs lost in the day. Nic Maddinson (17 not out) and Travis Head (10 not out) are at the crease.
David Bedingham top-scored for South Africa with 49 off 73 balls. The hosts were 197 for eight at one stage before a 52-run ninth-wicket partnership between Keshav Maharaj (34) and Simon Harmer (35 not out) reduced some of the damage.
South Africa is the reigning world Test champion and beat Australia in the 2025 final. It is Australia’s first trip to the country since the 2018 ball tampering scandal when they last toured here.
South Africa was down to 115 for four at lunch. Starting from 27 for one on day two, Aiden Markram (37) and Bedingham added 57 runs to their overnight partnership.
The breakthrough for Australia came just before drinks – Markram edged Starc to slip in the 21st over.
South Africa scored 59 for one in the first hour. In the second hour, Temba Bavuma (3) was out caught off Lyon – Steve Smith took a well-judged catch as Bavuma went for a reverse sweep.
Cummins then had Bedingham caught in the slips, with Smith taking another great catch to his left.
After lunch, Cummins struck again. Wiaan Mulder was the first to go – he scored 30 off 50 balls with three fours and a six, adding 56 with Tristan Stubbs.
Stubbs fell soon after for 32 – caught at square leg, again off Cummins.
Lyon had Kyle Verreynne caught at slip for 13 as South Africa stumbled to 197 for seven. Marco Jansen hit six fours for a 20-ball 26, before holing out off Hazlewood.
South Africa was 238 for eight at tea, with Harmer and Maharaj able to go past the follow-on mark. Their 50-partnership ended when Starc dismissed Maharaj.

The Supreme Court on Sunday directed that there shall be no detention of any individual except in accordance with the procedure established by law, particularly with respect to the assembly of peaceful and unarmed people beyond the area where prohibitory orders are in operation. A bench of Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana also issued a direction on pleas objecting to the closure of the Delhi metro station and internet restrictions in the wake of the CJP protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. The Supreme Court was hearing a contempt petition related to protests organised by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar in Delhi. According to Bar and Bench, the Supreme Court directed that: 1. Delhi Metro and railway services must operate normally. Restrictions are permissible only when justified under Article 19(2). 2. Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law, without affecting statutory powers to impose lawful restrictions. The court clarified, “When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act.” 3. Movement of people and vehicles across Delhi must not be unnecessarily obstructed. Barricades must be reviewed immediately in accordance with law-and-order and traffic requirements. 4. No unlawful detention is permitted. Any detention must follow a legally established procedure. 5. Peaceful assemblies must be allowed in accordance with law, especially outside areas where prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS are in force. 6. The Supreme Court said the State must explain the circumstances, manner and legal justification for the alleged detentions, observing that it is duty-bound under Article 32 to protect and enforce fundamental rights. 7. Any notice board announcing Section 163 restrictions near the Supreme Court must be removed, if still in place, to ensure unhindered access to the Supreme Court and other courts. 8. The Supreme Court recorded the assurance that lawyers, journalists and other professionals will not be obstructed in performing their duties. 9. Notice was issued in the contempt proceedings alleging violation of the Court’s October 9 order. Authorities must file a compliance report by Tuesday, October 13, including details of Metro restrictions and railway advisories. 10. Habeas corpus petitions alleging mass detentions and other connected matters will be heard with the main cases on October 13. The Supreme Court held a special hearing on Sunday on petitions challenging the preventive detention of thousands of protesters amid a massive crackdown on protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and various other political parties. Among those who have approached the Supreme Court are Trinamool Congress MP and Senior Advocate Menaka Guruswamy and advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi. Guruswamy reportedly challenged the detentions and the police action of picking up protesters from the streets. Tripathi filed a separate contempt petition, alleging that Delhi Metro stations remained closed on Sunday despite the Court's October 9 order against a “complete shutdown” of public transport ahead of the protests. The authorities had shut 45 Delhi Metro stations to prevent protesters from travelling to Jantar Mantar. More than 200 trains were cancelled and traffic restrictions were also imposed. Besides, as the protest began, more than 7000 protesters were arrested in the police clampdown, according to estimates shared by sources with news agency PTI. The protest was held to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar amid growing criticism of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has resulted in the deletion of millions of voters' names.
