Struggling Corinthians sign Seedorf as manager
Oct 11 : Former Netherlands midfielder Clarence Seedorf has returned to a managerial role after seven years, with Brazilian side Corinthians announcing the 50-year-old as their coach on Sunday.
• The former Real Madrid, Inter Milan and AC Milan player had last managed Cameroon, where he was sacked in July 2019.
• He has joined Corinthians on a contract until the end of the 2027 season, the club said in a statement.
• Corinthians, who are a point above the relegation zone in the Brazilian Serie A, sacked previous manager Fernando Diniz on Wednesday.
• Seedorf had terminated his contract with Botafogo to retire as a player and take up his first managerial role at Milan in January 2014.
• He took over at Milan when they were 11th, and helped them finish eighth, before being dismissed in June. He later coached Shenzhen and Deportivo La Coruna.
• Corinthians visit second-placed Palmeiras later on Sunday.

NASA on Friday released a much-anticipated “request” to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations that, as early as 2030, will succeed the International Space Station as a place for astronauts to live in low-Earth orbit.
In a cover letter accompanying the 360-page “request for proposals,” NASA stated its plan: “This will ensure NASA has a sustained human presence in LEO for crew members to perform science and exploration.” Several private companies that have worked for years on designing and developing such stations have been keen to learn exactly what capabilities NASA is seeking. These new documents finally provide some answers.
NASA’s solicitation can be found here. Industry responses are due back to NASA on December 8. NASA said it plans to select “two or more” contractors in this phase of the competition, and intends to make a final decision in April.
In LEO to stay
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement that accompanied the release of the new documents. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
Bidders for this funding phase will certainly include Axiom Space, Voyager Space, and Vast Space. Blue Origin won an earlier round of funding from NASA, but questions remain about the company’s commitment to the program. SpaceX appears unlikely to bid, at least for now. Phase 1 winners will be guaranteed at least $100 million.

- The claim that an image of U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth standing in front of an eagle emblem with his arms raised closely resembles a real image of Nazi leader Adolf Hitler is unfounded.
- The image of Hitler has strong indications of artificial intelligence generation. The image of Hegseth also has signs pointing to AI editing, although real video footage from an Oct. 3 speech authentically shows that the changes were minor and that Hegseth did raise his arms in front of a stylized version of the Department of Defense's eagle seal.
- The eagle emblem in the image of Hitler matches the "Reichsadler" symbol Hitler's Nazi regime used — but it's worth noting that the emblem was a highly stylized version of an eagle symbol used in Germany both before and after the Nazi Party came to power. The DOD has since 1949 used a seal featuring an eagle holding arrows above an olive branch; the version on display during Hegseth's Oct. 3 speech omitted the olive branch and had a more stylized design.
- We've reached out to the DOD to ask about the reason for the redesign and whether any similarities to the Reichsadler were intentional. The DOD denied any similarities existed.
On Oct. 3, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth delivered a speech at the U.S. Air Force Academy. Images from the speech of Hegseth with his arms spread wide in front of the Department of Defense's eagle seal went viral, drawing comparisons to Nazi leader Adolf Hitler and an official Nazi symbol.
Snopes readers shared the images with us, asking to confirm whether such comparisons were accurate. One Facebook meme showed Hegseth in front of a simplified version of the DOD's eagle seal without its traditional olive branch. Next to him, in a similar pose with his arms outstretched is Hitler in front of the "Reichsadler," the eagle emblem of Nazi Germany. The accompanying caption stated: 
On Saturday, Hegseth traveled to the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs to address the cadets.
As he walked on stage, the Department of War seal was visible behind him and on the podium in front of him.
Before he began, he raised both arms out to the side and told the cadets to take their seats.
That was all it took.
Within hours, critics were posting side-by-side images comparing the staging of the speech to old photos of Adolf Hitler speaking in front of an eagle emblem.
(Facebook user "Really American")
The image of Hegseth showed signs of artificial intelligence editing in the form of garbled letters in the seals behind and in front of him, but video footage of the Oct. 3 speech shows that the content was not meaningfully altered. The accompanying image of Hitler, however, carries signs of heavy manipulation and was likely entirely generated by AI.
That said, there are still other authentic photographs of Hitler that show him standing in front of a Nazi eagle emblem that in some ways resembles the new DOD one.
Given the heavy manipulation of the Hitler image, we found the claim that the image of Hegseth closely resembled a real image of Hitler unfounded.
We reached out to the DOD to ask about the reason for the redesign and whether any resemblance to the Reichsadler was intentional. Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Joel Valdez said to us over email: "The American bald eagle is an icon of our country and used on many state and federal seals, including the seal of the Department of War. If for some reason you see imagery of a bald eagle and begin having delusions about Nazi Germany, then you may need to get your head checked for serious brain damage."
The moment where Hegseth raised his arms wide occurred in the very beginning of his speech at the 5-second mark on the official DOD YouTube video. We captured a screenshot below:
(YouTube user "Department of War")
The image of Hegseth in the Facebook post appears to have been edited or manipulated. The color is much brighter and the "M" behind Hegseth's right arm appears misshapen. Hegseth's face also appears different. The image itself is similar to its original YouTube video.
There are several indications of AI generation in the purported photograph of Hitler. Firstly, the individuals on either side of him on the bottom left and right of the frame all have incomplete facial features, with sections of their heads cut off or blurred. The flags behind him also have inconsistent patterns that show signs of heavy editing or cropping.
Real photographs of Hitler standing in front of flag poles show that, even on draped flags, the swastikas are recognizable. The two swastikas on either side of Hitler's head are almost perfectly round circles. Considering they are placed over what could either be rounded pillars or curtains, they are clearly overlaid or heavily edited.
We compared the image to real photographs of speeches Hitler made, and found none that resemble the room in the image from the meme. One authentic 1939 image on Getty Images shows Hitler speaking to the Reichstag, or German parliament, with a much larger eagle symbol and the Nazi symbols farther apart. Images of Hitler speaking at Nuremberg rallies do not align with the one in the above meme. Videos show that Hitler often spoke with his arms held wide, but there are no specific videos corresponding with the image in the above meme. 
Despite the above image of Hitler being heavily manipulated, Hegseth's backdrop still has loose similarities to other real photographs of Hitler speaking in front of an eagle emblem.
During Hegseth's speech, many online noted the simplified (archived) version of the DOD seal, which removed the traditional olive leaves below the eagle, made the eagle's design more angular and replaced the 13 stars above the eagle with five stars.
We should note that the eagle symbol was used in Germany before and after the Nazi Party came to power. The DOD has been using the eagle seal since 1949. The DOD website, which still showed the version of the seal containing the olive branch as of this writing, explains its meaning thus: "The American bald eagle, long associated with symbolism representing the United States of America and its military establishment, has been selected as an emblem of strength. In facing to the right, the field of honor is indicated."
Hegseth has also been in the news for his Sept. 30 "State of the Force" address, in which he announced he was creating an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon and initiating "Project Meridian," which he described as "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
Snopes has frequently reported on rumors about Hegseth and the Department of Defense.

Hi there, it’s Sarah. Last night, STAT scored an awards hat trick, taking home a Gerald Loeb — the most prestigious honor in business journalism — for the third year in a row! This year’s Loeb recognized Lizzy Lawrence for her exceptional beat reporting on the Food and Drug Administration. This is also STAT’s fourth Loeb overall in our 11-year history. Not too shabby, y’all.
Does MAHA still matter to voters?
The Make America Healthy Again movement has been credited with helping to propel Donald Trump to a second term at the White House. But as midterm elections draw near, MAHA is nearly invisible on the campaign trail.
In today’s story, Isa Cueto, Daniel Payne, and Chelsea Cirruzzo take stock of MAHA’s current political influence, and its struggles to translate popular support for some of its core issues (like the dangers of ultra-processed foods) into policy. “This whole election in November is a contrast election. Democrats are making it about Trump, Republicans are making it about communists,” said Republican strategist Joel White. Read more.
What motivates two young scientists focused on breast cancer and abortion access
Amid relentless and sometimes depressing news cycles, one of the best things about working for STAT is that with projects like STAT Wunderkinds, we get to celebrate scientific achievements and the extraordinary talents who make them possible.
Yesterday, Allessandra DiCorato profiled cancer biologist and first-year resident physician Neal Carleton, whose work is focused on improving treatment for older patients with breast cancer. The hope, Carleton says, is to turn breast cancer into “more of a chronic disease” that can be managed with a daily pill and regular (but not too frequent) monitoring. And in today’s profile, Justin Chen interviewed researcher Betsy Pleasants, who’s using artificial intelligence to offer a more complete picture of online discourse about issues like abortion access and contraception.
Asking questions before we know why
Fifty years ago, researcher Robert Gallo and his colleagues made the landmark discovery of the protein interleukin-2, or IL-2. He reflects in a new First Opinion piece on the various reasons why that finding was so important. Not only did IL-2 make possible the discovery of the first human retroviruses, including HIV as the cause of AIDS, and become widely used in cancer cell immunotherapy, he writes, “its larger lesson is about the nature of scientific discovery.”
Gallo didn’t know all the things that IL-2 would make possible — and scientists shouldn’t be expected to answer questions about direct applications of their research in order to secure funding, he says. “If scientists must know the practical outcome before asking the question,” he writes, “they’ll never ask some of the most important questions.” Read more.
The census changes threatening public health
The Trump administration wants to make three big changes to the U.S. Census: eliminating questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation; excluding anyone who is not a citizen or “lawful permanent resident”; and changing how it determines where people like college students or retiree “snowbirds” reside.
These changes, if passed, pose a big problem for both public health research and real-world federal assistance, social epidemiologist Nancy Krieger writes in a new First Opinion. That’s because things like race and ethnicity data are essential for how we track trends in U.S. morbidity and mortality and how federally funded programs determine who is eligible and where resources need to be allocated. This isn’t the first flaw to be highlighted in the census system, but Krieger suggests it’s what tennis fans might call an unforced error.
The future of mifepristone
Mifepristone, a pill used to terminate early pregnancies, has been caught in a tug-of-war throughout the second Trump administration as abortion opponents push for crackdowns on its use. Now the Food and Drug Administration say its safety review will continue into next year, with a report on findings expected by March 2027. Read more.

Pakistan's president suspends provincial government led by Khan’s party ahead of march
Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari has declared a state of emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province
ISLAMABAD -- Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday declared a state of emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan and suspended its government, which is led by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s party, ahead of a planned march on Islamabad by supporters demanding his release.
Zardari acted on the recommendation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s Cabinet, according to a statement from the president’s office. The measures place the province under the authority of the governor, who represents the federal government.
The announcement came hours after Sharif’s office said that the federal Cabinet had recommended emergency rule, accusing the provincial government of “deliberate disengagement from the fight against terrorism.”
No protests were reported against the suspension of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s government, where police detained several supporters of Khan’s PTI party overnight. Authorities deployed additional police and security forces in the province and Islamabad to prevent unrest.
Shipping containers placed by police along key routes in Islamabad since last month to block potential rallies have disrupted traffic and forced residents in the capital and neighboring Rawalpindi to take lengthy detours.
Khan’s spokesperson, Zulfiquar Bukhari, condemned the suspension of the provincial government, calling it a disguised coup. He said the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government was the only one with a genuine popular mandate following the February 2024 parliamentary elections, which Khan’s party says were rigged.
“Now that little bit of democracy is also gone,” Bukhari said in a statement.
Referring to recent talks between Khan’s party and the federal government, Bukhari accused officials of having no intention of reaching an agreement. He said government representatives had focused on counterterrorism, while Khan’s representatives had come to discuss the imprisoned leader’s basic human rights.
Khan is Sharif’s main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated. Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan’s turbulent political landscape.
Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government last week held talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party’s chairman, said days ago that negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.
Beside Khan’s release, Khan's party demanded his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Sharif's government has said Khan is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintains that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.
The province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, on Saturday urged supporters to prepare to march on Islamabad. Afridi launched the protest campaign last week, leading marches through several districts in the province.
Sharif’s government has been urging Afridi since last month to postpone the march, citing a surge in attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. It has also accused Khan’s party of sympathizing with the militant group, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.
Khan's party said Afridi and his former Cabinet members had been detained.
Political analyst Azeem Chaudhry said the emergency measures gave Gov. Faisal Karim Kundi the powers of the provincial chief executive, removing Khan’s party from power in the only province it governed. He said the provincial assembly and Afridi’s Cabinet were also suspended.
Pakistan has witnessed a surge in militant violence in recent years, much of it blamed on the TTP, a separate group but a close ally of the Afghan Taliban, who returned to power in neighboring Afghanistan in 2021. Islamabad has repeatedly accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of providing sanctuary to TTP militants, an allegation Kabul denies.

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

Cardiac rehabilitation, a multidisciplinary approach to recovery and risk-reduction, is an important addition to medications, interventional and surgical procedures in heart patients. A cardiac rehab programme usually includes medical assessments, supervised exercise, nutritional guidance, psychosocial counselling and health education tailored to the clinical, cultural and behavioural needs of the patient.
Cardiac rehab has been incorporated into the routine care of patients in developed countries, while it is just now gaining inroads in low- and middle- income countries like India. The primary benefits of attending a cardiac rehab programme are faster recovery from cardiac procedures, reduced risk of future complications, improvement in blood sugar, blood pressure and lipid levels, increased cardiorespiratory fitness, adherence to a heart healthy diet, better weight management, abstinence from tobacco and excessive alcohol consumption, better emotional health and health-related quality of life, and decreased mortality.
The scenario in India
There is now a growing prevalence of heart diseases in the young Indian population, both in urban and rural parts of the country. According to the Global Burden of Disease, 2021, heart disease is the most common cause of death in India, accounting for 28.6 lakh deaths. Estimates indicate that nearly 27% of all deaths in India are due to heart disease, while 62% of all deaths due to cardiovascular disease in the country are premature, between the ages of 40 and 69 years. Among those who survive, the effects can linger for years, affecting productivity and quality of life. This has brought to the fore, the urgent need for more widespread and accessible cardiac rehab facilities. There is a wide gap in the number of heart patients requiring cardiac rehab and the actual numbers being referred for these services.
Barriers to rehab
Even among those who access and enrol in cardiac rehab programmes, not everyone completes the programme. The main barriers to completing the cardiac rehab program after enrolling include patients’ work commitments, family responsibilities, financial constraints, and medical complications. Programmes that can offer personalised solutions including flexible scheduling, return-to-work counselling, sliding scale payment options and close collaborations with the referring cardiologist to identify and treat complications early, could help decrease drop-outs. Programme facilitators must also be able to proactively identify cues for potential non-adherence and work with patients and their families to circumvent challenges and complete the programme.
What works
A ‘TRACK and CARE’ policy could help in improving patient engagement in cardiac rehab programmes. TRACK denotes establishing Trust, involving the patient’s Relatives, helping them set clear Aims for the programme, Checking on the progress made on a daily, weekly and monthly basis and finally remembering to say Kudos to every single positive behaviour change made by the patient. The CARE refers to multidisciplinary care, comorbidity care and holistic care, where various specialists work together to address the different medical and psychological needs of the patient.
Young people are increasingly contracting heart disease. Getting them back to be productive, healthy and happy members of society is vital. While prevention remains the most important goal, cardiac rehabilitation must become an important part of treatment, not just an add-on that is optional. And to do that, we have to proactively address the potential barriers to access, adherence and programme completion.
(Dr. Priya Chockalingam is the clinical director, Cardiac Wellness Institute, Chennai. drpriya@cardiacwellnessinstitute.com)

Where should you go in California for delicious food, sprawling vineyards, and the satisfying sound of a freshly uncorked wine bottle?
Let me guess, you're thinking of Napa.
But what if I told you there's a hidden gem on the central coast where you can get all of the above with fewer crowds, lower prices, and cooler tasting experiences?
Welcome to Paso Robles.
A wine for everyone
Growing up in the Bay Area, Napa Valley quickly became a special place for my family. With no relatives living in the US, my Greek parents took us there every Christmas to make the holidays feel special.
I've visited Napa over 20 times, but over the past few years, Paso Robles has stolen my heart.
Paso Robles is almost exactly in the middle of Los Angeles and San Francisco, about 200 miles each way. Parallel to the mountains and the sea, the region has a unique terroir due to big temperature swings. The topography's distinctive microclimates are perfect for growing a variety of grapes, helping Paso distinguish itself in a crowded California wine market.
"The diversity of this area really separates itself from the monoculture that Napa has become," Andrew Jones, the owner of Field Recordings Winery, told me.
Adding to that diversity is the low barrier to entry in the Paso Robles wine industry. Most of the wineries are small and family-owned, and the winemakers are often on-site to guide you. This refreshingly laid-back approach makes tastings feel intimate and approachable, and they're at a far more accessible price point than Napa, where the high cost of winemaking has trickled down to tourists. Silicon Valley Bank's 2026 direct-to-consumer wine report found that the average tasting fee in Napa is $79, while it's $27 in Paso Robles.
"Napa has a taller order; they have to live up to a brand that's worldwide," said Neeta Mittal, one of the first Indian women to open a winery in the US. "Where we thrive in Paso is we're able to etch our own identity, and that's a great nimbleness that we're allowed."
Tasting experiences with a twist
Mittal and her husband, Kunal, own LXV Wine, which offers the only wine-and-spice pairing in the US. I visited LXV on my first trip to Paso Robles and was delighted that my tasting included cheeses covered in various spices. I learned how ginger and black truffle salt can bring out the flavors of Cabernet and why Szechuan peppers and Nebbiolo pair so well.
I also love the tastings at Field Recordings, which prides itself on making wines that "are all about the flavor — with none of the pretension," as its website reads. Jones specializes in small-batch, single-vineyard wines. They're fun and funky, decorated with colorful labels and names like "Kitties" or "Super Gnario."
Field Recordings is in Tin City, my favorite part of Paso Robles. The converted industrial hub features over 20 wineries, all within walking distance of each other, where tastings typically cost between $20 and $30. It's perfect for a wine crawl, but there's also a brewery and the very fun Tin City Distillery if you're craving cocktails instead.
Where you can wine and dine
Another reason I keep going back to Paso Robles is the fantastic restaurant scene. I never skip a dinner at The Alchemists' Garden, which has a fun cocktail list and some of the best fries.
My parents still rave about the meal we had at Il Cortile Ristorante. Its pappardelle is handmade and paired with a rich, luscious Bolognese, and the branzino is light, bright, and cooked to perfection. But the star is the risotto covered in white truffles, a holiday splurge I've never forgotten.
The Restaurant at Justin, which earned its first Michelin star in 2022, bested any fine-dining experience I've had in Napa. I still have pictures saved from that dinner, where my fiancé and I feasted on maple-leaf duck breast, prime filet, and various veggies picked from their 26-acre farmstead.
And no visit to Paso is complete without a stop at Brown Butter Cookie Company, which has mastered the salty-sweet combo in a little treat. The hand-rolled cookies are made locally and available in a variety of flavors.
On my last visit, I grabbed a dozen bags for my family, friends, and myself, of course.
A destination for any season
Blessed with California sunshine, Paso Robles is a great vacation year-round. I've gone in the fall, summer, and winter — where it's festively decorated for the holidays — and have always been charmed by the small-town vibes and friendly locals. (Don't miss karaoke nights at the Pine Street Saloon.)
The winemaking world is slowly starting to learn about Paso Robles, but the town itself remains a hidden gem.
For now, at least, this is California's best-kept secret.

Ethiopian official promises change in Tigray after troops retake regional capital
A former Tigray leader now advising Ethiopia’s prime minister has promised a “visible change” in the region
NAIROBI, Kenya -- A former Tigray leader now advising Ethiopia’s prime minister on Sunday promised a “visible change” in the region after government-allied units retook Mekelle city following renewed fighting with opposition forces.
Ethiopian Airlines resumed flights to the city of Mekelle on Sunday for the first time since rebels led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front seized the airport on Sept. 23. They withdrew Oct. 3, when government-allied fighters entered the city.
Renewed fighting in Tigray has undermined the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year war, as mounting tensions between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea have raised fears of a wider conflict.
“I would like to assure you on this occasion that we will bring visible change, a change beyond mere hope,” Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, told supporters who greeted him and intelligence chief Redwan Hussein at Mekelle airport. He did not elaborate.
The 2020-2022 war in Tigray caused about 500,000 civilian deaths from violence, famine and the collapse of health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres on Friday urged all parties to cease hostilities and resume dialogue. He warned that fighting risked further destabilizing the wider region.
Ethiopia told the U.N. Security Council on Friday that it was taking self-defense measures, accusing Eritrea of sending troops across the border and occupying parts of northern Ethiopia. Ethiopian authorities previously have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, an allegation Eritrea has denied.
Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos did not specify the measures being taken. His letter to the council did not identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting the allegations. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims.
Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urged the council to condemn what he called a “deplorable declaration of war” by Ethiopia. His response did not confirm or deny the alleged troop crossings.
The dispute deepens a rift between the two countries whose armies fought together against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war.

Associated Press journalists Filmon Equar Hailu in Mekelle, Ethiopia, Khaled Kazziha in Nairobi, Kenya, and Amir Aman Kiyaro in Hamburg, Germany, contributed to this report.

Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said on Saturday that he would introduce the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” and bring it to the House floor through a discharge petition. The name draws on the defence philosophy that shaped US policy towards the Soviet Union in the 1980s. The proposed legislation is aimed at President Donald Trump’s newly announced deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, which the White House has promoted as a way to ease fuel prices. Fitzpatrick, who co-chairs the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, described the bill as bipartisan, although it was unclear on Saturday which Democrats would sponsor it. The legislation would block all purchases of Russian oil. “We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” Fitzpatrick wrote on social media. He added on X: “It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly.” Representative Don Bacon, a retiring Nebraska Republican, said he would support the measure. “I’ve already agreed to be an original cosponsor,” Bacon wrote on social media. “Congress must make a stand.” Bacon also told Axios he had “already agreed” to sign the petition. “Peace through strength” is a Cold War foreign policy doctrine that holds that stability is best maintained through overwhelming military power, deterrence and military preparedness rather than appeasement or passive diplomacy. Reagan championed the approach during the 1980s, although its roots can be traced to classical realpolitik. Its core principles included a substantial military buildup, the expansion and modernisation of the armed forces, and the development of strategic technologies. Reagan’s administration sharply increased defence spending, while the doctrine relied on the premise that superior US military capabilities would discourage Soviet aggression. Programmes such as the Strategic Defense Initiative, also known as “Star Wars”, sought to counter nuclear threats and shift the strategic balance of power. The doctrine also treated military preparedness as leverage for diplomacy. Rather than viewing strength and negotiations as opposing approaches, the strategy sought to encourage Moscow to engage in arms control talks. The 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty was one outcome of negotiations during Reagan’s presidency. Reagan also presented the rivalry with the Soviet bloc as an ideological contest between freedom and totalitarianism, rather than simply a geopolitical struggle. Supporters argue that the approach pressured an economically strained Soviet system, contained communist expansion and helped bring the Cold War to a peaceful end. Critics counter that an unconstrained arms race and proxy conflicts risked miscalculation, heightened tensions and brought the superpowers closer to a nuclear exchange. Donald Trump announced the arrangement on Friday. Under its terms, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with further shipments to follow. Putin said in a statement, according to Russian state media, that Moscow had confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and the wider global market. Energy analysts have questioned whether the additional diesel would meaningfully lower prices. Trump has presented the deal as a way to reduce fuel costs, but the arrangement could also generate revenue for Russia as its war against Ukraine continues. The arrangement has drawn objections from both parties. Representative Gabe Amo, a Rhode Island Democrat who sits on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned its logic on social media. “After signing a law to ramp up sanctions on Russia, Trump is paying Putin for oil to deal with the high gas prices caused by his choice of war with Iran? That’s not punishing Putin, that’s profit,” Amo wrote, adding: “Make it make sense.” The deal also intersects with existing US law. In 2022, Congress passed legislation banning imports of Russian oil and authorising further sanctions. That measure contained an exception allowing the president to permit energy already purchased before its passage, or imports deemed to be in the national interest. A discharge petition allows lawmakers to bring legislation to a vote without the approval of House leadership. It requires 218 signatures, a majority of the chamber, and has increasingly been used to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican. Fitzpatrick and Bacon have used the mechanism before. Earlier this year, they forced a House vote on Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions. The measure passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Time is short. The current Congress ends in January, and the House is not scheduled to vote again until after the 3 November midterm elections. Any legislation that passes the House would still need Senate approval and could face a presidential veto. Fitzpatrick is the latest Republican lawmaker to break with Trump in a high-profile dispute as the party fights to retain control of Congress amid mounting disapproval of the president. The proposed legislation sets up a fresh test of Republican support for the administration’s approach to Russian energy supplies and its wider policy towards the war in Ukraine. Sayantani Biswas is an assistant editor at Livemint with seven years of experience covering geopolitics, foreign policy, international relations and global power dynamics. She reports on Indian and international politics, including elections worldwide, and specialises in historically grounded analysis of contemporary conflicts and state decisions. She joined Mint in 2021, after covering politics at publications including The Telegraph.
She holds an MPhil in Comparative Literature from Jadavpur University (2019), with a specialisation in postcolonial Latin American literature. Her research examined economic nationalism through Eduardo Galeano’s Open Veins of Latin America. She also writes on political language, cultural memory and the long shadows of conflict.
Biswas grew up in Durgapur, an industrial town in West Bengal shaped by migration, which drew families from across India to the Durgapur Steel Plant. As the only child in a joint family, she spent years listening—almost obsessively—to her grandparents’ testimonies of struggle, fear and loss as they fled Bangladesh during the Partition of 1947. This formative exposure to lived historical memory later converged with her training in Comparative Literature, equipping her to analyse socio-economic structures and their reverberations.
Outside the newsroom, she gravitates towards cultural history and critical theory, returning often to texts such as Paulo Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed. As a journalist, she is committed to accuracy, intellectual rigour and fairness, and believes political reporting demands not only clarity and speed, but historical depth, contextual precision, and a disciplined resistance to spectacle. WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. For at least several months, people have attributed a quote to Oscar-winning actor Denzel Washington in which he allegedly praised and pledged support for U.S. President Donald Trump.
Snopes received website searches from readers looking for more information about the quote, which read as follows:
I've worked with a lot of people in my life, and I've never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. He's a great friend and an even better president. I'm proud to be a steadfast supporter, and I'll never apologize for it. God Bless America and our president.
Searches for Washington and Trump located users posting the rumor in quote memes, for example on Facebook, Threads (archived) and X (archived).
(Redline News via Facebook)
Some users' comments indicated they believed Washington truly spoke out in favor of Trump, while others expressed skepticism that the actor would say such a thing.
In sum, an extensive search for credible evidence turned up nothing at all, indicating Washington never said this. Also, we previously reported as similarly untrue that fellow Oscar winner Matthew McConaughey and musician Mick Jagger uttered the words after people reposted memes attributing the exact same quote to them.
As such, we rate this claim as an incorrect attribution.
Snopes emailed a representative for Washington for confirmation and will update this article if we receive further information.
Digging into the rumor
We performed an initial search for Washington and Trump on Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo. Those searches failed to locate any credible sources reporting that Washington praised Trump, either in the words displayed in the meme or in any similar manner.
Likewise, searches of the news media outlets ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News, MS NOW, NBC News, Newsmax and NewsNation found no reporting that Washington spoke favorably of Trump.
If any actor of Washington's prominence who had never publicly expressed such support in the past were to say the words attributed to them in the meme, national and international outlets covering entertainment and politics would have widely reported it. We found no such reporting.
We reported in 2016 that, despite another rumor, Washington did not publicly announce his support for Trump. We also fact-checked a false rumor alleging the actor said that electing Trump saved the U.S. from becoming an "Orwellian police state."
People who create and repost misinformation often exploit the names of actors known for portraying tough, "he tells it like it is" leading men in movies, for example Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck, Sam Elliott, Washington and others, to boost the credibility of their fabricated claims.

A heroic, 7-day bike ride made this teen a global star. Where is she now?
Fame is a strange beast. It brings applause, attention and promises of a better life. But when the spotlight moves on, those promises are often forgotten. No one knows this better than 22-year-old Jyoti Kumari.
When she was 15 years old, during the peak of India's COVID shutdown, she shot to international fame for cycling over 700 miles, from northern India to her village in the eastern state of Bihar, with her injured father riding on the back of the hot pink bike she'd bought for $20.
Her dad, Mohan Paswan, drove an autorickshaw for 20 years in Gurugram, a city near Delhi, sending money to his wife and five children in the village of Sirhulli. After he suffered a debilitating road accident in January 2020, Kumari and her mom took the train to Gurugram to care for him.
Five months later, he still hadn't made a full recovery and his family was running out of money for food and rent. The family decided they would all be better off at home. But at the time, authorities had shut down public transportation for the pandemic lockdown. No one knew how Mohan Paswan could make the journey. That's when Kumari insisted she would bring him back home, riding on a pad attached to the main seat of her bicycle.
She cycled for seven consecutive days on a relatively empty stomach at the height of the lockdown to get him to safety. Even though it was a test of sheer endurance, Kumari discovered that she loved cycling — it came naturally to her.
लॉकडाउन था, सो अपने पिता को साइकिल पर बैठाकर गुरुग्राम से दरभंगा ले गई बेटी...
वीडियो: मोहन भारद्वाज और सीटू तिवारी pic.twitter.com/Mc7hkmyB4O
— BBC News Hindi (@BBCHindi) May 19, 2020
Her epic ride grabbed headlines around the world. NPR's previous reporting noted promises of cash rewards, training for a career as a cyclist, even a movie deal.
Six years later
That was in 2020. "Now — life is hard," Kumari told NPR in a phone call from her home in Bihar.
What happened to all the promises made — for financial support, especially to support cycling as a competitive sport?
Many promises were not kept, she says.
"The politicians who made promises, saying they would give money for my sports or education — nobody actually gave anything," she says. "Whatever reward money we collected back then [from individuals who extended help and a government award that came with a cash prize], we put it all into our house, rebuilding it. We had a brick house before, but it only had bare walls. Now we have completed it, added a toilet, a bathroom, and a running water connection. By doing all that, the house has finally become livable," she says.
This is no small achievement. An estimated 300,000 people are homeless in the state of Bihar in spite of government programs. For a family living in poverty, having a home can make a huge difference in the fight for survival.
For Kumari's family, making their house livable meant securing something that burst of fame had failed to deliver on — a more stable place from which to build their lives.
But they are doing so without her dad.
Mohan Paswan passed away of a heart attack in May 2021, just months after his daughter brought him home. Kumari says she felt heartbroken. After his passing, financial security has been precarious for the family.
At the moment, her mother works as a cook. Her meager income supports Kumari and her three siblings at home (an older sister has married and moved out).
"There are days when we go to sleep hungry," she says. "Our brother-in-law used to help us earlier, but now he also has a child, a wife and his father to take care of. He works a small job in the city — how much can he really do? So now he isn't able to help us much."
Still she holds out hope for a better future.
"Once my education is fully complete, only then will I be able to do something else. Only then can I prepare for things and look for a job," Kumari says.
But she has yet to pass the final exam required to complete Class 12, her final year of secondary school. That's an important credential to apply to university or qualify for certain jobs. It's a stepping stone to a better life, especially for disadvantaged students.
A typical day
Finding time for her studies has been a challenge. Kumari's day begins at 7 a.m. She cooks and cares for her younger siblings after her mother rushes off to work. "I give my brothers breakfast for school and get things ready for my sister. Then, I clean the house, mop the floors, do the dishes, wash clothes by hand, take a bath," she says.
By the time she can turn her attention to her studies, she says it feels as if she has already done a gazillion chores. "There are days when I sleep because of the sheer exhaustion of it all."
What she hopes for
Whatever the future holds, she is determined to stay in their native village rather than seeking employment in the big city, as her father did. His experience showed her how precarious day labor can be — he had no savings and no medical support after his injury.
Kumari is firm about living in their native village. "Whatever I do, I want to do from here," she says.
She says she still loves cycling as much as ever. She loves the wind in her hair, the feeling of going somewhere, of feeling free. That's what the bike represents to her. But she doesn't have the time to do it as much these days as she's bogged down by household chores and small but persistent everyday worries. She can't just cycle for the joy of it or train as a competitive sport. She only cycles to do errands for the family.
With her own progress on hold, the family has quietly set their hopes on her younger sister who will take her 12th grade exams in mid-2027. If she manages to pass and get into a good college, their prospects will improve once she graduates and starts working.
But Kumari hasn't given up. "When you're poor, fame doesn't help. Only education can help you out of your difficulties. Otherwise, life becomes a never-ending obstacle course," Kumari says.

Hurricane Simon nears Mexico with 155 mph winds and flooding fears
PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico — The eye of Hurricane Simon was just off the Pacific coast of Mexico early Sunday and was expected to move inland later in the day as an extremely powerful storm.
Simon has strengthened to 155 mph (250 kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a Category 5 storm, the highest on the Saffir Simpson scale. It was about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west-southwest of Manzanilla and moving north-northwest at 6 mph (9 kph).
The hurricane could bring 10 to 20 inches (25-50 cm) of rain over parts of southwestern Mexico, with some areas in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco receiving up to 30 inches (76 centimeters).
"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the center warned.
Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors were fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.
Convenience stores, hotels and other businesses in Puerto Vallarta were boarding up their windows Saturday, and few were walking the streets under overcast skies.
"Let's hope it doesn't hit us, right? That it doesn't affect us," Jesús Gómez said as he stood outside a shop and handed out free samples of candied peanuts to passersby. "We'll be working as usual throughout the day, but when Civil Protection officials come and tell us we need to close, then we'll close and take shelter until the storm passes."
The hurricane center expected a dangerous storm surge along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. The agency warned that near the coast, large and destructive waves will accompany the surge.
Canadian tourist Ed Currie, who along with his wife still has five more days to enjoy Puerto Vallarta, said the hurricane had not yet affected his plans.
"Just stay in the hotel and look out the window hopefully," he said of what the couple would do. "I just don't know what to expect."

NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.
The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.
In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.
Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.
For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.
For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.
Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.
The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

The Trump administration announced Thursday that it is investigating nine universities for alleged fraud related to visas commonly used by postdoctoral researchers, a core part of the nation’s biomedical workforce.
Vice President JD Vance announced during a press briefing that Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the California Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the University of Pittsburgh, and UC Davis are under investigation by the Department of Labor. During the briefing, Vance asserted that these schools are improperly using J-1 visas, the main class of visa used by international postdocs, to bring in cheap labor rather than relying on domestic researchers.
“They’re using these visas way too much,” he said. “They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop.”
Vance asserted that these schools employ researchers on J-1 visas for work connected to federal grants at a rate of 61% compared to a national average of 38%. STAT contacted the White House and the Vice President’s office for clarification on where these figures came from but did not receive immediate replies. National Science Foundation data show that nearly 60% of postdocs in science, engineering, and health are temporary visa holders; most of these researchers would be on J-1 visas.
The labor department’s inspector general, Anthony D’Esposito, said during the briefing that his office has already issued subpoenas to the schools under scrutiny. He added that he will investigate whether “foreign influence, improper financial relationships, or visa abuse are compromising federally funded research.”
“If an American university is breaking the law to save a dollar while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal,” he said. “I don’t care how prestigious a university thinks it is. Break the law and screw the American people, and I will personally cuff you in the university square.”
Kimberly Allen, an MIT spokesperson, confirmed in an email to STAT that the university received a “very broad subpoena” on Thursday morning that it is now reviewing. She did not elaborate on the details of the subpoena or what kinds of information had been requested.
“Each J-1 visa holder at MIT has been vetted and authorized to come here by the U.S. government, and we take seriously our obligations to follow U.S. law,” Allen wrote.
Spokespersons for Stanford, Yale, and Harvard did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
It’s unclear how much evidence the administration has to support its visa fraud concerns, and D’Esposito’s office didn’t immediately respond to questions about the investigation’s scope or expected timeline. But Thursday’s announcement fits into a series of moves by the Trump administration to more tightly restrict the entry of international students and scholars into the U.S.
The Department of Homeland Security has attempted to place a four-year cap on how long foreign graduate students and postdocs can stay in the country, alleging that the current system allows these scholars to remain indefinitely and incentivizes fraud. On Wednesday, the Trump administration announced a proposed $70,000 fee for a popular work authorization program used by international students seeking professional experience. And DHS is attempting to revive plans to institute a $100,000 fee for H1-B visas, which are used by foreign workers in high-skill fields such as engineering and biotech.
These proposed restrictions have yet to take effect and have in some cases been temporarily blocked by lawsuits. But Elizabeth Goss, an immigration attorney in Boston, warned that these efforts send a clear sign to international scientists that their contributions are no longer valued, a message she worries could compromise U.S. scientific leadership.
“This is an incredible series of self-owns,” she said. “The government also knows that none of this will stand up in court. They just want to send a message: Don’t come here. But we will lose [out] on so much. It’s going to take decades for us to repair the damage when this is over.”

The federal government has released new quality ratings for Medicare Advantage insurers for 2027, with Humana emerging as the biggest winner.
But deep uncertainty remains around Medicare Advantage quality measures, which come with tens of billions of dollars in extra revenue for the highest-performing plans. One health insurance company, Alignment Healthcare, has already threatened to sue the government after its star ratings were downgraded — a now-common occurrence for almost any insurer that is unhappy with its grades.
Nearly 71% of Medicare Advantage enrollees are currently in a plan that will have at least four out of five stars for quality, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Getting at least four stars triggers bonuses, which total $13 billion across the industry annually. Ratings for 2027 lead to bonus payouts in 2028.

Pretorius breaks Gayle's T20 record score
- Published
CSA T20 Challenge, Bloemfontein
Titans 267-3 (20 overs): Pretorius 188* (79); Boast 1-46
Knights 143 (17.2 overs): Cloete 39 (25); Ferreira 3-16
Titans won by 124 runs
Lhuan-dre Pretorius has broken Chris Gayle's record for the highest score in a men's T20 match with an unbeaten 188 in a domestic fixture in South Africa.
The 20-year-old South African's knock off 79 deliveries, including 13 sixes and 15 fours, helped Titans post 267-3 against Knights in the CSA T20 Challenge.
It eclipsed the 175 made by Gayle for Royal Challengers Bangalore (now Bengaluru) against Pune Warriors in the 2013 Indian Premier League.
Pretorius, who has played 17 T20s, three one-dayers and two Tests for South Africa, finished with a strike rate of 237.97.
He made his half-century off 24 balls but only required 16 more balls to get to three figures and then got to 150 off just 58 deliveries.
Titans then bowled out Knights for 143 to wrap up an emphatic 124-run victory at the Mangaung Oval in Bloemfontein.

The State informed the Kerala High Court that in-principle approval had not been granted to Keralam for establishing an All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS).
The Division Bench of Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice V.M. Syam Kumar enquired into the reason why Keralam was not prioritised for building an AIIMS, even though the matter had been pending for almost 10 years. The Bench was considering a petition seeking establishment of an AIIMS under the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Yojana (PMSSY).
The court observed that the matter was presently at the stage of inter-ministerial consultation and any decision for setting up an AIIMS could be taken only after the continuation of the PMSSY scheme for the next five financial years, FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31, was approved.
In a previous order, the court noted that the idea of having an AIIMS in Keralam was raised in June 2016 and four locations were identified for this purpose. The court opined that Keralam should be considered on a priority basis considering the density of population, and asked the Union government to take a conscious decision concerning the proposal for the institute.
Prioritising other States
The Deputy Solicitor General of India, O.M. Shalina, informed the court that since Keralam had better health-care conditions than other States, the Union government was prioritising those States with a weaker health sector. At this point the court enquired whether the Union government’s stand was that Keralam did not require an AIIMS. The court orally asked whether the hospitals in the State were a disqualification or a ‘handicap’ to consider the establishment of the institute. The court orally remarked that Keralam had the highest density of population in the country, and that the existing hospitals would not be sufficient to provide medical facilities to the needy and poor.
The Union government responded that while considering all other States and Union Territories, Keralam’s status was much better, and that was the reason for the delay in approval. The court then enquired why there was an AIIMS in Delhi and two or three institutes in some other States, if the criteria was availability of medical facilities.
