In late September, two images circulated online purportedly showing ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats walking and resting on their owners.
One of the images shows a sculpture, possibly a wood carving, of a cat in a museum display as either standing or walking on a person at rest. The other image features a cat sitting right up against the chin of a person whose eyes appear to be open.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a graphic (archived) featuring the two images, with text reading, "4,000-year-old statues prove cats have always ignored personal space." The post's caption adds, "Cats Have Been Sitting on Their Humans for 4,000 Years." The pair of images also spread on Threads and X (archived, archived).
(Nathanistic via Facebook)
Reverse image searches uncovered examples of the standing cat image on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, as well as the resting cat image on Instagram, Threads and X.
Cats prominently feature in ancient Egyptian artifacts, including in mummification. That may be one reason why some commenters under posts have posted remarks indicating they believe the images are authentic. Others mention artificial intelligence, saying they are skeptical about whether the images show actual artifacts that truly exist.
In sum, the images are fake and appear to be AI-generated — as do other images of Egyptian sculptures depicting cats interacting with people.
The aforementioned reverse image searches indicate that the earliest posts featuring the image of the cat standing or walking on top of the person first appeared on Soft Cat Memes (@softcatmemes) accounts on Facebook, Instagram and Threads on Sept. 25, as well as on the possibly-affiliated @hardcatmemes X account. The image contains overlaid text, reading, "Cats have been bothering their humans since the dawn of time."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
The image of the cat sitting on a person also first appeared on the same accounts on Sept. 26, receiving more engagement. That second image also features overlaid text, reading, "Evidence suggests cats have never understood personal space."
(@softcatmemes via Facebook)
Snopes contacted the manager of the accounts to confirm the user created the images with an AI tool. We also asked for the name of the tool and the exact text prompts submitted to create the content. We will update this article if we receive further information.
How we know images are fake
Reverse image searches failed to locate any posts or websites containing the same two images prior to late September. With the ongoing popularity of internet cat content, the idea that no one, until recently, would share supposedly real photos of ancient Egyptian sculptures depicting cats acting silly is unlikely.
As one Reddit user has noted, scans of the images with OpenAI's free tool, that verifies content generated using the company's chatbot, display the results, "This content was generated using OpenAI tools," and, "We found a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI." For example, a scan of the image of the cat sitting displays the information shown below.
(via OpenAI)
There is also an inconsistency with one of the shadows in that image. The faint shadow nearest where the photographer is meant to be standing (running from left to right along the long edge of the bed) indicates there is a light source on the other side of the display. However, only a shadow of the bed is cast. If the image were authentic, the angle of the shadow suggests the viewer would also be able to see a faint shadow of the human and cat sculptures. That is not the case in this image.
A scan of the other image of the cat standing or walking displays the same result using OpenAI's tool. The absence of a shadow of the cat's tail also further suggests this image is fake.
For further reading, we previously reported about another feline rumor that wild cheetahs have never killed humans.

Police in New Delhi detained scores of protesters on Saturday as thousands of officers and paramilitaries patrolled India’s capital, metro stations were shut and mobile internet suspended to guard against a youth protest demanding India’s chief election officer quit.
The protest, called by the “Cockroach” youth movement, hopes to draw thousands of demonstrators who want the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to quit over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party.
Television images showed police in the city’s central business district chasing down a few dozen young protesters, before they were loaded into vehicles and taken away.
About 200 protesters were detained in the area, a police source told Reuters. Those detained outside Delhi included protest supporter Dhruv Rathee, a popular figure on YouTube, a police spokesperson said.
Touted by organisers as a protest to “save democracy”, it aims to be the biggest of the demonstrations that were launched last week after the Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar’s deputies had questioned and disagreed with him over the revision process that saw about 130 million voter names removed.
Opposition parties have long alleged the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage.
Kumar has not commented. The election commission and the BJP have denied the allegations.
The BJP says Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth are some of the reasons for its electoral dominance and that opposition parties are misleading the country because they are unable to win elections.
Near daily protests by opposition groups pose a new political challenge to Modi, just months after similar demonstrations forced his education minister to quit over exam paper leaks.
It also comes months before a series of important state elections starting in early 2027, including in the BJP-ruled most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
The protesters, led by the self-named Cockroach Janta party, that began as an online satire, said they would gather at Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning – a site designated for protests by authorities in the heart of New Delhi.
Delhi police said on Friday they had not given permission for the protest because the request did not come on time, adding that CJP had violated undertakings given during previous protests, and that authorities had to enforce the law and maintain peace.
Police said protesters would face the force of the law if they violated the ban.
Tens of thousands of police officers and paramilitary personnel have been deployed across the capital, with multiple layers of yellow metal barricades blocking roads leading to Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders rejected the police decision and said they would go ahead with the protest.
Authorities have ordered the closure of dozens of metro stations, and cancelled several trains coming to New Delhi. However, the supreme court on Friday said some trains must still run and there should be no blanket closure of metro stations.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” the CJP chief, Abhijeet Dipke, said on X.
“Imagine how many lives would be affected because of this shutdown by Modi.”
Mobile internet services in a radius of 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area were ordered suspended from Friday night to Saturday night, ANI news agency reported citing a government order.
The CJP has said “at least 10,000 people”, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
Some people detained in the central state of Madhya Pradesh were taken to hotels, The Hindu newspaper reported.
Police have not responded to the party’s broader allegations of mass detentions.
* With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

As what was left of Hurricane Isaias moved north on Sunday, bringing moderate to heavy rainfall across the central Appalachians and the mid-Atlantic region, nearly 396,000 customers across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama remained without power.
Heavy rainfall associated with the storm could bring isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts and remain a threat across the south-eastern US, especially near the southern Appalachians, according to the National Weather Service (NWS). That could bring scattered power outages and downed trees and power lines. Life-threatening surf and rip current conditions were expected to continue along the Gulf and south-eastern Atlantic coasts.
According to the National Weather Service, parts of the Carolinas and Virginia, including Raleigh, Richmond and Washington DC were under threat of tornadoes on Sunday.
At least four deaths were linked to the storm, including two people killed when trees fell on to homes in Florida and Alabama. Forecasters warned that flooding could stretch into the Appalachians.
Isaias came ashore as a category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. This has been the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024.
Despite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.
Hurricane-force winds in the Florida Panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.
In Florida’s Escambia county, sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home – and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. Four of the man’s family members, ranging in age from four to 72, were treated but were expected to survive, the sheriff said.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season, Isaias roared farther into Alabama with tropical-force winds.
One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, the city’s fire chief, Cory Moon, said. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour county, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency.
Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.
Donald Trump approved an emergency declaration for Georgia after the president did the same for Florida and Alabama, allowing for federal aid.
The US Energy Department authorized emergency exchanges of crude oil from the nation’s strategic petroleum reserve to address disruptions in supply because of the storm.
The NWS said parts of Georgia and the Carolinas could see heavy rain capable of causing flash floods.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Simon strengthened to 155mph (250kph), only just below the threshold for becoming a category 5 storm, as it approached Mexico’s coast. Simon was expected to bring heavy rainfall beginning on Sunday to parts of south-western Mexico with life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Forecasters say that conditions brought by Simon are spreading northward along a stretch of coastline that includes Puerto Vallarta. Rain could average 8-16in over sectors of south-western Mexico, with as much as 30in possible in places across Michoacán, Colima and Jalisco through Monday.
A woman, a man and their dog in Burke county, North Carolina, were rescued on the Catawba River after their camping trip was overflown by the rising water brought by remnants of Simon that caught them off guard.
Tropical storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and southern California. The National Weather Service has issued a flash flood warning in parts of San Diego, Riverside and Imperial counties. Officials issued mandatory evacuation orders for some residents in the Long Beach peninsula through Tuesday.
Eight buildings have been red-tagged, or deemed unsafe to enter, and one has been yellow-tagged amid conditions from Rachel. Long Beach officials have provided about 11,000 sandbags for the storm to protect homes from the rising tide.

In a tent camp in Ceuta, migrants weigh justice, safety and returning home
Migrants in Ceuta face a humanitarian crisis, with some alleging abuse by Spanish soldiers
CEUTA, Spain -- Many of the migrants in a sprawling tent village in Ceuta came searching for better economic opportunities. Others fled war and violence, or sought refuge in Spain because of their gender or sexuality.
With a humanitarian crisis unfolding, some have come forward with allegations of abuse.
Interviews at the now-demolished camp revealed migrants' motivations for seeking protection.
A Moroccan migrant recalled pressing his shirt against his head in the early morning. The blood kept flowing.
A group of Spanish soldiers had tied his head to a tree that September morning, he said, and struck him in the head, on the back and on his arms. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear for his safety.
The soldiers had approached him and another migrant and told them to follow, saying that their superior would register them, according to a police report he filed, which The Associated Press has reviewed.
“They stuffed us into the trunk of a car, locked us in and drove us to the forest,” he said in an interview on Oct. 1. His mouth was covered with gray electrical tape, he said.
“When they were beating me, I saw death, only death," he said. “Imagine your face being tied to a tree while they strike your head, taking hit after hit, right to the front of your face.”
He received staples in his head for his injuries, he said, and showed the AP his healing wounds. He said he wants to hold the soldiers to account.
Spanish prosecutors are investigating reports of torture and mistreatment of migrants in Ceuta, including minors. Amnesty International published a report in September detailing allegations of inhumane treatment by Spanish soldiers.
“I never thought anything like this could happen,” the artisan said. “We truly believed the people here are good and that the government is decent."
“Sometimes I ask myself why I even came here, but other times I tell myself that God will help me.”
A transgender teen swam to Ceuta in July from the Moroccan city of Fnideq. Soon, he thought, he would be in a shelter. Instead, he spent nearly two months at the beachside camp.
He left home because of the challenges of being transgender, he said. He spoke on the condition of anonymity due to fears of reprisals for his gender identity.
“People in Morocco don’t have any mercy," he said in an interview on Sept. 29. “They look at the outside of you, not the inside.”
In Ceuta, he said he briefly lived with extended family, but they kicked him out after learning about his identity. “They didn't accept my situation,” he said.
Spain's asylum law recognizes gender identity and sexual orientation as valid grounds for seeking protection. Cases are assessed individually.
In early October, he returned to Morocco after police cleared the camp.
A soft-spoken 34-year-old man left Tetouan, in northern Morocco, after his brother found pictures of him and his boyfriend on his phone and threatened to report them to the police.
The brothers were already in a bitter dispute over the sale of a family home. In a previous argument, he said his brother had burned him with hot oil.
He spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals from his family, community and the Moroccan government.
Consensual sexual activity with members of the same sex is illegal in Morocco, and can be publishable by fines and up to three years imprisonment. Hundreds of men and women are prosecuted annually under such laws, according to the U.S. State Department.
Homosexuality is regularly cited as an asylum claim for Moroccans attempting to flee.
“I left Morocco because being gay is so hard," he said.
A 28-year-old Moroccan asylum seeker said he received death threats for posting content online that is critical of Islam.
In 2025, he hosted TikTok livestreams focused on the religion. He began receiving death threats, and says he was kidnapped in Marrakech by a follower.
“That was the tipping point,” he said.
The AP was not able to independently verify his claims, but viewed a copy of his asylum paperwork in which he detailed them to Spanish authorities.
He spoke on condition of anonymity due to fear of reprisals. Publicly criticizing Islam in Morocco can lead to criminal prosecution, carrying prison sentences and fines.
He crossed into Ceuta in July, joining tens of thousands more.
“The first week was pure survival” he said. “It felt like running from zombies; some people wanted to attack you, others wanted to rob you.”
He fears for his safety if he is sent back to Morocco.

Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
- Published
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.
The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.
Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.
With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.
"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.
The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".
Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.
"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.
Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".
Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.
"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.
"But I did wrong."
It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).
Kim says Lisa’s in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.
"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.
"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.
"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."
The incident overshadowed what was supposed to be a triumphant launch for Lisa's debut solo album, Alter Ego.
In the film, the singer receives death threats, but presses ahead with public appearances while safety concerns are "spinning in my head".
"To a certain extent I have to take [criticism] and compromise," she says, exhausted, "but sometimes, it's too much".
In a world of sanitised celebrity profiles, Kim's portrayal of upheaval and discomfort is unusual. She asks Lisa about bad reviews, and captures the star being scolded by her vocal coach for lack of effort.
That said, the documentary was commissioned by the film division of the star's record label (which also made the recent, and much less revealing, Oasis documentary), so it is still ultimately a marketing product.
Even the most abrasive moments are calibrated to present Lisa in a good light - but the director credits the star with ensuring the film was not a mere puff piece.
"You never know when you meet an artist how transparent they'll be. And I have to give all credit to Lisa because she allowed us almost total access," Kim says.
"And when I showed her the film, she never asked me to remove a single scene. That's exceptional."
The film's main storyline is about Lisa taking a break from K-pop to pursue crossover success in the Western music market.
When we meet her, she is one of the world's most famous women, with millions of record sales and brand deals with Louis Vuitton and Bvlgari.
But she is trapped by a K-pop system that forbids her from drinking alcohol and having adult relationships.
"I don't want my dating to be the thing to hurt Blackpink's popularity," she says in the film. "But when I turned 25, I realised that this is not how you're supposed to live your life."
As a result, Lisa makes an early decision to cut ties with Korean entertainment company YG, who discovered her as a teenager, and signs a new deal with RCA Records in the US.
"Knowing her as I do, that took an immense amount of courage," says Kim.
"In general, she is a very kind, sweet person - and sometimes personalities like that, they don't want to rock the boat.
"Having been trained in the K-pop system from an early age, she grew acclimatised to obedience. Declaring that she wants a break is such a disruption to that way of life that I can only imagine it must have been building inside her for years."
The potential rewards for going solo were phenomenal – but so were the risks.
In the film, we see Lisa struggling to assert herself in the recording studio, and tearfully battling nerves over her singing voice.
At the age of 25, she is still curiously child-like. The fierce independence of her solo single New Woman sounds more like aspiration than fact.
Kim says that began to change as they filmed.
"I saw a person who was very tentative and unsure of herself slowly starting to unfold her wings. Making mistakes, but also getting back up on the horse."
Kim locates an inner confidence in early home videos of Lisa competing in talent shows, drawing parallels between that precocious seven-year-old and the young woman who is gradually reclaiming her agency.
She doggedly pursues a role in the third season of hit TV drama The White Lotus, self-taping an audition that wins her the role of kind-hearted wellness coach Mook Sornsin.
On set, she shrugs off the restrictive moral code of her pop career.
"Lisa threw more parties than anyone else," notes the show's executive producer in an interview.
"And the defining characteristic of a Lisa party is tequila shots."
Kim did not partake in the hedonism. In fact, the film-maker and her crew were regularly falling sick as they tried to keep up with Lisa's ridiculous schedule.
"But when we premiered the film in Toronto, Lisa found me and she brought bottles of tequila, and that was like the perfect christening of the film," she laughs.
The movie ends in June 2025 as Lisa returns to Seoul and rejoins Blackpink. As she unpacks her bags, she is clearly conflicted.
"It's bittersweet, and I think that's OK," says Kim.
"I don't think people should take it as like, 'Oh, she hates Blackpink'. It's more that she was reflecting on this year of freedom and worrying that she wouldn't be able to retain that. And that's a very astute fear to have."
In the year since, Lisa has already wrapped up her Blackpink duties and started phase two of her solo career with the single Sawadika. Kim says she is not surprised.
"Spending the year away from the K-pop system in the US really opened her horizons," the director says.
"She was exposed to a different kind of entertainment system where they're not held to a vow of chastity. If two star performers link up, it's almost like they get more power.
"That gave her a sense of like, 'Oh, I could have a different life. I might not lose my career if I want to get married and have children'.
"So I think part of the reason why Lisa's interested in continuing her solo career is that it might give her a little bit more personal freedom to be who she is."

Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent
- Published
Donald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.
The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.
The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.
The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.
That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia".
"Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.
The BBC has asked the White House for further details.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.
Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
"All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.
For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.
Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".
The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.
Earlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.
The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.
Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports.
"Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".
Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.
On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.
The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.
The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.
Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.
Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.
Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.
One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.

CJP renews protest call as Abhijeet Dipke, Dhruv Rathee remain detained; Delhi Police cite ‘broken promises’ amid crackdown
Delhi Police reportedly released all the detainees from the detention centers except CJP leaders. This comes amid a widespread crackdown in national capital.
Delhi on Saturday witnessed a major crackdown on a planned protest and the detention of thousands, including four former chief ministers, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijit Dipke, and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee. The action came amid CJP's call for protest against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, who faces allegations of carrying out irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
While the police released all the protesters after day-long detention, CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das, and Youtuber Dhruv Rathee remained in custody. The Cockroach Janta Party has given a fresh call for protest, urging people to begin march to Jantar Mantar at 10 am on Sunday.
Why Delhi Police stalled protests
The Delhi Police shared a video on X, explaining the reason for denying permission to hold the protest at Jantar Mantar. In the caption, the police wrote, "Broken promises, shattered trust."
Deep Dive
In the video, Delhi Police highlighted that the CJP failed to abide by its signed undertaking while protesting in June-July to demand the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over alleged examination irregularities.

Key developments from protests against CEC
From the closure of 45 metro stations in the national capital to the detention of actor Imran Khan in Mumbai, Saturday saw escalating developments as protests erupted in various parts of the country.
4 ex-CMs detained: Several opposition leaders, including former chief ministers Arvind Kejriwal (AAP), Mamata Banerjee (TMC), Pinarayi Vijayan (CPI-M) and Manik Sarkar (CPI-M), were detained from multiple locations across Delhi as they attempted to join the protest.
Abhijeet Dipke and others detained: Dipke and two CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained by Delhi Police from inside an aircraft as soon as their flight landed.
Dhruv Rathee detained from Gurugram: YouTuber Rathee, who lives abroad and had come to join the CJP protest, was detained by police from his residence in Gurugram.
CJP's Ajinkya Shinde calls fresh protest: Following the detentions, CJP's Ajinkya Shinde has renewed the call for demonstrations on Sunday, October 11.
"But we're not backing down! We will march to Jantar Mantar again tomorrow and stay there until all our demands are met," the CJP's post on X read.
Tushar Gandhi, actor Imran Khan detained: Police detained actor Imran Khan, activist Tushar Gandhi and CPI (M) workers from various locations in Mumbai for protesting without permission, news agency PTI reported.
Sonam Wangchuk's warning: Activist Sonam Wangchuk, in a post shared on his X handle, wrote, "Yesterday when I posted a message appealing for unity & peace in today's protest I had never imagined that the biggest democracy in the world would be under an undeclared EMERGENCY."
"I was happy there were so many leaders to lead the movement, but I now learn that they have all been arrested. I hope those arrested will be released soon. I will be compelled to consider an Anshan Fast or Padyatra March if they are not released by tomorrow," he warned.
BJP vs Opposition amid crackdown
Earlier on Saturday, BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra slammed Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and termed him a "nalayak neta" and an "anarchist".
Addressing a press conference, Patra criticised the remarks made by Gandhi outside Rashtrapati Bhavan on Friday.
"Yesterday a few politicians visited the Rashtrapati Bhavan. The statement of Rahul Gandhi after coming out of the Rashtrapati Bhavan was like that of a 'nalayak neta'... Never before was an attempt made to drag the President into a street protest. But a 'nalayak neta' attempted to do that. The anarchist Rahul Gandhi tried to pull the President of India to anarchism, which he is trying his best to conduct on the streets of India," the BJP leader said.
Meanwhile, Congress leader Gandhi, in a post on X, urged the youth to keep protesting.
"Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you," he wrote.
Delhi metro services update
Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), in an X post on Saturday night, informed, “Entry and exit gates of all Metro Stations of the Delhi Metro network are now open. The interchange facility at all the concerned Metro stations is also available.”

Monique Ryan ‘not bothered’ by Frydenberg comeback speculation
The release of Josh Frydenberg’s book this week has reheated speculation the former Liberal treasurer could have another go at his former seat of Kooyong in Melbourne.
But Monique Ryan, the independent who won the seat from Frydenberg in 2022, says she’s “not bothered” by all the chatter.
She told Nine earlier this morning Frydenberg seemed more interested in being prime minister than worrying about his electorate:
Josh does have a track record with the Kooyong community. Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
Something is breaking in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica, increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey.
The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem. The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species.
Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.”
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is among the most widespread of human viruses. More than 90% of adults are estimated to have been infected during their lifetime. Most people acquire the infection during childhood without developing symptoms. In some, particularly those infected during adolescence or adulthood, it can cause infectious mononucleosis. The virus then remains in the body for life.
A new analysis by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer agency of the World Health Organization (WHO), estimates that about 2.3 million new cancer cases worldwide in 2024 were attributable to infections. The analysis incorporates recent evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer and places EBV among the infectious agents responsible for a substantial cancer burden worldwide.
What is Epstein-Barr virus?
EBV, also known as human herpesvirus 4, belongs to the herpesvirus family. It spreads mainly through saliva, including through kissing or sharing drinks, food, eating utensils and toothbrushes.
According to WHO, many people infected with EBV have no symptoms. When illness occurs, symptoms can include fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and marked fatigue. Infectious mononucleosis generally improves within a few weeks, although fatigue can last longer.
After the initial infection, EBV remains in the body in a dormant state. In most healthy people, the immune system keeps the infection under control.
EBV is classified by IARC as a Group 1 carcinogen. It has established causal links with several cancers, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt lymphoma and Hodgkin lymphoma. The latest IARC analysis also incorporates evidence linking EBV with gastric cancer.
Who is at risk?
Most people infected with EBV do not develop cancer. The infection is therefore not, by itself, an indication that a person will develop cancer.
People with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of serious EBV-related disease. This includes some people who have undergone organ or stem-cell transplantation and those receiving treatments that suppress the immune system.
The cancers associated with EBV also vary geographically. Nasopharyngeal cancer, for instance, is particularly prevalent in parts of eastern and southeastern Asia. The development of EBV-associated cancer is thought to involve factors beyond the infection itself.
How is it diagnosed?
A person does not normally need to be tested simply because EBV is common.
When infectious mononucleosis is suspected, doctors may make a diagnosis based on the symptoms and clinical examination. Blood tests can provide supporting evidence. These include tests for heterophile antibodies and EBV-specific antibodies, which can help determine whether an infection is recent or occurred in the past.
In suspected EBV-related cancers or serious disease in people with compromised immunity, more specialised tests may be needed. These can include testing for EBV genetic material in blood or other samples and examination of tumour tissue for the presence of the virus.
A positive EBV antibody test does not mean that a person has cancer. Since infection is so common, evidence of past infection is expected in most adults.
What are the treatment options?
There is no treatment that removes latent EBV from the body and there is currently no vaccine against the virus.
According to WHO, treatment for uncomplicated infectious mononucleosis is mainly supportive. Rest, adequate fluids and medicines to control fever and pain may be advised. Antibiotics do not treat EBV because it is a virus.
People with mononucleosis may also be advised to avoid strenuous activity and contact sports for a period, particularly if the spleen is enlarged, because of the risk of splenic injury.
When EBV is associated with cancer, treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted treatment or a combination of these.
Can EBV be prevented?
There is currently no vaccine against EBV. Preventing transmission can also be difficult because infected people may spread the virus without knowing that they have it.
WHO advises avoiding the sharing of drinks, utensils, toothbrushes and other items that come into contact with saliva.
The development of an EBV vaccine is an important area of research. The latest IARC analysis adds to the evidence on the virus’s contribution to cancer and highlights the need for continued research into prevention.

For years, enterprises hired thousands of human executives to sell loans, answer customer queries and recover abandoned sales. Yet, even with massive teams, many high-value client interactions would slip through the cracks every single day. While some prospects were lost due to poor agent training, others were lost to long support queues. As a result, businesses consistently struggled to reach every lead on their lists. The common assumption was that companies simply needed better training for human agents or simply more calling executives. However, Arrowhead’s founders saw things differently. According to them, the core issue was that human-driven phone processes struggle to function effectively at enterprise scale. The realisation could not have come at a more opportune time. With rapid improvements in AI voice technology, they saw the future clearly – improving human-led call centres would soon matter far less than automating them entirely. This single realisation changed the direction of the startup. Founded in 2022 by Devyani Gupta and Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Arrowhead is building voice AI agents primarily for enterprises. It claims to power autonomous voice systems for many leading banks, NBFCs, ecommerce platforms and healthcare providers. The startup claims that its conversational agents automate everything, from loan sales and customer queries to abandoned cart recovery and collections. In January 2026, the startup raised $3 Mn in its seed funding round led by Stellaris Venture Partners. It claims to work with over 50 BFSI clients, including Tata 1mg, Bank of Baroda Cards, IndiaMART, Aditya Birla Capital, Paytm, Turtlemint, Kissht, InsuranceDekho and others. Yet, Arrowhead did not start with the technology it uses today. The startup’s pivot to enterprise voice AI was the result of a calculated gamble, which forced its team to rethink everything they had built. When Analysing Human Calls Was No Longer Enough Arrowhead didn't start in voice automation. The startup’s initial product was a conversation intelligence tool. Drawing on her experience at BCG across continents, cofounder and CEO Gupta initially built Arrowhead to identify mis-selling and compliance violations on recorded sales calls. Early clients, such as edtech platform upGrad, used the tool to pinpoint bad sales pitches that resulted in refunds. Then came the GenAI boom of 2023 and 2024, and the founders reached an uncomfortable conclusion. “We quickly realised that if we continued analysing just human sales calls, we would soon be analysing something that would potentially go extinct,” Gupta told Inc42. Recognising that human-driven call centres were on borrowed time, Arrowhead pivoted sharply to AI in late 2024. Rather than competing on building another chatbot, the startup focused almost entirely on voice-first enterprise workflows. Arrowhead initially targeted banks and financial institutions, where large calling operations remain critical for loan sales, collections and customer engagement. But, in a stroke of fate, many enterprises that originally bought Arrowhead's analytics software returned as buyers for its autonomous voice agents – this time, to replace their manual calling queues altogether. To scale its voice stack, Arrowhead quickly realised that off-the-shelf software simply would not cut it. The founders needed to control every layer of its underlying engine. Building A Voice AI Stack From Ground Up Instead of relying entirely on third-party API providers, Arrowhead has gradually built much of its voice AI infrastructure in-house. The startup recently launched internally fine-tuned small language models (SLMs), engineered specifically for live enterprise conversations. Rather than optimising purely for lower inference costs, the founders claim that the platform prioritises latency and conversational quality. According to the startup, its latest deployments have achieved response latency below 500 milliseconds, allowing conversations to feel significantly more natural during live phone calls. For context, even small delays in voice interactions can disrupt the flow of conversation, making latency a much bigger challenge than traditional text-based AI systems. To complement its language models, Arrowhead has also developed its own text-to-speech (TTS) models, powered by thousands of hours of custom speech recordings. The startup hired voice artists across specialised agencies to record speech across multiple Indian languages and emotional contexts. This primary data, instead of generic public datasets, enables Arrowhead’s AI models to master subtle human nuances, such as empathy, hesitation, filler words and natural speech rhythms, which generic TTS systems typically miss. Overall, its underlying AI stack also includes: Fine-tuned SLMs built on open-source foundation models such as Gemma and Qwen Proprietary TTS models trained using custom primary speech datasets Emotion-aware speech synthesis systems capable of responding with empathy and contextual tone Optimised inference infrastructure for sub-500 millisecond voice responses Support for multiple Indian languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam Enterprise deployments designed around data residency, privacy and single-tenant architecture for regulated industries Voice orchestration systems capable of integrating with multiple enterprise APIs during live conversations Speaking with Inc42, cofounder and CTO Srinivasan said that hosting proprietary language models provides cost savings, predictable latency and superior conversational quality while ensuring sensitive customer data stays safely within India for regulated industries such as banking. On the back of its in-house AI stack, the founders claim that over 90% of users cannot distinguish Arrowhead's voice agents from human representatives unless explicitly told that they are speaking with an AI agent. This conversational fluidity has enabled the startup to move beyond pilots to deploying its agents directly into critical, revenue-generating operations. Arrowhead’s BFSI Strength On the business front, financial services remain Arrowhead's biggest market. Around 80% of the company's revenue comes from banks, NBFCs and fintech companies, although it has also started expanding into sectors such as healthcare, ecommerce and edtech. Overall, Arrowhead’s voice AI platform is currently being deployed across three major enterprise workflows. The first is outbound loan sales, where its AI agents move far beyond basic lead qualification to complete much of the loan application journey. During a live call, the agent addresses customer objections, collects required documents, runs OCR-based verification and hands over fully completed files straight to underwriting. The second core area for Arrowhead is inbound customer support. Here, its AI agents first determine customer intent before tapping into the enterprise database to answer complex policy questions, fetch real-time loan statuses and retrieve account-specific records. This drastically cuts manual workload for enterprises that handle tens of thousands of support hours each month. The third area is abandoned cart recovery. For ecommerce platforms, Arrowhead’s AI agents contact customers shortly after they leave without completing a purchase. During the conversation, the system can modify cart items, apply discount codes, update shipping details, and process transactions without ever transferring to a human representative. The startup recently disclosed that its deployment with Tata 1mg generated conversion rates around 15% higher than human agents during abandoned cart recovery campaigns. But with healthy market traction and product-market-fit (PMF) in its kitty, how is Arrowhead monetising its customer base? How Arrowhead Makes Money Arrowhead employs a hybrid pricing strategy that blends traditional SaaS usage with performance-based monetisation. A portion of revenue is generated through per-minute billing, while another component depends on business outcomes delivered through AI deployments. The founders believe that outcome-based pricing creates stronger alignment with enterprise customers while reducing the long-term impact of declining AI infrastructure costs. While the founders did not disclose Arrowhead’s revenue figures, they said that usage-based contracts drive the majority of revenue and yield gross margins between 25% and 30%. They added that profitability varies depending on customer scale and committed call volumes. That said, the startup, despite operating with a lean team, has scaled rapidly to partner with most of the country's top banks, NBFCs, and fintechs. For the founders, replacing traditional call centres is just the opening move. Their bigger bet is that enterprise voice AI platforms will become completely autonomous, capable of completing entire business workflows on their own. But the road ahead may not be easy. The voice AI space in India is peppered with deep-pocketed homegrown startups such as Observe AI, Bolna, and Gnani.ai, among others. On top of this, unit economics also remains a real challenge, as LLM reasoning and TTS together can be an expensive purchase for early stage startups. Infrastructure and UX challenges also persist, particularly around mobile voice navigation and integration with existing enterprise systems. So, as India’s AI ecosystem matures and voice AI infrastructure turns into a commodity, Arrowhead is tasked with maintaining its tech edge to thrive in the long haul.

A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said.
The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said.
The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children.
The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes.
It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help.
The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.
Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.
Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm".

South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.
The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.
The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.
On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

“Even after I became the Prime Minister, I got the opportunity to work alongside with Jayalalithaa, former chief ministers O Panneerselvam, Edappadi K Palaniswami and DMK President M K Stalin,” he said.

Panama declares state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos
The government of Panama declared a state of emergency Saturday as the aftershocks of two powerful earthquakes that roiled the country shook communities for hours. Officials did not attribute any deaths to the quakes but reported damages in all 10 of Panama's provinces and two Indigenous territories.
The 7.7- and 6.6-magnitude earthquakes on Friday toppled buildings near the epicentre and prompted evacuations across the Central American country. Seismologists recorded more than 100 aftershocks, including ones measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2.
The earlier quake, also felt in neighbouring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometres southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometres.
Presidential Minister Juan Carlos Orillac announced the emergency during a news conference in the capital, Panama City. He said homes, schools, healthcare facilities, roads and hotels were among the damaged facilities.
Malitzie Rivera, deputy director of the National Civil Protection System, told reporters the state had reports of 27 people with injuries, ranging from minor to moderate.
Hundreds of homes were damaged
Most of the damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera, Cocle and Los Santos.
The Civil Protection agency tallied roughly 420 homes and about the same number of public schools damaged. It also reported that seven hotels, at least 13 churches and nine bridges were affected by the earthquakes.
In La Villa de Los Santos, a colonial-era community about 64 kilometres northeast of the epicenter, homes and a historical Catholic church collapsed. People who spent the night on the streets were waiting for the government's guidance on what to do next.
"We've been here since 1 p.m. yesterday; we haven't moved," Tony Jimenez, whose home partially collapsed, said while sitting with relatives under a tent. "It was a terrible thing. I can tell you with absolute certainty that in my 90 years, I had never experienced anything like it. It was intense -- truly intense."
The collapsed Church of San Atanasio was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Images of crumbling buildings and deep fissures slicing through roads added to fears across a Latin American region battered by a series of devastating earthquakes in recent months.
Two back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes roiled Venezuela's La Guaira state in June, killing more than 6,500 people and leaving 17,000 homeless. In August, a 7.4 magnitude earthquake in Colombia killed at least 289 people.
The notably lower toll in nearby Panama may have been due to the country's strict building codes, especially governing construction of skyscrapers in the capital, said Carlos Valdes, head of the Seismology Department at the National Autonomous University of Mexico.
Rising sea levels prompt evacuations
Officials did not report any missing people on Saturday but said some communities remained cut off due to landslides and road damage.
On Isla Cana, off the Pacific coast of Los Santos, approximately 300 people were evacuated because of rising sea levels and rough surf. Meanwhile, in the city of Penonome, around 150 kilometres from the capital, a shelter was housing 13 people, including five children. The earthquakes caused a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district's main square, as well as damage to the governor's office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
In Panama City, one of the water treatment plants supplying the area operated at 20 per cent capacity on Saturday, and tent facilities with cots were set up at six hospitals.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region's busiest airports with more than 20 million passengers in 2025, temporarily suspended operations after the first quake but said Friday but reopened hours later.
But hundreds of travelers on major Panama-based airlines like Copa Airlines were left stranded in airports around the region. Their connections through Tocumen — one of the biggest travel hubs in the region — were canceled or delayed. In Mexico City's airport, airline employees scrambled as families with babies were sleeping on the floor Saturday while one woman from Venezuela shouted in panic that the flight through Panama was one of the only ways she could return home to Caracas.
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.
The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica, killed 23 people, injured 559 and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas del Toro region.
A vehicle lies crushed beneath a collapsed building after an earthquake struck Penonome, Panama, Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. (Aris Mariota/The Associated Press)
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama's border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including the Cocos, Nazca and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the "Ring of Fire," a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world's earthquakes occur.
Countries offer help
Messages of support and offers of assistance flooded in from across the region shortly after the earthquakes. Mulino on Friday thanked fellow Latin American leaders for their support, saying he had spoken with the presidents of Chile, Uruguay and Guatemala, among others.
The U.S. Department of State on Saturday said it mobilized a disaster response team to help local authorities with search and rescue expertise as well as aerial and on-the-ground assessments.
The U.S. government also pledged $5 million for humanitarian assistance.
U.S. Southern Command also said two helicopters supported by the State Department's drug-control bureau had delivered 2,000 pounds of food to Panamanian communities affected by the earthquakes.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Is Amazon making a smartphone? A Reuters report from earlier this year revealed details about a device codenamed Transformer under development, with Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant as the focus of the experience.
With Amazon announcing a complete rebrand of its tablet line on Thursday—killing the cheap Fire Tablets and replacing them with premium Alexa Tablets that finally run Android with access to the Google Play Store—we now have a blueprint for what an Android-powered Amazon phone could look like.
Amazon's souped-up Alexa+ assistant is front and center on the tablets. There's a persistent “Ask Alexa” widget on the home screen that lets you call on the assistant to ask it questions—you can say “Alexa” to trigger it, too. But Alexa+ now finally has what Amazon calls On-Screen Intelligence. Like Google's Gemini on Android phones or Apple's Siri on iPhones, which can read your screen and answer contextual questions, Alexa now has the same functionality (if you opt in).
That can be for simple things like summarizing a web page, but it can be used for more complex tasks. Watching a YouTube video about a new product? Ask Alexa whether the product is on Amazon, and if so, add it to your Amazon shopping cart. Perusing an Infatuation article about new restaurants in your area? Ask Alexa to highlight the ones closest to your office.
Alexa also supports “live sessions,” just like Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode—it lets you have a free-form back-and-forth conversation with the assistant. Maybe you're focused on a DIY project and want Alexa to spell out instructions slowly at your own pace. It also supports visual intelligence: Point the tablet's camera at anything, and Alexa can identify the object and offer helpful advice. Got a water leak? Point the camera and ask Alexa how to fix it.
These are completely new experiences for Alexa. Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, tells WIRED the company “didn't really have the right product to be able to use” these capabilities, but that's now solved with its Android tablets.
But these features would fit right in on a smartphone, where they’d perhaps be even more useful. When I mentioned this to Keith, he laughed and said: “We have nothing to share on that. Interesting idea.”
Amazon notoriously tried to make a smartphone in 2014—the Fire Phone—a massive flop discontinued shortly after launch due to a limited app ecosystem, dismal sales, and an over-reliance on gimmicky features. (Even its designer recently said he was embarrassed by it.) That may partly be why Amazon is retiring the “Fire” branding and killing its budget tablets. People may forget the disaster and won't be reminded of the “Fire Phone” name when the company eventually introduces a new handset.
Switching its tablets over to Google's Android (rather than the forked version the Fire tablets ran) and adding the Google Play Store is a silent admission that it's hard to thrive without a healthy app ecosystem. It also sets the phone up for success, as it won't feel app-limited out of the gate like the original Fire Phone.
Alexa+ is right now a paid service that requires an Alexa+ subscription or Amazon Prime. However, Amazon says anyone with its new Alexa tablet gets Alexa+ for free, and this would likely also be the case with an Amazon phone. Amazon’s devices, after all, are vehicles used to drive users to buy stuff on Amazon.com. A 2022 Pew Research Center survey showed that 76 percent of Americans purchase products using a smartphone. It makes sense that Amazon would want more direct control over the hardware people use to make those purchases, especially if it paints Alexa as a helpful assistant that can shop for you.
Recently, Amazon has been on a mission to make its hardware more premium. This crusade seems to have ramped up after Microsoft Surface creator Panos Panay joined the company as head of Devices & Services in 2023. These upscaling efforts include the slew of Echo speakers it introduced in 2025, which saw marked price increases over their predecessors thanks to upgraded hardware. The Kindles announced at the start of October now come in sleek aluminum variants and are thinner and lighter than ever. The latest Alexa Tablets are more powerful, made from aluminum, and feel very iPad-esque.
Panay spent his final few years at Microsoft on the failed Microsoft Duo folding smartphone. When it launched, he was adamant it wasn't a phone but rather a productivity-focused device that belonged in a new category.
The Reuters report suggests Amazon's phone may feature an “AI interface,” what the industry often refers to as a generative user interface, that eliminates the need for traditional app stores. It could be that when Panay eventually steps on a stage to reveal an Amazon “Alexa” Phone, he'll once again claim it's not a phone, but a helpful AI assistant in your pocket that conforms to your demands—marking a clear departure from every other Android slab on the market.
The smartphone market is in a bit of a predicament right now. Devices are getting more expensive because of the memory crisis, shipments have declined for several quarters in a row, and the duopoly in the US market between Samsung and Apple makes it hard for other players to break through. Established smartphone companies have given up and left the market, like OnePlus this summer or HMD last year.
There isn't much choice left in for American buyers. However, an Amazon phone, made by a company that isn't based in China and backed by Amazon's retail dominance, could quickly swallow the slice of the pie Motorola and Google are fighting over.

Argenx disclosed that its blockbuster drug Vyvgart failed to outperform placebo in a Phase 3 trial of patients with Sjögren’s disease, a chronic autoimmune disorder, marking an unusual setback for the company, STAT says. Argenx has racked up a series of wins in autoimmune disorders en route to becoming one of the world’s largest biotechs based on market cap. William Blair analysts had projected $1.4 billion in peak sales from Vyvgart in Sjögren’s disease but described the trial as high risk, in part because Sjögren’s patients often have high placebo responses. That hold remains in place at U.S. study centers but enrollment continues in other countries, and additional clinical sites are being added. The FDA concern relates to the risk that some sodium channel blockers may trigger arrhythmias that can lead to serious cardiovascular events or seizures.

Mahmoud Abbas postpones Palestinian legislative elections another year
Palestinians won't head to the polls next month to vote on reviving a dissolved parliament
RAMALLAH, West Bank -- President Mahmoud Abbas postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.
Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority’s credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.
The internationally backed body is dominated by Abbas' party, Fatah, and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas’ presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.
The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization’s Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.
The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.
Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas’ Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.
The West Bank has grown increasingly violent in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority’s control are both regularly reported.
Though the U.S.-brokered ceasefire plan reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.
Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.
“Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.
