The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that there are approximately 19 million visually impaired children in the world, and 1.4 million are blind. In India, about 3 lakh children are said to be blind. Yet, nearly half of these cases are entirely preventable or treatable if caught in time.
This month, global campaigns will urge the world to protect child eye health. There will be calls for governments around the world to unlock funding and prioritise eye care so everyone, everywhere can access the care they need along with community screening camps, eye care in schools and global pledges. And while these are vital calls, as a clinician standing on the frontlines of an outpatient department (OPD), I am forced to confront a quiet, uncomfortable truth: threats to a child’s vision are not always due to a lack of access to healthcare; they are sometimes also due to a missed opportunity to identify visual problems within healthcare systems that the child has already accessed.
What happens in the system
Consider a recent encounter in my clinic. A couple walked in with their five-year-old daughter; I will call her Anu. I could immediately see that she was visually impaired. She was one of a twin. Her parents felt that her sibling was developing normally, while she seemed to have delays in reaching developmental milestones. Gradually they started to notice that Anu could not see clearly. On examination, I found that Anu had dense bilateral cataracts with nystagmus (involuntary movement of the eyes). The presence of nystagmus says that the visual impairment had been present since infancy. When I asked why they had waited five years to seek help, they explained that they were simply overwhelmed by the weight of raising twins and assumed it was best to wait until she was older so she could ‘cooperate’ during a standard eye examination. Now they had arrived, but a bit too late.
Childhood eye diseases that cause profound visual impairment need to be detected and treated early. A baby is born with an immature visual system, and the development of vision happens through the interaction between the eye and the developing brain. When clear images do not reach the brain during this critical period, amblyopia, or lazy eye, can develop. Once this period of visual development has passed, treatment cannot fully restore the lost visual potential. Anu had lost the chance of getting back her vision fully, even if she was operated upon now.
What doesn’t get seen
Anu had not been completely outside the health system; her vaccinations were perfectly up-to-date, and she had documented encounters with health personnel seven distinct times from birth to age five. Yet, across all these visits her profound visual impairment went entirely unnoticed. Why did this happen?
One of the reasons is the poor integration of vision screening with the vaccination schedule and general paediatric screening.
India has an extensive network of frontline health workers and child health programmes. The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), for example, is designed to identify and manage health conditions in children from birth to 18 years. Screening programmes, notably have demonstrated that large numbers of school-aged children with vision problems can be screened. The tools placed in the hands of mobile health teams to detect developmental delays are proven to be highly capable of detecting developmental delays at the community level. What then is going wrong?
Let’s take the example of Karnataka. There is no published standalone government data of the number of children screened, ocular morbidity detected and treated, for the 0–6 age category. However, according to the Karnataka Health & Family Welfare Department’s Annual Report 2023–24, the State screened 62,45,424 children (6 to 16 yrs) in government and government-aided schools. But only 1.2 lakh children received spectacles, representing a distribution rate of just 1.9%. This is in sharp contrast to localised epidemiological studies in Karnataka’s southern districts, which place the actual prevalence of paediatric refractive errors as high as 8%. This pronounced gap could be due to operational challenges such as drop-outs in the multi-tier referral system and supply chain delays. A study assessing the coverage gaps in child health screening under RBSK found that only 47.4% of children detected to have health problems received further care, indicating a significant treatment gap.
Even if the system successfully flags a child, the path from detection to actual restoration of sight remains riddled with problems. Independent field evaluations in Tumkur highlight that the system has some problems when dealing with younger children and follow-up care. The management process faces significant on-the-ground challenges, including parental non-cooperation for follow-up, logistical barriers, and potential training gaps among screening teams. In my own experience, when talking to the ASHAs in Tumkur district, they said they did not have the training required to detect eye diseases in children. If the parents or caregiver of the children specifically complained about any vision related issues, the ASHAs referred them to the paediatrician who visited the taluk hospital once a week. This exposes a significant gap in training frontline workers.
Bridging gaps
There is no need for an entirely new system. We need to make better use of the system that already exists.
The red reflex test: A simple red reflex examination using the direct ophthalmoscope is one example. The test takes less than 30 seconds, does not require a child to cooperate verbally, and can identify major, sight and life-threatening abnormalities such as cataract, retinoblastoma (eye cancer) and high refractive errors. RBSK mobile health teams, primary health centre nurses, and paediatric residents must be trained to perform this test. This simple check must become as routine as measuring a child’s weight and must get incorporated in the immunisation schedule, so it is never missed.
Improving frontline training for pre-verbal visual milestones: We also need to train ASHAs in simple ways of assessing visual behaviour in infants and young children who cannot read a chart or respond reliably to conventional visual-acuity testing. Can the infant fix and follow light and objects? Is there visual engagement? Is there an abnormal or asymmetric corneal light reflex suggesting a squint? These are not sophisticated examinations. They are observations that, with appropriate training and referral protocols, can help identify children who need an eye examination.
Strengthening referral pathways from the periphery to tertiary care centre: Detection, however, is only the first step. A child identified with a possible eye problem must reach the appropriate facility where treatment is available. Referral pathways need to be clear, practical and monitored. Where possible, digital systems could link frontline screening with appointments at district or tertiary eye-care facilities. Tele-ophthalmology could also help connect peripheral health workers with specialists and reduce some of the logistical barriers that cause families to drop out of care.
Anu’s story is not simply about a child who reached an eye hospital too late. It is about a child who was already within the health system, but whose eyes were never looked at. Young children cannot be expected to understand there is a problem; parents may not recognise signs or may believe problems will resolve with age. A child should not have to reach the age of five, with dense cataracts and established nystagmus, before a visual problem that could have been detected in infancy comes to attention.
India already has an extensive network of frontline health workers, immunisation services, RBSK teams, school health programmes and primary and tertiary healthcare facilities. The challenge now is to connect these pieces. The goal should, therefore, not be merely to increase the number of children screened. It should be to build a system in which every contact with a child is an opportunity to protect vision, every abnormal finding triggers a clear referral, and every referral is followed through to care.
As we mark World Sight Day, the question we should ask is not only how do we reach more children. It is also how many children are already within our health system whom we are failing to see. For children like Anu, finding the problem a few years earlier can mean the difference between having sight and living a life with visual disability, because preventing blindness in a child is not merely about saving sight. It is about protecting education, independence and the opportunity to reach their full potential.
(Dr. Vasudha Kemmanu is a paediatric ophthalmologist and a public eye health specialist at Narayana Nethralaya, Rajaji Nagar, Bengaluru. vasudhakemmanu@gmail.com)

In October 2026, a screenshot of an alleged post from U.S. President Donald Trump's Truth Social account spread online, showing Trump seemingly thanking billionaire Elon Musk for artificially increasing Republican votes ahead of the November 2026 midterms.
The purported post (archived) stated:
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool—Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dummods with massive turnout! THANKS TO THE GREAT ELON MUSK EVERY REPUBLICAN VOTE COUNTS AS 3 VOTES! SO IMPORTANT - PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE, AND MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President Donald J. Trump
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The above post is a doctored version of a real Truth Social post from Trump's account. The yellow highlighted line about Musk was edited into the post. As such, we rate this image as fake.
On Oct. 3, 2026, Trump wrote (archived) the following post on Truth Social. The fake highlighted line about Musk was added after "we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout!":
Republicans must WIN the 2026 Midterm Elections, and we must use every appropriate tool — Whether you vote early, absentee, by mail, or in-person, we must "swamp" the Radical Left Dumocrats with massive turnout! SO IMPORTANT — PLEASE GET OUT AND VOTE. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! President DONALD J. TRUMP
swampthevoteusa.com/
(@realDonaldTrump on Truth Social)
The post in the screenshot is clearly edited, based on the nonsense phrase "Dummods" which appears to be a garbled version of "Dumocrats."
Snopes also looked up variations of the phrase on Trump's Truth, a website that archives his posts "every few minutes" and makes it easier to find them — including deleted posts. There was no evidence of Trump thanking Musk on Truth Social for making "every Republican vote" count as three votes.
Trump has been speaking at campaign rallies nationwide, trying to drum up support for Republican candidates ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections.
For further reading, Snopes has debunked numerous posts falsely attributed to Trump over the years.

I've got my own questions on Man City case - Carrick
- Published
Manchester United boss Michael Carrick still has his "own questions" over the Manchester City case which he says "affected me personally".
There is a clamour among some for Manchester City to be stripped of their silverware and also be relegated after they were found guilty of multiple Premier League financial rule breaches.
The 45-year-old was on the pitch at Sunderland when he learned City had won their first Premier League title in 2012 thanks to Sergio Aguero's legendary injury time match winner.
He was still part of Jose Mourinho's squad when United finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City side in 2018 and was part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching staff when it happened again in 2020-21.
However, Carrick says getting a title winners' medal years after the event would not make up for missing out at the time.
"In football, the strive to win, the emotion and the feeling about winning, a lot of it is in the moment," he said.
"You can't take that back. It's the moment you strive for. That's essentially what we're all in it for. That's the feeling we all crave.
"The beauty of trying to win trophies is a little bit the journey towards it and then the finale. Does it go for you, does it go against you? Once that's done, there's no getting that back in any direction.
"I'm not getting blasé about it, but regardless of anything, in any sport in history, if later on you get the medal, it doesn't bring the feeling of when you initially win or you don't."
An independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
Manchester City have appealed against the decision. City boss Enzo Maresca has said he "trusts" his own club.
If the appeal adheres to strict Premier League guidelines, it should be concluded by Christmas Day, with a verdict to follow in the early part of 2027.
Carrick does not know how the situation will play out. However, as a very close bystander to the event, he feels there has to be a speedy resolution.
"It's thrown up a lot of questions," he said. "Some had answers, some haven't.
"Certainly, I've got my own questions about it. It's affected me personally in different ways over a period of time.
"As it's still not finalised, I think I'll hold that one (whether titles should be reassigned) until later on.
"What I will say is that the sooner it gets sorted, for everyone's benefit, is essential.
"It's unprecedented, a unique situation to be in at this level, with such a huge impact in so many ways. We all need to know what's going to happen."
Meanwhile, United's fans have delivered their own verdict by getting a 'ticker' banner showing the years since Manchester City last won a trophy rehung from the Stretford End.
The banner was initially displayed in 2000, at which point it was 24 years since City's last silverware - the 1976 League Cup.
It was increased by one each year until 2011 when City finally ended their trophy drought by beating Stoke City in the FA Cup final.
However, fans have a new version to display for this weekend's visit of Tottenham to Old Trafford, with the number 50 - signalling the years since their 1976 League Cup triumph, their final silverware before Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
An uninterrupted trip
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.
Volunteers went through the same four-part sequence twice, once sober and once on psilocybin. The sequence included putting participants in four different settings or contexts: eight minutes of lying at rest, a guided meditation, an 11-minute curated music playlist, and finally six minutes of eyes-open video of clouds moving across a sky. Each participant did all four inside an MRI scanner about 80 minutes after dosing, and again on EEG about 150 minutes after.
There were no cognitive tasks researchers routinely go for in brain studies, but there was a purpose behind this omission.
“We wanted ecological validity,” Stoliker says. “We wanted to know what the brain was like when somebody was having an authentic, uninterrupted psychedelic experience. If somebody took a psychedelic in a therapeutic setting, you wouldn’t have them completing tasks.” Stoliker also points out that there’s evidence that giving someone a task mid-trip pulls them out of the state—a phenomenon researchers sometimes call grounding. “Once you introduce these sorts of tasks, you’re actually interrupting the very phenomena you are seeking to measure.” And it worked.

Keralam Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan’s statement at a recent function about avoiding unnecessary angioplasty seems to have stirred a hornets’ nest with many doctors objecting to the “generalised statement,” while some lone voices pointed out that Mr. Satheesan was 100% right and that unnecessary procedures had become the norm.
In a Facebook post, Rajesh Gopalan Nair, Professor and Head of Cardiology at the Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, had appreciated Mr. Satheesan “for pointing out a truth.” But it set off an avalanche of comments from the doctors and public, with the latter narrating their harrowing experiences in hospitals and appreciating Dr. Rajesh for calling a spade a spade, while many doctors expressed disappointment at Dr. Rajesh’s stand.
Dr. Rajesh, however, made it clear in his post that a person coming into the emergency with a suspected heart attack should in no way distrust the doctor, for the situation may call for an immediate angioplasty.
Second opinion
He also explained clearly the situations when one could afford to wait and seek a second opinion, if angioplasty was suggested to a patient. He also cautioned the public against looking at every doctor or hospital with suspicion. Angioplasty should definitely be done when it is clinically indicated and these situations are clearly documented, he said.
Even though much of the medical fraternity expressed their displeasure at the “unsubstantiated” statement of the Chief Minister and the support that unexpectedly seemed to have come from one of their own, Dr. Rajesh refused to be cowed down. He maintained that he stood by his position that some of the angioplasty procedures done in hospitals were indeed not warranted.
On Monday, the Interventional Cardiology Council of Kerala (ICCK) said in a statement here that public’s apprehension over “unnecessary” medical procedures should not delay life-saving treatment during a heart attack emergency.
Responding to the Chief Minister’s remarks on avoiding unnecessary investigations and angioplasty, the council said it supported evidence-based and ethical medical practice and the principle that every intervention must have a clear clinical indication.
ICCK president Rajesh T. said that public discussion on angioplasty should clearly differentiate between elective intervention in stable patients and primary angioplasty during an acute heart attack, where treatment is highly time-sensitive.
What the data show
According to Statewide ICCK registry data presented at the council’s last annual conference, more than 70% of angioplasties performed in Kerala involved acute and emergency clinical situations.
He said the council welcomed any discussion aimed at strengthening evidence-based care, transparency and public confidence in the health-care system. “In stable patients, there is usually greater scope for detailed evaluation and for deciding whether medicines, further assessment or intervention would offer the greatest benefit. In an acute heart attack, however, delay can have serious consequences,” ICCK said.
However, the council cautioned that a general atmosphere of mistrust surrounding cardiac procedures could have unintended consequences, particularly when a patient develops severe chest pain or other symptoms suggestive of a heart attack.

Vivek Ramaswamy
 in Ohio (for the Governor’s mansion), the growing desi footprint reaches further down the ballot -- to state attorneys general, legislatures and local government.
One of the most striking examples is Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican challenging New York Attorney General Letitia James. Until recently, Komatireddy was hardly a household name outside legal and Republican political circles. But a combative televised debate with James on October 8 has given her greater visibility and a much larger platform.
It’s an uphill battle: New York is heavily Democratic, James is an established political figure who prosecuted Donald Trump, and Komatireddy is making her first run for elected office. 
Yet the challenger has turned her legal credentials and tough-on-crime message into a campaign that is attracting attention well beyond her prospects of actually winning, including an editorial thumbs-up from the Wall Street Journal.
Komatireddy, 41, was born in Brooklyn to parents who emigrated from India in the 1980s. A Harvard Law School graduate, she clerked for Brett Kavanaugh before his elevation to the Supreme Court, worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn, and served as chief of staff at the Drug Enforcement Administration under President Biden. Her prosecutorial career included terrorism and narcotics cases, and she was nominated for a federal judgeship that failed to materialise.
Komatireddy is not alone in seeking a statewide legal office. In Colorado, Hetal Doshi, a first-generation Indian-American and former federal prosecutor, entered the Democratic race for attorney general. She previously served as a deputy assistant attorney general in the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division. Her candidacy illustrates how Indian-American professionals are competing for offices that extend well beyond the familiar terrain of immigration and foreign policy.
The congressional contests offer another measure of that growing reach. Four Indian-American Democrats in the outgoing House -- Ro Khanna and Ami Bera of California, Pramila Jayapal of Washington, and Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia -- are seeking re-election. Meanwhile, Democrat Amish Shah, a physician born to Gujarati immigrant parents, is running in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, and Pia Dandiya, an educator and former school principal whose parents emigrated from India, is contesting Florida’s 22nd District. Both have received backing from the Democratic leadership.
On the Republican side, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Cincinnati-born son of Indian immigrants, is running for governor with President Trump’s endorsement. His candidacy offers a reminder that Indian-American political identity does not dictate party allegiance: Ramaswamy’s conservative message and Komatireddy’s law-and-order campaign stand in sharp contrast to the progressive politics of Jayapal and Khanna.
But the path to political acceptance is not always as straightforward as a Republican label might suggest. Some hard-line MAGA activists have made clear that conservative credentials do not necessarily trump race, ancestry or religion. Ramaswamy has faced attacks from within the right, including a primary rival who derided him as an “Indian boy” pretending to be American. Other critics have questioned how a Hindu can represent a state whose population is predominantly Christian.
The backlash against Indian professionals during the MAGA movement’s bitter H-1B visa debate has reinforced the contradiction: Indian-Americans can be celebrated as successful entrepreneurs and political allies while being cast by nativists as outsiders competing for American jobs and cultural influence. Even Indian-American Republicans have faced hostility over their heritage or religion. For candidates such as Ramaswamy, the test is therefore not simply whether voters accept their politics, but whether the movement they represent will accept them as fully American.

Lok Bhavan, the office and residence of West Bengal Governor R N Ravi, formerly known as Raj Bhavan, has declared a state-level essay writing competition for students from schools, colleges, and universities. The circular published on October 3 mentions two topics: Calcutta Massacre, 1946 – Causes and Consequences for students of Classes X to XII, and Direct Action Day by All India Muslim League – A Fatal Assault on Civilisational Bharat for college and university goers.
The competition carries handsome monetary awards going up to Rs 1,00,000.
Both the topics relate to the Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) also known as the ‘1946 Calcutta Riots’ and ‘Great Calcutta Killings’ which marked the beginning of a period of communal violence in Bengal that preceded and followed Partition.
However, the choice of topics raises questions because they do not seem to be framed neutrally. The term ‘Civilisational Bharat’ is ideologically loaded and is not standard historical terminology, and it gives the topic a distinctly Hindu nationalist framing.
Secondly, while the Calcutta killings of 1946 and Direct Action Day are important subjects for understanding the events leading up to Partition, the phrase ‘a fatal assault on civilisational Bharat’ embeds a particular ideological interpretation into the topic, rather than inviting students to examine the political circumstances, the causes and consequences of the violence and the competing narratives around it.
The wording is also problematic because it turns a complex period of history into a communal binary, with the Muslim League positioned as an assailant and ‘Bharat’ as the entity under attack. It is not just the inclusion of a controversial historical event that is concerning, but also the communal framing through which students are being asked to approach it.
Anwesha Sengupta, author and assistant professor of history at the Institute of Development Studies, Kolkata (ISDK), views the initiation of this competition in schools and colleges as an attempt to push a certain narrative and memory of the Direct Action Day and 1946 Calcutta riots.
“The history of the 1946 riots is very complicated. The government has, in recent times, tried to turn this event into an opportune moment for a particular brand of history-writing. The chief minister himself has routinely referred to it, in his speeches and on social media, helping create the figure of the ‘other’, in the demography of Bengali Muslims,” she said.
Sengupta also pointed out that one needed to have a certain degree of academic maturity to teach or write about riots. “How can school and college students be incentivised to turn out well-researched essays on this topic?” she questioned.
The essay competition notification comes close on the heels of another student-centric initiative by the West Bengal government that drew scrutiny for its political content. Alt News recently reported on the ‘Namo Seva: Untold Stories’ play, part of a month-long programme marking Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s birthday and 25 years in public service. The play, which was staged by students at schools and colleges, eulogised PM Modi on his achievements.
The play script sent out by West Bengal government to schools and colleges makes actors (which means students) shout ‘Jai Sri Ram’ and ‘Modi hai to Mumkin hai’ or wonder how ‘Modiji has been working tirelessly day and night for the last 25 years.’

A company called Steakholder Foods has launched a line of products under the brand name Perfecta. While the meat is 3D-printed, it is made from a formulation of plant material like other plant-based meats are. It is not made from cultured animal cells, which is often what people refer to when they mention "lab-grown meat." It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers are selling Perfecta-branded food, though the company has said its products have reached shelves in certain Northeastern U.S retail locations.
Between September and October, social media users claimed that 3D-printed, lab-grown meat had started being sold in U.S. stores from early September.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claims the 3D-printed meat "has federal clearance" but will not have a "lab-grown meat" label on its packaging. The post reads, in part:
The first 3D printed 'meat' has federal clearance and is about to be sold in the United States.
Packaging will not say 'lab-grown meat' because there is not a law that requires the packaging to say it was printed.
3D-printed plant-based food is already on shelves in the U.S.
Federal labels for cell-grown chicken and pork fat must be pre-approved and have used the words "cell-cultivated."
The printed food was in stores on September 3 of this year.
The company Steakholder Foods put its Perfecta line into Northeast supermarkets.
The rumor has appeared elsewhere on Facebook (archived) and on Instagram (archived). Numerous Snopes readers also emailed us to ask if the story is true.
In short, on Sept. 3, Israeli company Steakholder Foods, which specializes in making 3D-printing technology for plant-based meats, announced the launch of its 3D-printed, plant-based meat products in Northeastern U.S. retailers under the brand name Perfecta. Therefore, the claim is true.
Steakholder Foods' news release says its "Premium Plant-Based Meat" products were launched at retail locations in the Northeastern United States on Sept. 3, "marking the brand's first commercial placement on U.S. store shelves."
According to the webpage, the launch "focuses on building awareness and consumer trial throughout the Northeast U.S. market while establishing a foundation for broader expansion across additional regions."
It is not clear which grocery stores or retailers have started selling or stocking the products.
Snopes reached out to the company via a contact form on its website for more information. We will update this article if we hear back.
According to Steakholder Foods, the company uses plant-based ingredients and cultivates cells to create what ultimately becomes the 3D-printed meat.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Food Safety and Inspection Service do regulate "lab-grown" meat and require a label for such products. However, this regulation is specifically for food made with cultured animal cells, not for food made with other kinds of cells, which is what Perfecta products consist of.
Snopes reached out to both the FDA via contact form and the FSIS via email to confirm that there are not similar kinds of regulations for food made with other cultured cells, such as plant cells. Additionally, we asked both agencies to confirm if Perfecta products had received federal approval, as the above Facebook post states. We will update this story if we receive responses.
Based on how the product boxes appear on the website, there does not appear to be any text identifying the food as 3D-printed or made with cultured cells. The boxes do clearly identify the meat as "premium plant meat" and "plant-based."
Manufacturers of plant-based meat products usually have to process their ingredient mixes in a way that allows them to mimic the texture of conventional meat. According to the Good Food Institute's Asia-Pacific website, the most common processing method requires putting shear stress on the ingredients to align them into a meat-like texture. There are several other methods of processing plant-based meats, including 3D-printing.
For further reading, Snopes previously fact-checked a claim that a plant-based meat manufacturer was 3D-printing meat products in the Netherlands in 2024.

Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, was caught on an audio recording raging about not being invited to a dinner party with the Trump family, according to a report.
Guilfoyle, who was engaged to Donald Trump Jr. before they called it off in 2024, had a meltdown in January after learning that she wasn’t on the invite list for a dinner organized by Greek House Davos with Eric Trump, The Wall Street Journal reported.
“You don’t have the f****** U.S., you know, ambassador to Greece not come. She should be kissing my f****** ass,” Guilfoyle appears to have said of the event’s organizer.
Guilfoyle allegedly flexed her connections to wealthy Greek businessmen who were paying for her luxury travels at Davos before convincing an American businessman to help her snag an invite, according to audio reviewed by the Journal.
“You know, I can deliver the world to you, which you deserve,” she appeared to have said, according to an audio recording reviewed by the Journal. “I’m going to make you a lot of f****** money.”
While Guilfoyle managed to weasel her way into the event, organizers indicated that things had not gone smoothly and that Guilfoyle ended up leaving early.
Organizers “had to manage a small crisis [that] affected a number of high-profile guests,” the chairwoman of the venue, Irene Vantaraki, told the newspaper, adding that “some were disappointed.”
The report alleging Guilfoyle traded access comes days after news broke that she pressed wealthy MAGA donor Eric Deters for $100,000 to pay off her American Express bill, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.
In exchange for the funds, she offered Deters help getting the Trump administration to look into his personal tax and legal issues. However, a lawyer for Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages to the outlet.
“I just heard about it. It’s too bad,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report on Friday. “I mean, I don’t know. She’s an ambassador….She was always very nice.”
The State Department Office of the Inspector General is also investigating whether Guilfoyle received gifts or favors from private businessmen during her time as ambassador, according to the Journal.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.

The Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famous Cray-1 supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple’s founding.
Mac Minis from over a decade ago might not seem like the obvious first choice for building a cluster supercomputer, but when networked together, the developers can orchestrate the 64 active processing cores into a combined 1.3 teraflops of performance in their most recent tests. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops previously using all 70 available cores, prior to one node going offline. Benchmarks were obtained using a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Five PCs are quad-core i7s, and the remaining 25 are dual-core i5 models. Except for two units from 2014, the rest of the array dates to 2012.
The replica is a valuable tool for museum-goers to understand the shifts in computer architecture since 1976. The original Cray-1 used vector processing, applying a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster. The peak theoretical performance of the original Cray-1 was approximately 160 megaflops. What was originally a purpose-built research machine has been re-created with consumer hardware that’s vastly more capable than the machine that inspired it.
Rather than opting for a more standard Linux distribution, the team found that macOS Mojave (10.14) met their project needs by harnessing macOS’s built-in support for MPI (Message Passing Interface), the software layer that allows all the nodes in the cluster to pass tasks to one another.
Guests at the Museo de Historia de la Computación can watch in real time as the system runs matrix algorithms, mapping the scale of system performance from a single core to the full suite running in parallel.
Stealth supercomputing
Combining 30 consumer PCs into an operational cluster wasn’t the only engineering challenge the team faced. If you’ve ever stepped inside a server room, or, like me, foolishly installed one in your own basement, you know that fan cooling can be loud. The museum team used passive convection cooling via a steel rack chassis and aluminum tray mounts for each Mac Mini. Compared to the roaring thunder of a modern data center, this cluster is nearly inaudible.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

The increased instances of indigenous and imported cases of malaria over the past five years have left the health authorities a worried lot.
Imported malaria is acquired outside Keralam, while indigenous malaria is acquired through local transmission, when a local mosquito picks up the parasite from an infected person and transmits it to another person.
Going by the Health department statistics, as of October 5, four confirmed indigenous cases were reported in 2026, and 974 imported cases.
One death due to indigenous malaria and six deaths due to imported cases have been reported this year. Last year, no deaths due to indigenous cases were reported, while two deaths occurred due to imported cases.
The number of cases began to rise after 2021, when 252 imported and one indigenous death case were reported. The highest number of indigenous cases was reported from Malappuram, Kozhikode, and Kannur. Kollam, which earlier showed a high incidence of these cases, is in a recovery phase.
Health officials attribute the abundance of mosquitoes and the frequent influx of travellers to the increase in the number of infections.
“Over the past several years, the number of imported malaria cases has increased substantially. We need to strengthen surveillance measures, screening of migrants for the disease and ensuring intensive screening and testing for the disease in asymptomatic fever cases,” said the official.
The Health department plans to introduce insecticide-treated bed nets, which will kill mosquitoes on contact, in houses in regions where indigenous cases are reported. Steps are being taken to intensify malaria prevention activities to prevent the development of malaria-endemic regions in the State,” said the official.
“The increasing number of malaria cases in the past few years is a concern,” said. T.S. Anish, associate professor, School of Public Health, Kerala University of Health Sciences, Thiruvananthapuram.
“The consistent efforts by the Health department back in the 1960s succeeded in freeing the State from malaria. However, with increased travel and the influx of the migrant population from disease-endemic regions, malaria cases are getting reported. The delay in timely detection and intervention measures will contribute to the rise of indigenous cases. The local conditions are ideal to facilitate the spread of the disease,” Dr. Anish warned.
Climate change
He further added that climate change can also emerge as a key concern.
He warned that malaria could spread to hitherto unreported regions due to climate change-induced developments. “The climate in Keralam and the frequent movement of domestic workers are favourable to the spread of the disease,” he said.

The tropical Pacific has seen heat build for months as a “super” El Niño takes shape.
A climate phenomenon that forms every few years, this year’s iteration of El Niño has been on a tear of daily records and is forecast to reach unprecedented strength this winter. While it’s characterized by hotter-than-normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific, El Niño is a global problem.
It’s fair to wonder how another global problem is interacting with El Niño: climate change, driven by burning fossil fuels. While a hotter climate begetting a hotter El Niño might seem like a done deal, “I have more questions than I have reactions” to what’s happening, says Christopher Callahan, a climate researcher at Indiana University. In other words, the relationship is still an area of active research—and this year’s event could provide vital insights.
El Niño’s added ocean heat affects the atmosphere, causing weather patterns around the world to shift. Consider it kind of like a domino run, where one tile starts a chain reaction. Such a major slug of heat in the Pacific will act more like a shove then a light flick on the atmosphere, and the resulting shifts in weather are expected to be generationally intense.
The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting 100 percent odds of an extremely strong El Niño through December and above 80 percent odds it stays that way through February. Data shows this El Niño has already set multiple all-time daily heat records including a recent peak of 3.4 degrees Celsius.
NOAA issues its El Niño forecast as a three-month rolling average, and the agency predicts heat could peak at 2.7 degrees Celsius above normal for the period from October to December. (It’s not out of the question that heat could surpass 3 degrees Celsius, though.) If the forecast holds true, it would smash the previous record of 2.4 degrees Celsius, which was set during the 1982-1983 event.
How Is Climate Change Impacting El Niño?
There is a growing body of evidence that climate change is likely playing at least some role in influencing El Niño. The magnitude and frequency of the phenomenon has increased over the past 60 years, says Francisco Estrada, coordinator of the Climate Change Research Program at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, and so has the variability and how the effects are distributed around the world. He says there shouldn’t be a debate framed as a choice between a “natural El Niño” and an “El Niño caused by climate change” but rather as an interaction between the two processes.
“You can’t separate El Niño from global warming—they’re inextricably linked,” he explains.
Modeling also indicates that El Niño is likely to strengthen as the planet warms, though Callahan notes that many models struggle to accurately represent long-term temperature trends in the eastern tropical Pacific. That can give researchers some pause, but there’s also other evidence that climate change is juicing El Niño.
“The majority of climate models say that El Nino amplitude shall go up in a warming climate, and all of our paleoclimate records say that we're currently in a more active period of El Niño than the last several 1,000 years,” Callahan says.
Research published in August uses data collected from ancient coral, and provides that 1,000-year glimpse Callahan mentions. (He wasn’t involved with the study.) The scientists found an uptick in El Niño amplitude that neatly mirrors when humans started pumping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, though they didn’t attempt to attribute the shift to climate change.
This year’s El Niño will provide another data point to help researchers suss things out.
How Is El Niño Impacting Climate Change?
But as Callahan notes, there’s also an important question about how El Niño is layering on top of climate change.
“Even if climate change has not made the event itself stronger, even if the [sea surface temperature] anomalies are totally natural, the presence of those SSTs in a climate that has been changed by global warming might produce unprecedented impacts,” he says.
El Niño’s impacts on weather—known as teleconnections—are well known, from increasing the odds of drought in the Amazon and Indonesia to juicing precipitation in the Southwest US and lowering the odds of Atlantic hurricanes.
Such an extreme event layered on top of climate change doesn’t mean teleconnections get thrown out the window, though. In fact, some of them may be even more intense.
“We can no longer place as much confidence in the knowledge we’ve gathered from data regarding how El Niño manifests in terms of weather and climate in different parts of the planet,” says Estrada.
What El Niño Means for Climate Risk
From a risk perspective, Estrada believes it’s important to understand how the two phenomena interact and how that combination will affect societies.
He and Callahan’s main concern is not merely whether this El Niño will be the most intense on record but rather the combination of an exceptional event with a climate that has warmed significantly.
“Surprises are the last thing you want when you’re trying to manage risk,” Estrada says.
Callahan’s work shows that the impacts of El Niño on society are extreme, with the most severe events knocking off trillions of dollars from the global GDP. Ecosystems also suffer greatly, particularly coral reefs, which are facing a mass bleaching event.
Given this scenario, the United Nations and other international organizations have called for urgent adaptation measures to safeguard the well-being of the at-risk populations and ecosystems. Some places are already doing that: California preemptively declared a state of emergency last month.
“El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world. Impacts will hit even harder, travel even farther, and cross borders with devastating speed,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said last month.

We got our first look at Prime Video’s new sci-fi series Blade Runner 2099 in July at San Diego Comic-Con. With the show’s premiere roughly six weeks away, the streamer unveiled the full trailer this weekend at New York Comic-Con. Co-stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) joined showrunner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) onstage for the big reveal.
As Luisa described the show during the NYCC panel Saturday night:
We are 50 years after [Blade Runner] 2049 and, bad news, the worst has happened. The replicant uprising that has been bubbling up in the films has taken place and the humans have lost. So the creations have surpassed their creators. And the series, the big question it asks is, ‘What happens when our time as a species ends?’ 2099 is taking place at a junction point when one species is ending and a new one is rising. The first film, something I loved about it, was that it was looking at mortality on a micro level. Roy Batty and the other replicants were fighting for more life. This show asks that same question but on a macro level. Mankind—what happens when we realize our time is running out? And are we going to accept that loss? Can we hold on to our humanity during it?
Yeoh stars as Olwen, the dying Replicant, while Schafer plays Cora. The cast also includes Hugo Hamlet as Buster Friendly, as well as Dmitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Matthew Needham, Tom Burke, and Maurizio Lombardi—all in as-yet-undisclosed roles.
Prime Video will drop all eight episodes of Blade Runner 2099 on November 25, 2026.

Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers say
- Published
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.
Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition in hospital.
Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.
Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to reschedule Pike's execution.
The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
After Pike survived two lethal injections, she lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital.
She eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyers said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"

India’s cleantech startups attracted substantially more capital in Q3 2026, with large electric mobility rounds driving funding growth alongside an increase in deal activity. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026, cleantech startups raised $433 Mn across 23 deals, compared with $118 Mn across 16 deals in the year-ago quarter. The report tracks funding announced up to September 24. The increase stood out against a subdued funding environment. Overall startup funding rose just 5% YoY to $2.2 Bn, while funding for fintech and ecommerce startups declined 11% and 31%, respectively. However, the cleantech funding surge was heavily concentrated in electric mobility. River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette attracted $85 Mn. Together, the three startups accounted for $298 Mn, or nearly 69% of the sector’s funding. Adding to this, Simple Energy raised a mega $180 Mn round at the end of the month of September, further adding to this trend. The numbers raise two questions: what is drawing investors towards these businesses and how far does the momentum extend beyond a handful of large EV rounds? Commercial Viability Shapes Investor Bets For investors, the appeal is increasingly tied to whether technology can solve a tangible problem and support a commercially viable business. “What's different this cycle is that capital is backing businesses and not just the energy transition,” Elev8 Venture Partners managing partner Navin Honagudi told Inc42. The VC firm led River’s $120 Mn Series C in August. The round alone accounted for nearly 28% of the quarter’s cleantech funding. Shubham Jhuria, CFO and partner at Aeravti Ventures, also pointed to a shift in how investors assess the sector. “The biggest change we are seeing is that the cleantech conversation is moving beyond the climate-impact narrative towards businesses solving very specific economic and infrastructure problems,” he told Inc42. Funding activity extended beyond the three largest EV rounds, with Omega Seiki Mobility, Electric.AI, Simple Energy, and Yuma also raising capital during the quarter. Cleantech deal count increased about 44%, while the average cheque size rose to approximately $19 Mn from $7 Mn in the year-ago quarter. EVs accounted for 57% of deals, according to the report. This suggests that the increase was not solely the result of larger cheques, although electric mobility remained central to both funding value and deal activity. EV Adoption Supports The Investment Case Rising EV adoption is giving investors a more tangible basis to assess demand and business models. JMK Research estimates that 15.41 Lakh EVs were registered in H1 2026, up 43% YoY. According to Vahan, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in September. E2W registrations increased 12.2% to 2.07 Lakh units from 1.84 Lakh in August. Honagudi said electric mobility has matured into a demand-led market. He pointed to River’s position among India’s top seven electric two-wheeler brands by registrations, despite having far fewer retail outlets than established players, as evidence of product-led demand. Over the next 3-5 years, Elev8 expects deeper localisation of motors and electronics to improve margins and supply-chain resilience. Honagudi cited last year’s rare earth magnet shortage as an example of the vulnerabilities that localisation could address. He also expects consolidation to leave “a handful of scaled independents” alongside established incumbents. Can The Momentum Broaden? Stronger adoption does not automatically translate into attractive investor returns. Jhuria cautioned that investment appetite could moderate if businesses struggle to convert technological capabilities into scalable solutions or continue to require substantial capital without improving their unit economics. The quarter’s numbers reflect both wider deal activity and substantial concentration. More cleantech startups attracted funding than a year earlier, but three EV businesses still captured more than two-thirds of the capital. For the momentum to broaden, investor conviction will need to extend beyond large electric mobility bets. Within EVs, the test will be whether rising demand and deeper localisation translate into stronger margins and businesses that can scale without repeatedly requiring outsized capital infusions.

Spirit of Hong Kong Awards: Gaza nurse’s obstacle-laden road to becoming a professor
Border closures and travel restrictions prevented Hammoda Abu-Odah from leaving Gaza on six occasions. Today he is a lauded Hong Kong nursing professor
On six occasions, Hammoda Abu-Odah, a Gaza nurse-turned Hong Kong scholar was offered an opportunity to study overseas. But each time, border closures and travel restrictions prevented him from taking them up.
Abu-Odah had obtained a nursing degree in his native Gaza but set his sights on an academic career abroad. He kept working, teaching and conducting research, despite the many challenges that prevented him from leaving.
Finally, on the seventh attempt, he made it to Hong Kong, where he eventually completed his doctorate at Polytechnic University in 2021 after receiving a Hong Kong PhD fellowship.
“If I had given up after losing six scholarship opportunities, I would not be here in Hong Kong teaching today,” he said.

‘If a sibling uses a skin-lightening product, you may be more likely to use one too’. This was among the findings from behavioural research cited by the World Health Organisation (WHO) during a discussion on colourism in Hyderabad on Wednesday (October 7, 2026).
The discussion was part of ‘Complexion of Change: Challenging Colorism Through Policy, Art, and Science’, held at Goethe-Zentrum in Hyderabad. A documentary exploring global skin colour bias and the deep-rooted societal association of fair skin with higher status, beauty and success was also screened as part of the programme.
“Skin-lightening product use was not a single behaviour but was influenced by psychological, cultural and environmental factors,” said Ammaarah Martinus, Behavioural Insights consultant at the WHO.
The psychological dimension includes motivations such as wanting to appear fairer, younger or to fit into society. The cultural dimension includes the influence of families, communities and social networks. Mr. Martinus said research had found that people were more likely to use a skin-lightening product if a sibling used one. She also spoke about access to such products . In India, skin-lightening products could be easily purchased in local markets and supermarkets. “Interventions to address skin-lightening therefore need to work across all three levels rather than focus on only one aspect of the behaviour,” she added.
Psychologist and researcher Bharti Upparu said children begin receiving messages about skin colour at a very young age, often without anyone explicitly telling them that one skin tone is preferable to another. They observe who is complimented, who is bullied and who is teased, and gradually learn which physical characteristics society values. “A person perceived as fair and attractive may unconsciously be associated with other positive characteristics such as competence, goodness and trustworthiness. Such biases can compound into an overall perception of a person’s character and affect how others interact with them,” she said.
The discussion also highlighted that colourism is not restricted to women. Arpit Bhutani, co-founder of Circular Innovation Lab and moderator of the session, pointed to products marketed specifically towards men and noted that the pressure to conform to lighter-skin beauty standards also affects men.
Former Miss America Nina Davuluri recalled an incident involving a friend’s baby, when an older family member cautioned against taking the child into the sun because the child could become darker. “Such comments are not necessarily made with malicious intent but can come from a desire to see children succeed in a society where lighter skin is perceived to offer advantages,” she added.
Mercury in skin-lightening products
In remarks before the documentary screening, Monika Stankiewicz, executive secretary of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, said mercury was among the chemicals of highest public concern according to the WHO and that cosmetics were one pathway through which people could be exposed. “Mercury-containing skin-lightening products can damage the skin and may also contaminate households, potentially exposing other family members,” she added.
Ms. Stankiewicz stressed that the issue was not solely a chemical problem but also a social one linked to beauty standards and the pressure to conform to them. She said meaningful change could not come through regulations alone and that activism, art, culture and storytelling also had important roles to play.

- The claim that Matthew Ingalls, one of seven Cornell University students accused of rape in a September lawsuit, fled to Dubai is still under investigation.
- The rumor stems from an article in the Daily Mail, a British tabloid, which cited an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle, who said they believed the accused man is in Dubai.
- Using old yearbook photographs and searches of public records, Snopes was able to determine Matthew Ingalls also was known as Umar Matthew Ingalls, an alumnus of Dubai International Academy. While we know Ingalls lived in Dubai at some point, we cannot confirm his current whereabouts.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We have reached out to Ingalls, the Dubai International Academy, Ingalls' former school in Washington state and the person tabloids identify as Ingalls' father in Dubai and are waiting for responses.
In October, several weeks after a lawsuit was filed accusing seven male students at Cornell University of drugging and raping a female student in 2024, a rumor spread about the whereabouts of one of the accused men. According to the claim, Matthew Ingalls — who reportedly initiated the encounter with the accuser, named in court documents only as Jane Doe — fled to Dubai, where he previously lived.
Posts on Facebook (archived) and Instagram claimed Ingalls, who the posts said also goes by Umar Matthew Ingalls, was in Dubai with his family:
Umar Matthew Ingalls, one of the "Cornell 7" accused in the alleged 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi house, is now reportedly in Dubai, where he grew up. Neighbors of his relatives in Connecticut told the Daily Mail they believe he's back in the Middle East with his dad. How convenient.
Quick refresher on Mr. Ingalls. He's the one Jane Doe says invited her to the house that night. He's also the one who, according to messages filed in her lawsuit, shared a photo of her in the frat's Snapchat group chat and wrote "Like you can walk in and whip it out." The New York Post reports he added "Boys come whip it out." Truly the words of a gentleman.
(Facebook user Feminist News)
The rumor originated from a report in the Daily Mail, a British tabliod, that relied on anonymous sources. Snopes is unable to verify Ingalls' whereabouts as of this writing, so we have left this claim unrated. We have, however, found records of an Umar Ingalls who studied at the Dubai International Academy in Emirates Hills, Dubai, whose appearance matches that of Matthew Ingalls.
We have reached out to Ingalls — whom The New York Times reported had been expelled from Cornell — via his old college email address, to a person believed to be his father, to the Dubai International Academy and also to the Annie Wright School in Tacoma, Washington, where Ingalls reportedly studied as a child. We will update this story as we learn more.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls as Umar Matthew Ingalls and spoke to an anonymous neighbor of Ingalls' uncle in Connecticut, where Ingalls' address was listed in court records. That neighbor reportedly told the tabloid Ingalls hadn't been seen at the home in some time and that they thought he was in Dubai.
Our public records search for Umar Matthew Ingalls found his name appeared connected to an address in South Dartmouth, Massachusetts, that also was linked to the name Matthew B. Ingalls.
The Daily Mail identified Ingalls' father as a Yale-educated professor at the American University in Dubai. We found a Matthew B. Ingalls listed as an associate professor of Middle Eastern studies at the American University in Dubai. Snopes reached out to him to verify his identity and relationship to Ingalls and will update this story as we get more information.
Several purported photographs of Matthew Ingalls have circulated, including one showing him wearing a Cornell rugby T-shirt and another from what appears to be his now-deleted LinkedIn account. According to the university's student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, the school's rugby club confirmed Ingalls was previously a part of its roster.
We found that Ingalls' image from his deleted LinkedIn account had SynthID markers — which are inserted into images created with some generative artificial intelligence platforms — and was thus likely edited with AI. However, the photograph of Ingalls in his rugby shirt did not. We then compared that photograph to other images we found of him and found several matches.
Dubai International Academy's 2022-23 yearbook identifies Umar Ingalls as a member of the class of 2023 and part of the athletics team. The person in the yearbook photo appears to be the same person wearing the Cornell rugby shirt.
(Dubai International Academy)
Umar Ingalls also was mentioned in a 2022 story in the Khaleej Times, a Dubai newspaper. The article reported on a group of students who created their own version of a lunar rover. The accompanying photograph is blurry, but the student in the back right has a strong resemblance to Ingalls.
A 2020 blog post on the website for Annie Wright Schools, an elite private school in Tacoma, Washington, identified Umar Ingalls as half-American. He appeared to have studied at the Lower School until 2016 and lived in Dubai at the time the article was written. He commented on how Americans were perceived in Dubai after the election victory of U.S. President Donald Trump.
For further reading, we have previously reported on numerous rumors about the Cornell rape case.

South Africa hope to host first African Olympics
- Published
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has confirmed South Africa have shown an interest in becoming the first African host of the summer Olympics in 2036.
Hungary, India, Qatar and Turkey are also working towards becoming first-time hosts, while Germany and South Korea are in discussions with the IOC having held previous summer Games.
The IOC stated that the seven countries are engaged in "continuous dialogue" with the governing body and have set a deadline of 31 October for submissions of stated interest.
Virtual presentations will be given by interested parties to the body's future host commission in November, with IOC feasibility assessments to be carried out by March 2027.
After that, the national Olympic committees, all of whom have previously announced an intention to explore hosting bids, will enter strategic dialogue with the IOC.
The South Africa proposal involves hosting between three cities - Cape Town, Durban and Johannesburg.
Durban had been set to host the Commonwealth Games in 2022, but withdrew in 2017.
Ahmedabad, which will welcome the Commonwealth Games in 2030 and has bid for the 2038 Asian Games, will be the host city in India's bid.
The city has also staged four of the last five finals in cricket's Indian Premier League at its Narendra Modi stadium, which is reported to have a capacity of 132,000 and is named after the current prime minister of India, who hails from the city.
Budapest and Doha, the capital cities of Hungary and Qatar respectively, are the hosts in their country's bids.
Qatar hosted football's 2022 World Cup, with multiple stadia in the capital, while Budapest has staged the 2022 World Aquatics Championships and 2023 World Athletics Championships.
Istanbul is the nominated city in Turkey's bid, having previously bid unsuccessfully for the 2000, 2008 and 2020 Games.
The largest city in Turkey will host the 2027 European Games.
Germany has hosted the Olympics in 1936 and 1972, in Berlin and Munich respectively, while the latter city is bidding again for 2036.
Meanwhile South Korea capital Seoul, which hosted the Games in 1988, is part of a bid that also involves the province of North Jeolla.
The IOC also confirmed that a number of national Olympic committees are taking part in non-committal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036.
The UK government said in May that it is in "discussions about supporting potential bids" for the Olympics and Paralympics in the 2040s.
The 2028 Games will be held in Los Angeles, while Australia will host the Olympics for the first time in 32 years when Brisbane stages the event in 2032.

Trump has spent a majority of his days back in the White House bashing the nation’s election integrity
Trump has accused Democrats of cheating in 2020, in state-wide races and in the November midterm elections

President Donald Trump has questioned the credibility of U.S. elections on 440 separate days of his second term, according to a new report by The New York Times.
That is more than 70 percent of the days since he returned to office in January 2025.
One of his most repeated claims is that the 2020 election was fraudulent and that Joe Biden was not the duly elected president. The claim has no basis in evidence. Recounts, court proceedings and investigations — including by Trump allies — have found no widespread fraud that changed the outcome.
Trump wasted no time in calling U.S. elections into question upon his return to office. At a luncheon after his inauguration, he called the 2020 race "rigged," a claim he had repeated many times before. The comments kept coming.
“I have had more people ask me to have a third term, which in a way is a fourth term because the other election, the 2020 election was totally rigged,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One in March 2025.
He has also used unjustified claims to push for policies he wants adopted. These include the SAVE America Act, which would require new voters to provide proof of citizenship, and restrictions on mail-in voting.
“We cannot, as a country, put up with this any longer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in May. “Voter I.D. and proof of citizenship must be approved, now. Crooked mail-in voting must be stopped.”
At times, Trump has also accused Democrats of cheating in state-level races, including California's gubernatorial primary in June.
"The Dumocrats are at it again! They are trying to STEAL THE GOVERNOR OF CALIFORNIA PRIMARY, AND THE MAYOR OF LOS ANGELES, PRIMARY, AWAY FROM TWO GREAT REPUBLICAN CANDIDATES," the president wrote on Truth Social on June 4.
His accusation, which came before the final results were tallied, was not accompanied by any evidence.
With the November midterms less than a month away, the 80-year-old president is now alleging that Democrats intend to rig those contests as well.
“Vote by mail or vote in person on Election Day, November 3rd, so we can defeat the radical left Dumocrats in a midterm victory that is too big to rig,” Trump said in a video released this month.
Democrats have spent years condemning the president's comments about U.S. elections, accusing him of undermining faith in the democratic system and laying the groundwork to dispute any result that does not favor him.
When reached by the Times, a White House spokesperson said “the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up,” and that Democrats’ opposition to the SAVE America Act is “keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections.”

Last month we covered the winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. But allegations surfaced about Xu’s use of AI while making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).
According to a BBC report, some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed extending restrictions on advertisements of prescription medicines to drug retailers, wholesalers and distributors, seeking to close a regulatory gap in the Drugs Rules, 1945.
A draft amendment notified through Gazette notification G.S.R. 861(E) on September 28 proposes inserting a new sub-rule under Rule 65 to prohibit holders of licences to sell, stock, exhibit, offer for sale or distribute drugs listed under Schedules H, H1 and X from advertising these medicines without prior sanction of the Central government.
Under the existing framework, pharmaceutical manufacturers are prohibited from advertising drugs covered under these schedules without prior government approval. However, the corresponding restriction does not explicitly cover entities involved in the retail and wholesale sale and distribution of medicines.
The proposed amendment seeks to extend the requirement across the drug supply chain, strengthening oversight of the promotion of prescription medicines and reducing the risk of inappropriate self-medication.
Misuse of prescription drugs
The medicines covered by these schedules include drugs that require medical supervision, including certain antibiotics and psychotropic medicines. Unauthorised promotion of such medicines can encourage their use without appropriate medical advice, raising concerns over patient safety and the misuse of prescription drugs.
The proposal follows recommendations made at the 93rd meeting of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) on February 16, 2026, which examined the need for provisions regulating advertisements by holders of drug sale and distribution licences.
The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days of the date on which copies of the Gazette notification containing the draft rules are made available to the public.
The submissions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the Central government before the amendment is finalised.
