The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has announced a protest march to Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on 10 October 2026, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The party’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced the protest after demonstrations in Mumbai on 02 October and in Delhi in the days that followed. CJP leaders have said they will continue the protest even if the police stop them from reaching Jantar Mantar. As of 09 October 2026, Delhi Police had not granted permission for the proposed gathering and had tightened security ahead of the demonstration. CJP has also alleged that authorities were detaining its members and volunteers across the country to prevent them from participating in the protest, with party leaders vowing to continue the agitation (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows women police personnel assaulting students during the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi on 04 October 2026.
Fact: The video predates the October 2026 Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest and shows a confrontation between the family of a man found dead under suspicious circumstances and the police in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, in July 2026. Although clashes between protesters and police were reported in Delhi during the first week of October amid demonstrations demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, the viral video is unrelated to those protests. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) dated 01 August 2026 featuring the same video, confirming that it predates the October 2026 CJP protest. According to these posts, the video shows an incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, where a young man named Ganesh was found dead in a rented apartment. Following the incident, his family staged a protest by blocking the road and making serious allegations against the landlord. The posts also describe a clash between women and police personnel during the protest.
We also found news reports (here, here) published around the same time covering the incident. According to these reports, tensions erupted in Budh Vihar, Rohini, Delhi, after the body of a 30-year-old man named Ganesh was found under suspicious circumstances at his rented house on 31 July 2026. His family accused the landlord of murder and staged a roadblock, during which they alleged that the police assaulted them. The reports also state that a woman dressed in black, identified as the deceased’s aunt, alleged that a police officer had snatched her mangalsutra and pulled her hair. These findings confirm that the viral video shows a confrontation between the family and police in July 2026, unrelated to the CJP protest in October 2026.
Meanwhile, during the first week of October 2026, clashes broke out between protesters and police in Delhi during demonstrations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Police detained several protesters and stopped groups from reaching protest sites, while some demonstrators alleged that police personnel pushed, dragged, and assaulted them (here, here, and here). However, the viral video predates these demonstrations and shows an unrelated incident in Budh Vihar, Rohini, in July 2026.
To sum up, an unrelated video is shared as showing women police personnel assaulting students during the CJP protest in Delhi.

AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn. AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn. The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters. Investors Want More Than AI Exposure Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples. For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price. Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value. Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each. Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure. Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts. The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint. The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology. Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum? The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds. The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent. “One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds. This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector. Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector. However, India's AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period. For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers. The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market. Delhi CJP protest: Metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, more than 250 trains were cancelled, a traffic advisory was issued, internet services were temporarily suspended and markets across the national capital, including Khan Market and Connaught Place, were also affected — all this to thwart a protest led by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has been under fire after an Indian Express investigation alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll and flagged 14 objections raised by Kumar’s deputies over 10 months. These objections included the change in Form 6 and ECINET — where the voter list is published.
To protest against Kumar, the CJP and several political parties organised a protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10, prompting the Centre and police to take pre-emptive steps to avoid a July 20-like situation (when the CJP protest over NEET turned violent).
Quick answers to key questions
The estimated cost could reach around ₹90–91 crore for the weekend, according to a Times of India report cited in the article. The figure combines estimated losses from market closures, liquor shop closures and Metro restrictions.
The estimates include around ₹58.5 crore from a one-day closure of liquor shops, roughly ₹31.8 crore from closing Connaught Place and Sadar Bazar markets for a day, and ₹0.52–1.30 crore from the Metro shutdown.
The article says the costs are passed on to the public. Shopkeepers, workers and commuters are among those affected by lost business and disrupted travel.
The reported estimate for closing Connaught Place and Sadar Bazar for one day is about ₹31.8 crore. Khan Market’s traders’ association president said a single day’s closure could cost each shop ₹1–1.5 lakh, with perishable goods adding to losses.
Forty-five Metro stations were closed for a period, trains were cancelled, liquor shops were shut and internet services were temporarily suspended in designated areas. Markets, including Connaught Place and Khan Market, were also affected.
But how much do these restrictions on the metro, internet, railways, and markets cost, and who pays for them?
The cost of these curbs would be passed on to the public, the Times of India reported, while sharing a breakdown of the estimated losses incurred due to the October 10 restrictions, which the Opposition has widely labelled a “shutdown.”
The lockdown of the national capital could reach around ₹91 crore for the weekend, the TOI reported. It stated that when a capital city is locked down for one protest, shopkeepers, workers and commuters pay for the loss.
The report claimed that the shutdown of the Delhi metro may cost around ₹0.52 crore to ₹1.30 crore, while the closure of the Connaught Place and Sadar Bazar market for just one day may amount to roughly ₹31.8 crore.
Dry days (liquor shops shut for one day) may cost around ₹58.5 crore. All this roughly adds up to ₹90 crore-91 crore loss in this weekend alone, the TOI report claimed.
Meanwhile, Khan Market Traders Association President Sanjiv Mehra told ANI that a single day’s closure can cause losses of ₹1-1.5 lakh per shop. “Perishable goods, such as fruits and groceries, add to the losses,” he added.
Delhi Metro closed 45 stations from 9 pm on Friday till 6 pm on Saturday for security reasons, an advisory said.
Internet services were suspended within a 4-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar from 10 pm on October 9 to 10 pm on October 10. However, the Hindustan Times reported on Sunday that the internet suspension was extended to at least eight places across Delhi that had been designated astemporary jails for Saturday's protest.
The order, dated October 9 and approved by Union home secretary Govind Mohan, suspended mobile internet within 500 metres of each site from noon to 10pm on Saturday, the report added.
Liquor shops across Delhi were ordered to remain closed on October 9 and 10 as a preventive measure.
Railway services were also disrupted, with several trains scheduled to arrive at or depart from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations between 4 am and 2 pm on Saturday reported cancelled.
Hotels, lodges, guest houses and dharamshalas were checked as part of the preventive security exercise. Police are also issuing appeals from various mosques and temples, urging people to maintain peace.
No such restrictions were announced for October 11 as the CJP decided to continue its protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

Disappointed, angry, excited: Albertans weigh in on looming referendum
CBC News heard a lot about unity and unease at a pop-up in a Calgary library
Jim Fedor booked Oct. 19 off work to make sure he can vote in Alberta’s referendum.
“I'm looking forward to it. Never voted in a referendum like this before, so it'll be something new,” said Fedor, who stopped at the CBC News pop-up at the Seton library branch in southeast Calgary last week.
“I'm gonna vote Option 1 on the separation question, for Alberta to stay in Canada, and the other nine questions I plan to vote no for each one,” he said. “I'll get there early, and I'm willing to wait to get in and vote.”
“I think it's important for everyone to have their voices heard. A lot of places in the world don't allow voting on much of anything. So I feel quite lucky to be able to vote and make my vote count.”
CBC News set up at the library to get a sense of how Albertans are feeling as the referendum campaigns head into their final week. We set out Post-It notes and markers, and invited patrons to share their thoughts on the question: What are you thinking about as you get ready to vote?
Library patrons left their thoughts at a CBC News pop-up in the Calgary Public Library's Seton branch. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Parents came by with their kids; high school students stopped in after their classes ended; seniors swung by to pick up books on hold. A low hum filled the busy building.
Some Albertans frustrated at the vote
A few people were excited to vote, like Fedor. Others were just starting to follow the process and had not yet decided how they would cast their ballots; several expressed frustration at even having the vote.

- Exclusive Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll
That’s how Christine Nelson was feeling.
“I'm really disappointed. The majority of people do not want to separate, and we have to spend taxpayers’ money to vote on something that's not going to go through unless there's some kind of, you know, crookedness going on. It's ridiculous,” said Nelson.
Charmaine Coutinho, who stopped by with her young daughter, had a similar sentiment.
“I am feeling anger about the increase in racism and otherness caused by legitimizing these extreme perspectives through government actions,” she said. “I am saying no to everything, and we are, and I am, very much in favour of staying in Canada.”
From left to right, Michael Chudleigh, Charmaine Coutinho and her daughter, and Christine Nelson. They all stopped by to share their thoughts at the CBC News pop-up in Seton on Thursday. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Michael Chudleigh said he is voting the same, but trying to stay open to difference.
“I'm trying not to be angry about the whole thing and understand that those who disagree with me have their reasons, even if I can't see them.”
Friends at odds over separation
One pair of seniors were laughing and chatting as they stopped by on their way for coffee. The two women said they are good friends, who meet regularly.
One is passionate about staying in Canada, while the other is casting her vote to explore leaving.
They don’t talk about the referendum. “We might not be friends after!” said the pro-unity friend. She didn’t want to be interviewed, but earlier said her father fought for Canada and she’d never want to see it splintered.
The other friend came back later to write her thoughts on the whiteboard: “I think the Oct. 19 [referendum] is more like a memorandum of understanding thing and gets people talking and looking into our rights and fairness/democracy. But many people have been led to be afraid it’s a final say or referendum to leave their country or be taken over by Trump!”
She wrote that separatists fear the way Ottawa has been asserting control over individuals, such as freezing bank accounts during the trucker convoy.
- First came the blockade. Then came separatism. Old tensions revived in Coutts
- Analysis How anti-COVID activism injected life into Alberta's separatist movement
Newcomers express love for Canada
As the afternoon wore on, our board filled with messages, with a lot of love for Canada.
“I love Canada; I’ll vote to stay here,” wrote one person.
“I love Canada, this is my home,” wrote another.
David Aldana immigrated from Colombia and has been following the referendum campaigns, even though he can't vote. Other Albertans with permanent residency but no Canadian citizenship also left messages on the board. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Several people with permanent residency but not Canadian citizenship stopped by. One was David Aldana, who moved to Canada from Colombia.
“If I could vote, I would stay with Canada, and because I feel that unity is better,” he said. “I think unity is better for the country itself. I'm in love with Canada. I'm in love with the freedom that we have here.”
Concerns the vote could backfire
In Alberta, support for independence had been polling at about 27 per cent this spring, according to a poll from Janet Brown Opinion Research commissioned by CBC News.
That softened to 23 per cent in a similar poll by Janet Brown in September, which also found Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party lost some support, likely due to frustration over the vote.
One man at the library called it a nightmare. He wrote: “Talk about backfiring. Rather than more consideration from Ottawa we are now facing a potential NDP resurgence (the worst outcome you could imagine).”
On the left, a Ukrainian newcomer left her concerns: the referendum reminds her of separation votes in the Ukrainian regions of Crimea and Donbas. On the right, a public servant wrote a note about his hope for a transparent referendum process. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who stopped by after class at the nearby Joane Cardinal-Schubert High School. He said at school they tried to look at the separation arguments from both sides.
“Surprisingly, a lot of my class wanted to stay. And I really found that fascinating ‘cause there's just one of my friends who is heavily right. He always agrees with whatever right-wingers say but this time … he wants to stay in Canada,” Asher said.
“It kind of just shows that as a country — it sounds a bit corny, but there's a lot of love and unity. I think that's really special, and I think we just can't give that up.”
Muaaz Asher is a Grade 10 student who discussed the Alberta referendum question at school. (Elise Stolte/CBC)
'Strong opinions on both sides'
The voices for unity were loudest and most common at the library Thursday. But it’s one location, on one afternoon.

- Fight for independence won't end after referendum: Alberta Prosperity Project leader
Destiny Fox stopped by and suggested you can’t judge how people in general are feeling by those most willing to speak up.
“I don't think that a lot of people are being very open about their opinion to leave Canada as honestly as people who want to stay in Canada,” Fox said. “So you're just not hearing as much … You're not going to see the lawn signs on people's personal property because they don't want to get into it with their neighbours. But I think that there are a lot of strong opinions on both sides.
“I'm glad that we're having this referendum because I feel like it's giving everybody an opportunity to voice their feelings. And I don't necessarily feel that I want to separate from Canada, but I do want the premier to have the power to go back to Ottawa and say this is how Albertans are feeling.”

Srinagar, Oct 11: PDP youth leader Zuhaib Yousf Mir on Sunday said that suffering of protestors in Delhi deserves justice in its own right, but solidarity shouldn’t come at the cost of erasing Kashmir’s distinct and deeply painful history.
“The suffering of protestors in Delhi deserves scrutiny, solidarity, and justice in its own right. But solidarity should not come at the cost of erasing Kashmir's distinct and deeply painful history. One injustice does not diminish another, equally, one cannot invoke Kashmir merely as a metaphor for every instance of state repression elsewhere,” PDP youth leader said on X.
He termed the ongoing protest in Delhi and elsewhere in the country as “Kashmirisation of India”.
“To call what is happening in India today the “Kashmirisation of India” is, therefore, both a misnomer and an oxymoron. It risks turning decades of Kashmiri suffering into a political slogan while overlooking the specificity of what Kashmiris have endured,” PDP leader added.

Australia veterans shine against South Africa
- Published
First Test, Durban (day three of five)
Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*
South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54
Australia lead by 139 runs
Australia's modern Test side remain a fascinating one to unpick.
Viewed by many in England as there for the taking in last winter's Ashes despite a 4-1 win, they are also labelled too old by many observers at home.
The victims of recent shock defeats by West Indies and Bangladesh, they are still unbeaten in their past nine Test series.
But while their struggling batting line-up was bailed out by Matt Renshaw across the first two days of the first Test in Durban, they took control over South Africa on day three in an all-too familiar way.
Nine years after they first appeared together as Australia's bowling quartet, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon produced their latest relentless performance to dismiss South Africa for 284. There was even some magic from Steve Smith thrown in too.
Cummins took three wickets, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon two apiece, in doing so brushing off any doubts about their effectiveness at the start of a run of Tests against the world Test champions, in-form New Zealand, India and England.
How Australia's quartet turned the screw on South Africa
At 82-1 in response to Australia's 390, South Africa appeared well in the Test.
Australia's bowlers searched for early swing and Aiden Markram and David Bedingham countered with a second-wicket partnership which progressed at almost 4.5 runs per over.
It was then, at the 20-over mark, captain Cummins reverted to Australia's tried and tested - Lyon one end, the quicks rotating at the other.
Having bowled 34% of their deliveries full in the first 20 overs, Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins dragged back their lengths. There were only 19 deliveries pitched fuller than six metres between the 20th and 60th overs.
With deliveries easy to hit scarce, Markram and Bedingham attempted forced back-foot drives and edged to slip for 37 and 49 respectively.
Wiaan Mulder was caught in two minds and bounced out by Cummins. Tristan Stubbs top-edged the Australia captain to fine leg.
In Australia's first innings, Renshaw, who ground out a superb 190, faced 52 deliveries pitched as short and played a pull or hook shot to four of them. He scored runs with only one of those shots - when he had 176 runs to his name and had faced 368 balls.
The contrast to Renshaw's application could not have been greater.
Six overs after Stubbs was caught, Marco Jansen, who had struck six fours in quickly reaching 26, also tried to pull Hazlewood off a fuller length and was tamely caught at mid-off.
The quality of the bowling and fact the Proteas are playing their first Test since November were other factors in South Africa's slide.
Smith soars back to number one
At the other end, off-spinner Lyon bowled 19 overs at less than three runs per over.
The 39-year-old had a more worn pitch to utilise than South Africa's spinners and found significantly more turn and threat.
He also had the sprawling Steve Smith to his advantage.
Both of Smith's catches off Lyon, first to dismiss Temba Bavuma and then Kyle Verreynne, were feats of anticipation. He saw both right-handers shape to reverse sweep, gambled and clung on at close range. The first was good. The one-handed second was spectacular.
In between, Smith's leaping catch at second slip after Cummins found Bedingham's edge took the 37-year-old back above Joe Root as the non-wicketkeeper with the most catches in Test history on 223.
While he ended the day with three more catches than Root, he still has a catch percentage about 77%, which sits below the format average.
He creates, and occasionally drops, chances such as these - chances others would not have created.
Pace cartel appears as good as ever
The result is Australia's fabled foursome now have 607 wickets in Tests in which they have played as a quartet.
The next most successful bowling four-pronged attack is James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Ben Stokes and Moeen Ali, who took 415 wickets in their 31 Tests together for England.
Much has been made of Australia's ageing side and a perceived lack of succession planning.
At 37, Starc is the oldest of the three quicks but his average pace of 141.21km/h in 2026 is higher than any of his past three years. He is also averaging his most swing in a calendar year since 2015.
The concern for Australia comes when they are not fit, with Hazlewood having missed all five of last winter's Ashes Tests and Cummins four.
Australia's issue right now is keeping each of their quartet on the field, because they appear as good as ever.
At 33-0, Australia lead South Africa by 139 runs.
Even with bad light halting play early again, they should have the time to press home an advantage across the Test's final two days.

A student hated reading for years. Her podcast explores finding the right diagnosis
LONG ISLAND, N.Y. — Cora Walsh walks home from middle school every day. It's only a few tree-lined blocks in Rockville Centre on Long Island, but the movement helps clear her head of the school day. She probably thinks about how the brain works more than most seventh-graders.
"I want to be a doctor," she says. "And I want to go to Princeton and major in neuroscience."
Her fascination started a few years ago when she was struggling to figure out what was happening in her own head.
"It's kind of confusing what it is like in my brain," she says. All she knew back then was that reading was hard. Even when she spent more time working on it than her friends, she could never reach their level.
Like millions of Americans, Cora has dyslexia, but it took her almost five years to get the correct diagnosis.
Her podcast about the journey to understanding her own mind is the grand prize winner for middle school in this year's NPR Student Podcast Challenge. "Dyslexia and MEE" was chosen from nearly 1,500 submissions from 42 states and the District of Columbia.
"I feel really excited," Cora says about her victory. Her parents, who spent the whole journey right by her side, are thrilled too.
"This is a kid that works so hard and has such a good attitude," says her mom, Emily Johnson. "I'm so proud of her."
Finding the right learning style
Cora has come a long way. She has received tutoring for her dyslexia for two years now.
Her podcast takes the listener along to one of her lessons. She sounds out words over Zoom, and her tutor gives her feedback and tips. They don't move too fast, making sure Cora really understands something before moving on.
It can be tedious, but her hard work outside the classroom is starting to pay off.
"I think I'm a better reader now, and I enjoy it a lot more," she says. "I feel more comfortable reading bigger books, but not too big!"
Her mom says that this summer marked a turning point: She saw her daughter reading the first book in the Hunger Games series.
"She would pick it up for fun, and she would go read to [her pet] rabbit. Or we were traveling this summer, and she read on the train," Johnson says. "I mean, it's the first time that's ever happened."
It was a winding road to get to this point, but Cora and her parents are excited to see where it goes. Winning NPR's national competition is another bright spot.
"I'm kind of just proud of myself that I overcame this hard, annoying thing," she says. "And proud of myself that I created something really cool and interesting that everyone can listen to."
Cora hopes that her podcast might help dyslexia feel a little less scary for listeners and maybe even reach younger students who are still trying to figure out their own learning styles.
"I would say: Always try your hardest, and don't sell yourself short," she says. "I think trying is … the best thing you can do."
Cora Walsh is still trying: She just checked out that second Hunger Games book from the library.

Before the 2017 ODI World Cup, journalist-turned-broadcaster Gaurav Kalra led a media training session for the women’s cricket team in Mumbai. In an ecosystem rife with clichés like ‘trust the process’ and ‘control the controllables’, Kalra was tasked with helping the women get comfortable with media engagements, pushing them to be honest about their stories and journeys so their own lives inspire at least one other.
Kalra remembers Harmanpreet eagerly raising her hand to say, “ Sir, aap bol to rahe ho ki apni story bataon, par koi sunna hi nahin chahta” (Sir, you’re asking us to tell our stories, but no one wants to listen).
Life for the ecosystem nine years on looks starkly different. India has become a force to reckon with, taking its place among the game’s competitive (and not just monetary) elite. It enters tournaments among the favourites. Its players are household names now, not just in India, but also in pockets abroad where some feature regularly on the franchise circuit.
The roots of this new era of the women’s game can be traced back to this eager 28-year-old (relatively) newly appointed full-time T20I captain. She forced people to stop and listen, eventually becoming the protagonist of the vertical’s most cherished chapter (so far).
Taking space
“Sardaran hai. Ladne ki thaakat toh uski khoon mein hai” (She’s a sardarni, that fighting spirit is in her blood) - this is former chief selector of the Indian national team Neetu David’s first adjective for Harmanpreet. Fighting is a three-act phenomenon in the life of this maverick from Moga, Punjab.
First, there was the fight to play.
Young Harmanpreet was a sports buff, playing anything and everything she could. She even tried hockey, where the stick and ball ultimately became part of a game of cricket, much to her school teacher’s chagrin. “ Bohot mushkil se bacchon ko cricket se hockey tak le aaye hai hum. Aap yeh na karein (It’s taken a lot to get kids to pivot from cricket to hockey. Don’t do this now),” she once cheekily recalled.
“ Pehle hi dekha ki jo log six marte hain, unki bohot value hai (It was evident to me very early on that those who hit sixes, their value is a lot higher),” Harmanpreet said of her formative days in the sport. Her coach Kamaldeesh Pal Singh Sodhi spotted heroics of the sort watching her smack the ball while playing with a group of boys. He didn’t know if she was a boy or a girl, given her long locks were tied up in the trademark sikh high bun.
Young Harman only knew the bat and ball in her hands. She knew not of any pathways of progress, or what would come of her life should she stick with cricket and nothing else. The 80s and 90s had no women’s cricket on television, so there were no ambitions for her to soak off a screen.
But Sodhi did and he saw what Harmanpreet would mean for the sport if she could extrapolate the raw spunk he saw into enduring legend. So did her father Harmandar Singh Bhullar. Given his own sporting success at state level, he wanted his daughter to go past him and clinch the honour of donning an India jersey some day. All when his daughter did not even know of the existence of the women’s side.
Sodhi built a women’s team around Harmanpreet and she repaid the faith by eventually building a new culture of excellence which ultimately led her and her pack to the sport’s biggest podium.
Simple pleasures
Former India international Soniya Dabir’s earliest memory of Harmanpreet is one from the manual - a six she hit in the U-19 inter-zonal match in Pune. She was the local manager then.
“That was the first time I saw a player at that level hit such a long six. She could smack sixes at will and the difference was immediately apparent in the stance, the backlift… She decides ki abhi aane wala hai and we prepare,” Soniya says.
In a domestic Challenger series, the pair were teammates and eventually even became roommates during the 2010 T20 World Cup in the West Indies.
That Harmanpreet was naive, untouched by the burdens of spotlight and just grateful to make cricket her life’s fulcrum. She would happily eat the same food regularly, diligently follow workout regimes on repeat and also, unfortunately for Soniya, play the same song on loop for days on end.
“I would keep a lot of songs loaded on my phone, but hers had just one song called Tere Liye. For almost 12-16 hours, she would play it. I had enough eventually. There were no Hindi channels in the Windies at the time.”
“She had a routine she followed strictly. She prayed everyday, she did her things a certain way. It stopped for nothing, no one and no result. She used to be able to switch off really well. Kuch carry forward nahi hota tha pichle match ka (Nothing carried forward from one match to another) . That was a good thing, to take each day for what it is.” Fifteen years later, that very trait would help Harmanpreet bhangra her way towards the ODI World Cup trophy before a manic crowd at the D.Y. Patil Stadium in Navi Mumbai on a dewy November night.
Legendary Indian legspinner Neetu David, who was the chair of selectors when India reached the One-Day zenith, fondly remembers the Punjaban who took on Railways in the domestic circuit.
“Back then, the Indian Railways was as good as the Indian national side,” Neetu says. “The way she fearlessly tackled our bowlers and as good as led the batting effort made us feel like this girl would go places and maybe even captain India someday.”
After getting employed by the Western Railways, Harmanpreet – who now can’t venture out into any street in India without being mobbed – would sprint through streets to catch the Mumbai local, shuttling between work and training at Bandra Kurla Complex. She unabashedly admits to sitting on Diana Edulji’s head to get exemptions sanctioned so her stomach wouldn’t kill her heart’s desires.
Diana’s condition was clear: help Railways win the domestic tournament first. The rest eventually fell into place.
Unending hunger
From here, Harmanpreet realised just how much ‘change’ would come to define her chapter in Indian cricket. She moved from the Railways to Punjab Police to be able to be closer to home. The Women’s Big Bash League came calling in 2016 when she became the first Indian to feature in an overseas league, having signed with Sydney Thunder.
It reinforced a love affair with the systems Down Under that began in the late 2000s when she and M.D. Thirushkamini were sent for an exposure trip there.
Former India captain Purnima Rau, who had selected her for that tour in 2007, took charge as head coach in 2014, two years after Harmanpreet had stepped up in the absence of an injured Mithali Raj and Jhulan Goswami to lead India to the first of what would eventually be four Asia Cup triumphs.
“She was a very raw, energetic kid who was very hungry for knowledge. That ambition was evident in her eyes,” she says.

Bring up Harman and her thoughts go back to an earnest 26-year-old who stayed back for advice after the dressing room had cleared post a series win against New Zealand.
“I am usually the last one to get out of the dressing room or the team bus so I can check if players have left anything behind. One such day, I found Harman standing there. She held my hand and said, “Ma’am, I want to do much better than what I’ve done. What should I do?”” Purnima remembers being asked.
She recalls copious notes on technique, on how she urged Harman to be audacious on the front foot and tweak her elbow placement to extend her field of strokemaking.
In Purnima, the evangelist Harmanpreet would eventually become for Indian cricket found her first believer. Both agreed on one fundamental element - India was talented enough and gutsy enough to win not one ICC title, but three. This was without the Women’s Premier League, little to no media attention and a system that made it a point to tell the girls they were good, but just not good enough.
A disappointing home T20 World Cup campaign, where India sank in the group stage, meant India found itself increasingly jaded by Mithali’s steady, risk-free brand of leadership. Harmanpreet’s aggressive, unbending style of batting was already turning heads. It wasn’t long before Mithali made way for her deputy in the shortest format.
But all of that would be eclipsed by a superhuman effort in Derby in the 2017 ODI World Cup, a monstrous knock that would lay the foundations of ‘Harmonster’ as she would come to be called, and a particular penchant for treating the world’s most decorated and dangerous side - Australia - like a puppy slinging around a rope toy.
Harman vs the odds
That unbeaten 171, which both made and, many times, broke Harmanpreet has to be among the most documented knocks in the history of the game. Like a raging Spanish bull, a red-faced and hungry Harmanpreet hacked Australia down.
For Purnima, however, it was Harman’s effort 149 days prior to that knock that has her respect.
“Everytime I’ve coached a side, I gave my captains a book when they won a series. Mithali got seven books from me. Harman got one, for the ICC qualifier before the 2017 World Cup. One by Shiv Khera,” she remembers.
Chasing 245 for victory against South Africa in the final, India needed eight runs off the last two balls. Harmanpreet, the stand-in skipper, smacked the ball over the midwicket ropes and then ran two to send her dugout into a tizzy at the P. Sara Oval in the heart of Colombo.
“She fought with the last wicket (Rajeshwari Gayakwad). That six she hit sums up everything about her. Forget her captaincy. She did well, that’s a given. But for me, as a player, tagda thi wahan pe (She was tough),” Purnima declares.
2017’s big high and equally ravenous low came and went, but what remained was the adulation and then fascination of the general public, all waiting for the next big news from this bunch.
Unfortunately, the squad served rotten meat to vultures waiting to feast and from singlehandedly sculpting a memorable pièce de résistance, Harman suddenly became the face of one of the biggest controversies to rock the system. A bitter tussle for power which involved leaks and snide comments and much in between saw Harmanpreet and Mithali on two sides of what looked like an irreparably torn national side.
The 2018 T20 World Cup became the battleground.
Facing England in the semifinal, skipper Harman made a temerarious decision to drop Mithali for the knockout fixture. Mithali had batted in just two games in that campaign, scoring 50s on both occasions. She picked up a knee injury and didn’t feature in India’s 48-run group stage win against Australia. Harman defended her decision saying she wanted to stick to a winning combination.
Things, however, didn’t go as planned, with India folding for 112 in 19.2 overs, its last eight wickets falling for just 23 runs. England didn’t blink as it sealed an eight-wicket win.
“Whatever we decided, we decided for the team. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, no regrets. I’m proud of the way my girls played through the tournament,” she said defiantly then. But the apple cart had been blown to smithereens.
The fallout of this incident added to an already tumultuous time for the side, with two coaches – Purnima and Tushar Arothe – finding themselves out of the scheme of things rather unceremoniously, documented to be at the behest of the players. Ramesh Powar, earlier an ally to Harmanpreet, was also shown the door, not once but twice. W.V. Raman, too, was not retained, and with no explanation.
Team first
Raman unenviably walked into a broken dressing room masquerading as a team.
“Harmanpreet was obviously hurt, and she felt she was blamed for no fault of hers about a lot of things that happened before. It’s very easy for us to live in the past. I sat them both down and said I didn’t intend to go back there. Let’s try and start with a clean slate.”
He pushed Harman to be large-hearted and focus on the time she has to leave her imprint behind as captain and player.
“I told her that she needed to try and make an identity for herself. Of course, she had been doing that as a player but for her to make an impact as captain, she couldn’t afford to be distracted by the past or by how people outside were trying to box her in. At some point, I even read an interview where she said she contemplated leaving the game. Fortunately, she carried on,” he says.
Harman was not one for diplomacy and Raman cites that as one of her attributes he values the most.
“A lot of things have been said about her for the simple reason she just spoke her mind. She did not have the finesse like some of her predecessors to try and convey things in such a manner. No matter what the implications were, no matter what people might think about her decisions, she came across as somebody who did things the way she felt she needed to do. Perhaps, that’s not something people always look at kindly. But that is Harman for you. It’s always good for people to be different, or the world would be a very boring place,” he shrugs.
The musical chairs in leadership positions is an Indian cricket staple, particularly in the women’s game. Purnima remembers how friends quickly became foes as selectors rolled in and rolled out ‘one series captains’ in their blind quest for results, which is why she underlines that permanence as the enduring legacy of both these players.
“Stability is important for any captain,” Mithali says. “But a long tenure also has to come with accountability. You have to keep assessing whether the team is progressing and whether the captain is still the right person for the next phase.”
“Harman had that time, and there were different phases to her tenure, good and difficult. But that continuity allowed her to shape the team in her own way. That is ultimately the value of giving a captain a long rope,” she adds.
Breeding belief
In the eight years that passed, Harmanpreet first defined her (in capital letters) side as one that could enter tournaments as favourites, that could give Australia and England a run for their money.
India’s march to the final in the 2020 T20 World Cup was imperious. The campaign was propped on the captain’s unflinching faith in the prodigious abilities of a 16-year-old Shafali Verma. However, like it had many times before, India’s ambitious castles were watered down by the mighty Aussies, with nearly 90,000 people watching at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

“It would have been the perfect gift if we were to win on that day because it was played on her birthday. That was not to be, unfortunately. It would have kept the side going through the COVID-19 pandemic which followed for a year and a half right after. That was a challenging phase,” Raman reminisces.
“Maybe it was the early stages of her captaincy or the fact that India was so near yet so far all the time… That victory could have perhaps proved to the world that they’re capable of winning a World Cup, that she is capable of winning a World Cup. And that’s something that she wanted for the team to do because India was always looked upon as an entity that didn’t have the wherewithal to win the World Cup. She wanted to change that. A lot of things were riding on that particular final. So it was a bit frustrating.”
This was around the time calls for a women’s Indian Premier League were growing increasingly louder. Losses saw even board officials lament about not having sufficient talent to stage a league. Harman credits former BCCI secretary Jay Shah for breaking that cycle, breaking the unending chase the women’s team was set on to first achieve before having the guts to ask for foundational sporting architecture.
Another opportunity presented itself in 2023. Once again, Australia stood in India’s way and would eventually push India back like a bully cordoning off privileged territory. An unfortunate run out involving Harmanpreet and some stinging yet nonchalant criticism from new captain Alyssa Healy triggered the makings of a memorable rivalry to spice up a vertical bedrotting in the lull of Meg Lanning – its most decorated commander – shockingly calling time on her international career.
The group stage exit in the 2024 T20 World Cup, by their own admission, hurt the side the most. Systems were changing. The Women’s Premier League had turned two. Harmanpreet and Smriti Mandhana, her eventual successor, had won the first two editions. With new coach Amol Muzumdar, experiments and fresh perspectives were the Women in Blue’s oxygen. But the side returned from the arid Emirati deserts with their tails tucked between their legs.
A desolate Harmanpreet, spacing out at the post-match presentation after yet another gutsy fight against Australia, became the image of that dismal campaign. That perhaps explains why the tears were so unaesthetically raw in 2025, when India overcame the mighty Aussies before a raucous home crowd in the semifinal in Navi Mumbai.
When Jemimah Rodrigues and Amanjot Kaur brought India home, Harmanpreet sat with trenches for creaselines on her forehead in the dugout, Smriti hugging her as they saw victory inch closer. As Smriti led the entourage out to embrace a tired and emotionally broken Jemimah, Harmanpreet roared away into the dugout, with Deepti Sharma and Muzumdar enveloping her from either side.
“I would actually say the World Cup victory. For me, that will define her captaincy more than anything else. Indian women’s cricket had waited a long time for that ODI World Cup, and Harman was the captain when it finally happened. There were different phases to her tenure, but that achievement will naturally stand out. That is a significant part of what she leaves behind as captain.”Mithali Raj
She might have enjoyed one single song on loop for days on end all those years ago in the West Indies, but she was tired of the same old taunts, disbelief and the “go back to the kitchen” jibes.
History repeated itself.
Once, Harman validated the aspirations her father and coach saw for her. On October 30, 2025, Harman’s team realised hers. The coronation a few days later, the unquestionable cementing of her legacy, may have taken some doing, but was a mere formality.
India’s own angry, young woman
Amitabh Bachchan popularised the trope of the angry, young man in Indian cinema, allegorical of the mood of the nation then. Harman became that symbol for the women’s game. Remember how she rained down on poor 19-year-old Deepti when she almost ran Harman, then on 98, out. Evidently, Harman was not hunting the ton, but the win. The pair hugged and made up soon after and India clinched that epochal win.
That same Deepti she reduced to tears in Derby had Harman’s complete backing at Lord’s in 2022, when she ran out Charlie Dean at the non-striker’s end which helped India seal 3-0 ODI series sweep.
When asked, Harman snapped back at why the other nine wickets weren’t as interesting to talk about before unequivocally stating, “I will back my player. She’s not done something which isn’t in the rules. It shows our awareness.”
Little under a year later, Bangladesh faced Harmanpreet’s wrath enough for her to become a yardstick for bad behaviour for the system there. Stumps were smashed, nasty things were said, umpires were accused of favouring the home side and a prompt two-match ban was slapped on the Indian skipper too.
Harman, consistency personified, quietly served the ban without an ounce of regret. “I don’t think I said anything wrong to any player or any person. I just said what happened on the field. I don’t regret anything,” she said later.
That unbridled anger is something Raman remembers from his early days with the mercurial (now) former Indian skipper.
“In the run-up to the 2020 World Cup, there was a murmur in the side. The girls were a little scared, a bit peeved by Harman giving everyone a piece of her mind. One of our warm-up games was rained out, so I sat her down and began talking about a couple of other captains. Harman knows me to be direct and was a little puzzled by why I was beating around the bush and asked me in so many words.
“I then told her that different captains have different methodologies but this cannot be a system of top-down management all the time. It might not always work. She needed to do what was possible to get the best out of her teammates.
“Apart from the World Cup title, she’s won so many Test matches for India as captain. That’s an equally good record. India, for the longest time, didn’t play Tests. It’s not easy to win these against England and Australia when you’re leading a side in all three formats. Winning that Test match at Lord’s after exiting the T20 World Cup, where they had to sit and watch other teams get through the end and push for a win in the Lord’s Test, was incredible. Credit to her for that record too!”Soniya Dabir
“I suggested that if she wanted to let loose, we could nominate a player for every game to be her punching bag (not literally, of course) and we’ll get on with it. She slept over it and came back back and said there was merit in what I said. Things then suddenly changed. She hardly said anything on the field.”
“Players came raising issues with that too and all I said was, ‘You can’t complain about everything.’ Harman controlled was better than her letting loose,” he quips.
Legacy and a wheel that refuses to break
A year is a long time. India soaked in the hysteria of a World title far too many thought would never arrive. Soon, it was time for another World Cup, but a disastrous campaign in 2026 and another group stage exit followed.
Harmanpreet Kaur’s captaincy record: 211 games across formats
A now 37-year-old Harman, with diminishing returns with the bat, could not fight the pendulum swinging towards Smriti, long understood to be India’s captain-in-waiting and in the form of her life. The 30-year-old growing increasingly vocal of her ability and willingness to lead the nation only fanned a flame that needed no help spreading.
That image from 2025, the camaraderie from the ones before that, all seemingly made way for subtle distances that rabid fanbases of both players frothed at the mouth to blow up online.
In early October, images emerged on an Assamese news portal of Harman and Smriti in Guwahati with BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia. A day later, Harmanpreet announced her decision to step down from Indian captaincy.
This is a woman who jumped up for the World Cup-sealing catch in the final with an injury in her left knee. The same woman who played that 171 knock with a dislocated finger had to be held back by the team doctor from venturing out for the second innings despite severe dehydration. Somehow, though, the words of her resignation felt loaded with far more pain.
ALSO READ: India wins first gold medal of Asian Games 2026 after women’s cricket team beats Sri Lanka in final
There is an interview with Harmanpreet where she describes how the balance and make of the bat don’t matter, but the grip does. If it doesn’t feel like she has full control, it ruins the full experience. Now, the grip has been yanked away.
For a Punjabi girl growing up on a sporting diet, the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics was the perfect carrot to push her ageing and hurting body through a few more sporting summers for that one coveted gold medal. She comes from a hockey and athletics hotbed and a State that values Olympic golds like divinity. She still has a shot at it, but not as the bird leading the migration.
She won the fight to play and the fight for collective belief. But she couldn’t prolong the fight to lead.
Paisa and pyaar
Harmanpreet’s journey cannot be detached from the financial whirlwind that has embraced the women’s ecosystem. Noopur Kashyap, her manager, has seen Harman’s “value’ grow into a bankable commercial face for big brands.
“In 2017, women’s cricket was still emerging. Viewership was still quite limited. We began with digital campaigns so she could at least be seen,” Noopur explains.
Harman got a lot of webinars around the lockdowns and that gave her team the confidence that people want to hear what she has to say. That translated to on-ground events and activations and eventually to big brand deals, the arc hitting its peak right after the 2025 ODI World Cup. When Navi Mumbai woke up to continue ringing in India’s triumph barely five hours after the final, Harman had already been named brand ambassador for real estate firm Omaxe Ltd. And that was just the start of more to come.
Harman loves a photoshoot but the larger world of brand engagements was alien territory for her for quite a while.
“For her to be at a shoot for eight hours would be draining, with the lights, arrangement and people. But send her to a cricket field for as long and she’d be totally fine. That shift came about with the WPL. It taught players to balance training and matches with shoots thanks to how advertising and appearances are coded into franchise operations,” she explains.
Noopur stepped in for Harman at a time when the math involved in being a ‘brand’ in sports left her utterly confused. The fear of being misled or cheated was there too and since then, Noopur has been Harman’s firewall. Over the years, a girl who was once mistaken for a boy now loved seeing herself on posters, cover shoots and ad films.
Noopur sees this next phase of her career as an opportunity for Harman to finally make her life’s favourite thing – cricket – about herself.
“Harman’s never been one to have a big circle. You won’t see her doing dinners, outings etc very often. She has missed out on all this and wants to experience it all. She’s drawn her legacy. She also wants to be more socially available. Captaincy and its responsibilities came with several personal restrictions. Even going home was a challenge. She lives away from her parents to be close to an airport so she can report for duty anytime. Those are things she will be able to address now,” she says.
In the 2025 final, after a job well done, Harmanpreet running to her father and Bhullar lifting her up like she was five again was among the unforgettable frames of that triumph. It was anything but just the adrenaline from the night, Noopur suggests.
“Harman comes from a very simple, non-city background. She wants time with her family. Her parents are getting older. She watched her sister’s wedding on video call. Both her siblings stay abroad. She doesn’t talk about all this but it really matters. It’s why that hug with her dad after the final means so much. That’s what she misses.”
Epilogue
This exercise of documenting Harman the captain might seem like an end-of-career tribute piece. It’s perhaps inevitable considering how much of Harman’s life in this sport has gone into taking the lead in some form.
“Captaincy suited her. She wanted things to happen all the time and wanted the team to win. It suited her personality and her mindset. She’s been a captain all along. She now has a chance to show what kind of a leader she can be. It’s time to create an ever bigger legacy,” Raman says.
“Captaincy does add pressure, because you are thinking about the team even when you are batting. But I wouldn’t put Harman’s batting inconsistency entirely down to captaincy. She has always had periods of outstanding batting and periods when she hasn’t been as consistent, even before she became the all-format captain,” Mithali explains.
“What captaincy does is add another layer to that. When you are not scoring, you are answering questions about both your batting and your leadership. Now she doesn’t have that additional responsibility. So she has the opportunity to concentrate on her batting and let her performances speak for her,” she adds.
Harman has been the genesis of the rule of fitness and form in this ecosystem and now stands consumed by the very frameworks she cemented in place.
She was part of a side that is infamously reported to have pushed for a male coach – which led to Purnima’s sacking. But she is now also part of a franchise setup — Mumbai Indians — that has always championed women in the coaching staff, from Charlotte Edwards and Lisa Keightley to India’s own Jhulan Goswami and Devika Palshikar.
It’s been a long vigil for an unapologetic servant of the game, who now finally has the space and reason to fire up this next chapter just for herself.
As one of her early coaches told Harman (as documented in Sidhanta Patnaik and Karunya Keshav’s “ The Fire Burns Blue”), “No bowler can get you out unless you want to get out. Everything is in the mind.”
Chardi Kala, Harmanpreet.

Yemeni attack on Riyadh airport kills 12 and injures over 300 as Houthi-Saudi war escalates
It was the third strike on the capital’s airport this week

At least 12 people were killed and over 300 injured following a strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday – the third attack this week – as Yemen’s Houthi forces stepped up their campaign against the kingdom.
The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the casualties, saying four Saudis, two Bangladeshis and a person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan, and Egypt were killed.
At the latest count, officials said 309 people were injured.
Hospitals were overwhelmed with casualties brought in by ambulance and helicopter, according to people briefed on the situation. Some of the injured were reported to be in critical condition.
The attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in almost a decade, struck without warning, as no alert was issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. Two earlier attacks this week targeting King Khalid international airport left four people dead and severely damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac.
The fatal strikes highlight vulnerabilities in the country’s defence capabilities while it conducts an air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen. A Saudi-led military coalition promised to retaliate.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni forces backed by it claim to have launched hundreds of strikes against targets in Houthi areas in recent weeks. The Houthis say the air raids have killed civilians, including women and children.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said operations at the Riyadh airport were temporarily suspended on Saturday and all flights were diverted. The airport serves a city of about eight million.
Following the strike, the head of the Houthi media office posted on X that the movement had "shut down Riyadh international airport".
The Houthis warned commercial airliners to avoid Saudi airspace, declaring it a military operations zone after the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched an offensive on Monday.
In the US, president Donald Trump was asked by reporters if Washington intended to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen.
"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio condemned the raids, saying they "demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life”.
An eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then several casualties lying injured on the ground inside the facility. More than a dozen ambulances were seen heading towards the building, with video verified by Reuters showing emergency vehicles at the scene.
An injured passenger told Reuters they saw an object flying through the sky outside the terminal before part of the ceiling collapsed near a departure gate.
Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015, leading an Arab coalition to attempt to drive the Houthis from the capital Sanaa after the rebels had seized the city the previous year.
The war resulted in a devastating stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and starvation.
Saudi Arabia subsequently signed a 2022 agreement with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.
That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a rapid Houthi advance that seized the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el Mandeb from Saudi-backed forces. The Saudi-supported forces launched a new offensive this week to reclaim that territory, making slow progress even as Houthi forces placed Taiz, the country's third-largest city, under siege.
Flight-tracking service flightradar24 showed that all incoming flights to Riyadh were redirected or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one stage.
Houthi strikes earlier in the week had already driven several airlines to suspend or cancel flights to the Saudi capital, shortly before it was scheduled to host major energy and investment conferences.
Organisers of those events stated prior to Saturday's attack that they would proceed as planned.

The visuals in the footage have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer.
On Oct. 4, a social media user posted a video purportedly depicting a man leading a group of Arkansas farmers in prayer, asking "baby Jesus" for "more Mexicans" to replace the "Mexicans we had deported" to save their farms.
The user posted the footage to Facebook (archived) and Instagram (archived). The audio seemingly shows the man leading the prayer saying:
Dear Baby Jesus, please help us. We're losing our farms. We know we sent all the Mexicans away. Dear Lord, please send us some more Mexicans to replace the Mexicans we had deported. We're going to lose our farms; please, Baby Jesus and all things holy. Amen.
The clip spread amid numerous reports of rising prices and trade wars impacting U.S. farmers.
In short, the visuals in the video have an authentic origin, but the audio has been edited to significantly change the meaning of the prayer. Therefore, we rate the audio as fake.
The authentic footage originates from a broadcast by KATV 7, a TV news station in Little Rock, Arkansas. The channel posted the segment to YouTube on Sept. 2, 2025 (archived), more than a year earlier than when the edited clip was circulating. It shows hundreds of Arkansas farmers in a school gymnasium seeking the federal government's help regarding their financial struggles.
At about 2:24, the video cuts to a man leading the farmers in prayer. He can be heard saying:
Farmers, in my opinion, dear Lord, and it's only my opinion, are closer to you than anyone else on this Earth because we deal with your Earth every day. Dear Lord, we're hurting, dear Lord. We can't help what's happened to us.
According to KATV 7's article about the event, also published on Sept. 2, 2025, the farmer then said, "We need help, dear Lord."
Another piece of evidence that the "more Mexicans" iteration of the clip is edited is the quality of its audio. The prayer in the edited version is sharp, clear and lacking an echo. Inside a school gymnasium, the audio of the farmers praying should, in reality, feature an echo, like the man's voice does in the original footage.
Both Facebook and Instagram identified the audio as original to Aaron Beltrán, the person who appeared to first post the edited clip on both platforms.
Snopes reached out to Beltrán to ask whether he originally edited and posted the manipulated video, if the voice is his own and if the content was meant to be satirical. We will update this story if we receive a reply.

The newspaper subscription rate in Japan fell below 50% for the first time, a survey has found.
According to the fiscal 2026 survey by the Japan Press Research Institute, the proportion of respondents who have monthly subscriptions for newspapers dropped 0.3 percentage point year on year to 49.8%, the first reading below 50% since the survey started in 2008, when the share stood at 88.6%. The survey results were announced Saturday.
The latest survey, the 19th of its kind, was conducted between July 17 and Aug. 16, covering 5,000 people age 18 or over across the country and receiving valid response from 2,676.
The share of respondents who get news from newspapers in a given week also slipped below 50% for the first time, at 49.7%, coming in fourth in a ranking of media sources. Television programs of commercial broadcasters ranked first, at 84.2%, followed by the internet, at 74.4%, and TV programs of public broadcaster NHK, 69.7%. Radio programs ranked fifth, at 27.6%.
The latest survey asked questions about the Cabinet of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who took office in October 2025, for the first time.
The approval rate for the Cabinet stood at 62.3%, thanks to strong support from younger generations.
By policy, 50.1% said they support her Cabinet’s diplomacy toward the United States, while 52.6% disapproved of its measures to address inflation.
Although 65.6% said that they are interested in the issue of revision of the Constitution, about 50% said they are not sure whether the supreme law should be amended or not.
The proportion of respondents in favor of constitutional revision came to 31.2%, while that of those against ws 15.3%.
Asked about items deemed appropriate for constitutional revision, with multiple answers allowed, 32.6%, the largest group, said that the existence of the Self-Defense Forces should be added to the Constitution.

Delhi braced for a second day of youth protests demanding the resignation of India’s election chief on Sunday, as a court ordered the release of the “cockroach” movement founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and two other senior leaders.
Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), and the other leaders were detained when their plane landed in Delhi on Saturday, as the movement planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi.
Indian authorities on Saturday deployed a sweeping crackdown across Delhi and detained thousands of protesters as the youth “cockroach” movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fuelled anger at the prime minister, Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.
Reuters reported police detained more than 2,000 people to thwart Saturday’s protest. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel continued to be deployed across the city on Sunday although metro stations reopened and mobile internet services were back up.
Most detained on the first day of protests were released on Saturday night, police said.
Opposition parties and critics of Modi’s government criticised what they said was the high-handed use of force against the protesters.
The UN human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests.
UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said: “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled.” He urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed.
India’s foreign ministry said the UN’s approach was “selective” and its statement constituted “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.
The protests are calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), which has been in power for more than 12 years.
Sporadic protests have been going on across India since the Indian Express newspaper in late September reported Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, registration procedures and digital systems.
The commission says differing views are normal in internal deliberations, and has denied favouring any party.
Modi’s BJP has accused groups opposed to it of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Election Commission data cited by the party shows about 130 million names, more than the population of Japan, have been deleted from electoral rolls during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated and 30 million who could not be traced.
The BJP and the commission deny allegations of manipulation, although opposition parties say Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The “cockroach” movement, which began as an online satire, rapidly evolved into a pressure group, with street protests against exam paper leaks culminating in the resignation of Modi’s education minister.
The CJP has called its protests against Kumar “Season 2” on its social media handles, and said it would not stop until India’s election system was reformed.

How to Craft in Anime Zero
Once you collect the required materials through quests, story, or Anime Zero codes, follow these steps to craft accessories:

- Select Crafting to teleport to the crafting area.
- Find Yugi, the Forger NPC, and open the crafting menu.
- Select the Craft tab.
- Choose an accessory from the list and select Quick Craft to create the accessory.

That is everything you need to know about crafting in Anime Zero. Did you create any accessories that are featured in the S tier of the Anime Zero tier list? Let us know in the comments.
Where do you craft accessories in Anime Zero?
You can craft accessories by visiting Yugi, the Forger NPC, in the Crafting area. Open the Craft tab, select an accessory, collect its required materials, and click Quick Craft.
How do you get crafting materials in Anime Zero?
You can obtain crafting materials by playing Story Mode, progressing through Infinite Mode, and exploring areas for breakable objects. You can also buy materials with Coins from the Material Shop or convert existing materials into the items you need.

‘System can’t be honest when you win and rigged when you lose’: 124 ex-bureaucrats defend Election Commission, SIR exercise
Defending SIR, the ex-civil servants described it as a necessary process to maintain accurate electoral rolls by identifying deceased voters, duplicate entries
After 42 former judges raised concerns over what they described as a sustained campaign against the Election Commission of India (ECI), 124 former bureaucrats have written an open letter defending the poll body amid allegations of irregularities in the electoral process.
In their letter to the citizens of India, the 124 former IAS, IFS and allied services officers said the country’s electoral system had undergone a significant transformation from the era of booth capturing, ballot box stuffing and election-related violence. They highlighted safeguards such as polling agents, the sealing of electronic voting machines (EVMs), strong-room security and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) verification.
Also Read | Delhi protest: Right-wing groups assault protesters, journalists amid heavy security deployment
The letter comes amid protests in Delhi and Mumbai against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of electoral irregularities.
“A system cannot be honest when you win and rigged when you lose,” the letter stated, according to ANI, noting that the party ruling at the Centre had lost several state elections under the same Election Commission. The officers also referred to the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, in which the ruling party failed to secure an outright majority on its own.
Defending the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, the former civil servants described it as a necessary process to maintain accurate electoral rolls by identifying deceased voters, duplicate entries and individuals who had permanently shifted residence.
They also maintained that the SIR process included safeguards to address concerns over wrongful exclusion, including the publication of draft electoral rolls, opportunities to file claims and objections, hearings and provisions for appeals.
“Questioning is every citizen’s right. Proving is the accuser’s duty,” the officers said, adding that unsubstantiated allegations could weaken public confidence in democratic institutions and the electoral process.

Meanwhile, in a separate open letter, 42 former judges and retired constitutional officeholders said they had no political brief and were speaking out because “silence is no longer a neutral choice”. They alleged that constitutional bodies were facing attacks driven by political interests and warned of the consequences of undermining public trust in the country’s democratic institutions.
“Our concern is grave. India's constitutional bodies are under sustained attack. The Election Commission of India stands at the centre of this assault,” the letter read.

Pope Leo will undergo surgery to remove a nodule on his lung
Pontiff to undergo surgery in coming days, with an expected recovery time of a week, Vatican said
Pope Leo announced Sunday he will undergo surgery in the coming days to remove a nodular lesion on his lung that was recently discovered during medical checks.
The 71-year-old Pope said the nodule was found at an early stage and was "circumscribed" or well-localized. The Vatican later said Leo would undergo surgery in the first days of the week, with an expected recovery time of a week.
The American Pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than three centimetres that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.
Leo, elected Pope by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He has no previously known health problems and is considered physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo.
The Pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.
In his remarks, delivered in Italian, Leo said during a recent medical check, "doctors found a small, localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is circumscribed. The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it."
"The surgery is already scheduled for the coming days. Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers," he said.
Before mentioning his health issue in his address on Sunday, the Pope referred to the trip, thanking Catholics for their prayers "for the pastoral visit I will undertake."
Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
Leo is expected to undergo surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, where Francis and popes before him were treated and where there is a special apartment for pontiffs.
Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni, among the few outsiders to visit Francis during his long final hospitalization, expressed her support, and that of the Italian government, to Leo "as he faces this challenge in the coming days." In a statement, she added that "the serenity and calm with which he spoke about it" were reassuring.
A nodule on the lung is a small, localized lesion that can be benign. The American Thoracic Society says fewer than five per cent of lung nodules overall prove cancerous, although risk rises with age, size and other factors.
