The Mumbai Police on Sunday (October 11, 2026) detained several people gathered near Shivaji Park in Dadar to participate in a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar. The agitators alleged they were prevented from reaching the protest site despite assembling peacefully.
The protesters claimed police personnel had been deployed at multiple entry points around Shivaji Park and that several people were detained even before they could join the demonstration. Some alleged that people who were merely standing or walking in the area were also taken into custody.
Shafqat Khan, a protester, said demonstrators were denied entry through Gate No. 6 and other entrances to Shivaji Park. "We came to Dadar for the protest, but we were not allowed to enter through Gate No. 6. We tried other gates as well, but were stopped everywhere. Even some people who had not come for the protest were detained simply because they were moving around in groups," he alleged.
Mr. Khan accused the police of using excessive force while detaining demonstrators. "We did nothing wrong; did not misbehave with the police and did not engage in any violence or raise provocative slogans. We are protesting to protect our voting rights, which are among our most important rights in a democracy," he said.
Meera Shah, a resident of Mulund, said she had decided to participate in the demonstration after seeing reports of police action against Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protesters in Delhi a day earlier.
"I was not sure about coming here, but thanks to the Delhi Police, they did that with Dhruv Rathee, and that is why I am here today," Ms. Shah said, referring to the reported detention of the YouTuber. "I am neither for the Congress, nor for the BJP, nor for the Shiv Sena. I am for India, and I feel our democracy needs to be saved from whatever is happening."
Another protester Chetan Patil criticised the detentions and said the demonstrators were demanding the withdrawal of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the resignation of the CEC.
"From Jantar Mantar to Mumbai, people are gathering to demand that SIR be cancelled and Gyanesh Kumar resign. But the police are picking people up and putting them in detention as though a 'Jail Bharo Andolan' is underway," Mr. Patil said. "We, as young people, will continue fighting till our last breath."
Leslie D'Souza, another demonstrator, questioned the government's response to the protests and accused the authorities of attempting to suppress dissent.
"For the last two or three days, attempts have been made to silence people's voices. My question to the government is, who are you afraid of? You are serving the nation, so why should you be afraid of questions and answers?" Mr. D'Souza said.
"You all are not even taking any press conferences for the situation that has arisen in this country," Mr. D'Souza added.
‘Extremely rough’
Manya Yadav (name changed), 24, alleged that male police personnel dragged demonstrators by their shirts and verbally abused them. Ms. Yadav said she was detained around 5:50 p.m. and released around 7 p.m., alleging that women protesters were kept in custody beyond 6 p.m. “They were being extremely rough, extremely aggressive. They were hurling abuses at us," she said. She also alleged that police personnel filmed the women as they stepped out of the police vehicle.
Several protesters alleged that they were detained without giving a clear reason. "We were just standing quietly. We didn't say a word to anyone," a woman seated inside a police vehicle said.
Another protester said the police had detained him despite his willingness to cooperate. "They told us to move to the side, and we complied. But even after that, they detained us without any reason," he alleged.
A man speaking from a police vehicle claimed that he and another person were detained while walking along the road. "Two of us were just starting to walk this way, and they just forcefully shoved us into the bus. We kept asking why they were putting us inside, but there was no answer," he said.
A 25-year-old man who was among those detained was taken to Nair Hospital after suffering a panic attack. Deputy Commissioner of Police (Central Zone-1) Jayant Meena said the man was now doing well and was expected to be discharged from the hospital within 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, Mumbai-based student leader Rohit Dhale, a member of Chattrabharti Vidhyarthi Sanghthna, claimed he was allegedly taken into police custody from his residence in Parel ahead of the scheduled protest. A press note issued following his alleged detention questioned the police action and sought clarification regarding the grounds on which he was taken into custody.
"Questioning the authorities should not be treated as a crime in a democracy," the press note stated, urging the Mumbai Police to disclose the legal provisions under which Mr. Dhale was detained and clarify on his whereabouts and current status.
Samya Korde of the Progressive Students' Union alleged police personnel had been stationed outside her residence, restricting her movement.
The Yuva Sena also warned of protests if demonstrators were detained unlawfully. In a statement, its core team said if the Mumbai Police illegally detained anyone from Shivaji Park or elsewhere, the organisation would stage protests outside Shiv Sena Bhavan and police stations.
MNS leader’s charge
Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) leader Sandeep Deshpande accused the Mumbai Police of attempting to instigate residents against CJP protesters by allegedly asking representatives of Navratri festival mandals in Dadar to confront those expected to gather at Shivaji Park.
Mr. Deshpande claimed that representatives of festival mandals from Dadar and surrounding areas were summoned to a police chowky near Chaityabhoomi around 12:55 p.m. on Sunday (October 11). According to him, the meeting was attended by a Shivaji Park police officer and a local Bharatiya Janata Party functionary, identified as Kewal Chavan.
"The mandal representatives were told that CJP workers would be coming here to protest and that they should stand there as local residents and oppose them. They were assured that the police would stand behind them," Mr. Deshpande alleged.
He claimed that the police were attempting to create Opposition to the demonstration by involving residents rather than allowing the protesters to gather peacefully.
“Around 300 protesters were detained. They have also been released. FIR registration is in progress,” Deputy Commissioner of Police Zone 5 Mahendra Pandit said

The era of Amazon's Fire tablets—cheap slate computers ranging from $60 to $280—is over.
All of the Fire tablets are being replaced by the all-aluminum Amazon Alexa Tablet. These tablets will, in a first for Amazon, run official Android and have full access to the Google Play Store. The lack of proper app support was always a sticking point for the Fire tablets, which ran a custom version of Android and had a much more limited app library.
The new Alexa Tablet series comes in three models: the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro ($500), Alexa Tablet 11 ($330), and Alexa Tablet 8 ($230), with the numbers corresponding to the display size. Amazon is also offering kids' editions of the latter two devices at the same prices. These include bumper cases for extra protection, a one-year, worry-free guarantee to replace the device if it breaks, and a year of Amazon Kids+ service to fill the tablet with age-appropriate content.
As for Fire tablets, Amazon says it will stop shipping the devices in the next month or two. It will support them for four years from the last ship date. Amazon is committing to at least four years of software updates for the new Alexa tablets, which will launch with Android 16 and will receive Android 17 early in 2027. Preorders for the new Alexa Tablets are open now, and they'll begin shipping on October 14.
Premium Tablets
The experience is largely the same on all three tablets, with aluminum builds designed to mimic the new aluminum Kindles. The MediaTek Dimensity 8189 chip powers the two smaller tablets, whereas the 12-inch device gets a little more power from the MediaTek Dimensity 8400.
The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is the outlier of the trio, as it's the only one with two display variants: a standard 12-inch LCD screen or a 12-inch Nanomatte display with anti-glare and anti-reflective properties. Upgrade to the Nanomatte—starting at $550—for a matte, paperlike look and feel. With a peak brightness of 500 nits, it should still be bright enough to view in sunlight.

Amazon says it developed this screen in partnership with Corning (the company that makes most of the glass that protects smartphone displays). It's similar to the matte displays found on devices like TCL's Nxtpaper series, though Amazon's vice president of devices, Kevin Keith, says the hexagon-shaped imprint on the Nanomatte display can push out vivid colors and crisp blacks while still retaining those matte properties.
The screen also offers a “really good” writing experience, according to Keith. He says the same engineers who worked on the Kindle Scribe worked with Corning to get that paperlike feel. The screen works with Amazon's new Alexa Tablet Pro Pen ($90), which has 4,096 levels of pressure sensitivity, plus tilt detection. The pen can magnetically dock to the top of the slate for charging and pairing. Amazon also sells a Pro Keyboard ($150) for the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, which attaches to the device via the pogo pins on the bottom edge—no Bluetooth needed.
Now that Android has recently gained multiwindowing features, attaching the keyboard turns the largest Alexa tablet into a productivity machine: split apps across the screen, resize them into various windows, and “save” several desktop arrangements so you can pick up where you left off.
For the kids’ versions of the Alexa Tablet 11 and Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon says the software is still Android with a heavily customized interface for kid-friendly content and built-in parental controls. Keith says one in five kids in the US has an Amazon tablet, so it'll be interesting to see how that changes now that these devices start at a higher price.
Alexa Front and Center
It may look and feel like Android, but Amazon has tweaked the interface to make these Alexa Tablets feel like Amazon hardware.
The top-left corner of the home screen features a persistent widget called the Dynamic Tab. This scrollable widget lets you dive into Amazon content you may have been consuming on another device—say, if you were reading on your Kindle, watching a movie on Prime Video on your iPhone, or snapped some photos and you want to view them on Amazon Photos.
Swipe right, and instead of Google's Discover feed, you're instead greeted with Amazon's For You experience. Amazon's Fire tablets were a vehicle to put Amazon content in front of your eyeballs, and that hasn't changed with the Alexa Tablets. Again, you can continue consuming content here, with tabs for movies and TV, games, and Kindle. There's also a news feed, and you can tap Alexa prompts for more information on a story.
Uniquely, opening the Kindle app triggers “Kindle mode,” which disables all notifications, turns on the blue light filter, and extends battery life to 20 hours (less on the smaller tablets). You can also choose one of three display treatments in this mode: subtle warmth with natural color, a softened paper tone, or monochrome. There's even a fun page-turn effect that mimics turning a page in a book. As soon as you exit the app, notifications turn back on, and the screen returns to normal. Annotations you make with the stylus will sync with Kindle apps on pen-supported devices, like the Kindle Scribe.
As the tablets’ names suggests, Alexa+ is front and center. So far, Amazon has restricted Alexa+ access to paid subscribers or Amazon Prime customers, but Keith says you don't need to subscribe to anything to use Alexa+ on these devices.
In the bottom-right corner, a persistent “Ask Alexa” chat box lets you call up the virtual assistant immediately. You can also trigger it by saying, “Alexa,” just like an Echo device. It can control your smart home devices, but the marquee addition is Alexa's On-Screen Intelligence. It's opt-in—with an on-screen indicator whenever it's active—allowing the assistant to see what you're looking at and answer contextual questions.
For example, if you're traveling to a new city and are looking at a guide filled with restaurant recommendations, you can ask Alexa, “Which of these is closest to my hotel?” and it can filter the list. Got a schedule for your kid's soccer games? Bring up Alexa and ask it to add all the events to your calendar.
Alexa+ also supports live sessions—much like Google's Gemini Live or ChatGPT's Voice Mode, you can have a real-time back-and-forth conversation with the assistant without speaking the wake word at every turn. Watching a TikTok and wondering whether a product in the video is available on Amazon? Naturally, you can ask Alexa, and the assistant can even add it to your shopping cart.
The hardware may finally have the look and feel of other premium Android tablets, but these slates are still built to keep you hooked on Amazon's retail empire.

Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
- Published
A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.
Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.
Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.
The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.
Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault
Catching My Teacher
Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia
Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube, external.
The student detectives
Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.
They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.
By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.
Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.
Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.
Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.
In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.
Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.
In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.
Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.
Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".
The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.
More students come forward
The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.
One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.
"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."
Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.
"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."
Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.
"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.
Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.
"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.
Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.
The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.
NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.
In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

MacBooks have taken most of the spotlight away from Mac desktops in recent years. Now that mobile performance and battery life have improved so much, there's less of a reason to buy a desktop that chains you to your office.
But Mac desktops are getting a resurgence. The Mac Mini and Mac Studio were finally refreshed with brand-new chips and a newfound focus on running local AI. But which one should you buy? And where does the iMac land these days? I've been testing Macs for over a decade and have tested all these Mac desktops, so I can recommend what's right for you.
Also check out our complete guide to the Best MacBooks, Best Desktops, and Best All-In-One Desktops.
The Best for Everyone: Mac Mini
Apple's lovable mini PC was just upgraded with the M6 chip, and it's a big deal on a couple of fronts. Before the refresh, these little computers were sold out for months, and it has AI to thank.
The Mac Mini isn't the ultra-cheap mini PC it used to be. It's $300 more than in the past, but the base model now has higher specs and a focus on running local AI. If you want a truly affordable little desktop PC for occasional use, you'll have to opt for a Windows machine. The good news is that the Mac Mini remains a compelling offer across its configurations. You can choose between two new models: one with the M6 and one with the M5 Pro. The M6 model is the one most people should buy, especially if you're looking for a fast, reliable Mac desktop.
The new M6 chip is especially fast in terms of GPU performance, an area Apple continues to make strides. If you're a fledgling video editor or designer, the base configuration packs plenty of performance for creative applications. Unfortunately, it's only a couple hundred bucks cheaper than a similarly configured MacBook Air, which makes the buying decision frustrating given how much more versatile a laptop is. But for the first time, the Mac Mini's form factor is a benefit over a laptop. AI enthusiasts get excited about the prospect of an always-on, agentic AI box that sits on their desk and can then be controlled remotely from a MacBook or iPhone. That's exactly what the Mac Mini can do (just be sure to upgrade the memory). And given memory prices across the industry, you won't find many comparable options on Windows or Linux—at least not with this much performance and RAM.
I haven't tested the M5 Pro model yet, but the main difference is in the enhanced graphics. Despite the improvements I mentioned on the M6, you can configure the M5 Pro up to 20 GPU cores, which really come in handy for tasks like gaming, 3D modeling, and video rendering. As the name suggests, I wouldn't consider the pricier M5 Pro config unless you're a professional who sits in front of Final Cut Pro or DaVinci Resolve all day. If you're more of a hobbyist or dabbler, the M6 will likely do you just fine.
Shipping times on the M6 Mac Mini have improved to the point where you can buy one and pick it up today from an Apple Store. The M5 Pro models, however, may take up to four weeks to ship.
Only for Pros: Mac Studio
Like with the Mac Mini, there are really two distinct versions of the Mac Studio. The base configuration comes with an M5 Max (the same chip in the MacBook Pro), sporting some really impressive GPU performance in particular. And that's the main thing to consider when deciding between the M5 Pro Mac Mini and the M5 Max Mac Studio. Like choosing between those two chips in a MacBook Pro, the main upgrade is in graphics performance. Going with the M5 Max also lets you configure it with up to 128 GB of unified memory, which matters if you plan to run heavy local AI models. On the other hand, this puts you over the $5,000 price point rather quickly.
And then, there's the M5 Ultra. This massive chip is literally two M5 Max dies stitched together, and to my surprise while testing, it sometimes resulted in double the performance, such as in GPU performance. But look, don't even bother considering this unless you know exactly what you intend to use it for. Just so you know what you're getting into, the model I tested had 256 GB of memory and cost over $11,000. You read that right. It's definitely the most expensive computer I've ever had on my desk.
But I downloaded and started running on the M5 Ultra some of the largest and most powerful AI models I could find, and soon enough I had a foundation-tier LLM running completely on-device—no cloud needed. That means direct access to your computer for a powerful agentic AI to run wild with, all without the privacy and security concerns. Some simple agentic tests I ran on the M5 Ultra took minutes, whereas it took five times as long on my M5 Max MacBook Pro.
And while this thing is clearly not intended for gaming, I was pretty blown away by how fast games like Cyberpunk 2077 ran. I've definitely never seen games play this smoothly on a Mac before.
Unfortunately, shipping times on the Mac Studio are still dicey. If you want anything with 128 GB or more of memory, you'll be waiting up to a month and a half for the M5 Max models. The M5 Ultra Mac Studio, meanwhile, will take up to four months to ship at this point.
Don't Buy the iMac Right Now
The iMac has been downplayed in recent years. The once-iconic all-in-one computer, which comes with the display, stand, and accessories, used to be an affordable go-to choice for students, families, businesses, and even content creators. But as Apple has shifted focus, the iMac seems less and less of a focus, with sporadic updates over the years. It hasn't been updated since 2024 and still uses the M4 chip.
It's not a bad computer, though. The screen is brilliant, and the performance is solid, even by today's standards. Its age, however, isn't reflected in the price you'd pay right now: $1,499 gets you 16 GB of RAM, 256 GB of storage, the M4 chip with an eight-core GPU, two Thunderbolt 4 ports, and a 4.5K IPS display. A second M4 model with a 10-core GPU and four Thunderbolt 4 ports starts at $1,699. (Like nearly all Apple products, the iMac got a price increase.)
The main issue for me is that there's currently only a 23.5-inch model, which is smaller than what most people will probably want. Until Apple releases a 27-inch model (as it has in the past), perhaps with an option for a “Pro” M-series chip, I can't see the iMac as a good choice for most people. The simplicity will be a draw, especially if researching and buying a separate monitor and peripherals sounds daunting.
Interestingly, it is also the only desktop-size Mac monitor that isn't at least 5K (it's 4.5K). So, while it's cheaper than buying a Studio Display paired with a new Mac Mini, the iMac also locks you into a one-time purchase you can't upgrade later. And as the focus on local AI only grows, I can't imagine the iMac regaining the relevance or attention it once had. On the plus side, it's the only Mac desktop available in seven colors.
At the very least, I hope it gets a refresh to the M6 in the next couple of months. It'll have been long overdue! Either way, now's not a good time to buy an iMac.
Why Is Everyone Buying a Mac Mini?
Before the launch of the M6 model, Mac Minis had been sold out for most of this year. Orders for Mac Studios were similarly backlogged for months before you could get one. The reason? Well, according to Apple on an earnings call, both computers are “amazing platforms for AI and agentic tools,” and that “customer adoption of that is happening faster than we expected.” In other words, they were caught off guard. AI frameworks released in 2026, such as OpenClaw, run best on a dedicated machine that never turns off and has lots of available RAM—such as a Mac Mini.
What Happened to the Mac Pro?
The last incarnation of the Mac Pro was one of Apple's most short-lived Macs. The most recent design was relaunched in 2019, alongside the Pro Display XDR. When it was unveiled, it was an exciting re-entrance for the Mac, focusing not only on Pro-level performance but also on upgradability. Unlike the current Mac Studio, the Mac Pro had modular components you could swap in and out—or upgrade. The design was much more akin to a traditional tower PC. For a company that had been moving in the opposite direction for so long, it was a breath of fresh air.
But it wasn't meant to last, and it survived only a few upgrade cycles. With the advent of Apple silicon and the rapid scaling of these system-on-a-chip (SoC) designs, the Mac Pro's focus on modularity made less and less sense. Apple didn't officially discontinue the Mac Pro until March 2026, but by then it had been almost three years since the Mac Pro was last updated. The Mac Studio with the “Ultra” chips has since fully replaced the Mac Pro.
M6, M5 Pro, M5 Max, or M5 Ultra?
Both the Mac Mini and Mac Studio have two configurations to choose from, which gives a clean delineation between the two in terms of performance. When you move from the base chip to the Pro and Max chips, the main differences are GPU cores and, in some cases, the maximum amount of RAM you can upgrade to. Certain applications and tasks benefit greatly from stronger GPU performance, speeding up things like video rendering, 3D modeling, gaming, and AI inferencing. These are the same chips that are available in the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro.
The jump between the Max and Ultra chips, however, is much more significant. This is where you enter performance territory not possible on a MacBook. It has twice the CPU and GPU cores of the standard Max chips, delivers far stronger performance, and lets you configure it with up to 512 GB of unified memory.
The iMac is still holding onto the M4. For most people, the chip is more than capable, but considering the age and the price of the iMac today, it's outdated for a new machine.
Here's a list of the different Apple silicon available for the Mac Mini, Mac Studio, and iMac.
Mac Mini update history:
- Mac Mini (M6): 2026
- Mac Mini (M4): 2024
- Mac Mini (M2, M2 Pro): 2023
- Mac Mini (M1): 2020
Mac Studio update history:
- Mac Studio (M5 Max, M5 Ultra): 2026
- Mac Studio (M4 Max, M3 Ultra): 2025
- Mac Studio (M2 Max, M2 Ultra): 2023
- Mac Studio (M1 Max, M1 Ultra): 2022
iMac update history:
- iMac (M4): 2024
- iMac (M3): 2023
- iMac (M1): 2021

Pope Leo XIV to undergo lung surgery this week
Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday that he would have surgery this week to remove a "localized nodule" in his lung.
Leo said the nodule was found at a "very early stage" with doctors recommending surgery.
"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," Leo said during his weekly Sunday noon blessing in St. Peter's Square.
The surgery is due to occur at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which is the primary location for popes to receive medical attention.
Leo has had no known previous health problems.
"I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers," Leo said to the crowds on Sunday.
According to the American Cancer Society, a lung nodule is a small abnormal area, less than or equal to 3 cm, found during a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. These tests are often conducted as routine screenings for "trauma, heart disease, non-cancer related lung disease, or lung infection."
Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said in a statement that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of this week and the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week."
Leo's next major international trip is scheduled for early November to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear if the surgery would affect his travels.
During his papacy, Leo has been outspoken about peace throughout the world. He spent part of his Sunday address renewing calls for peace in Ukraine.
"I make a heartfelt appeal to the parties to the conflict to allow the safe transport of grain across the Black Sea," Leo said. "The daily bread of millions of people cannot be held hostage by war."
On Saturday, the Pope also called for the death penalty to be abolished, saying on X that it is "inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person."
"The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption," Leo said.

Why investment-linked policy sales have surged even as complaints rise
Simpler sign-ups and welcome bonuses may be driving demand for investment-linked policies in Singapore, industry experts say.
SINGAPORE: Sales of investment-linked policies (ILPs) have more than doubled in three years, even as claims over alleged misrepresentation and inadequate disclosure keep climbing.
Weighted new business premiums – a measure of new sales – have risen for three consecutive years after falling in 2022 amid rising interest rates and market volatility, said the Life Insurance Association (LIA).
They reached S$2.88 billion (US$2.2 billion) in 2025, up from S$1.31 billion in 2022, said the association’s executive director Chan Wai Kit.
“This represents growth of approximately 120 per cent over three years, including a 27.8 per cent year-on-year increase in 2025,” he said.
Over the same period, claims related to ILPs at the Financial Industry Disputes Resolution Centre (FIDReC) rose from 42 in 2022 to 164 in 2025. This included a spike in 2024, which saw 211 claims.
The industry mediator saw 104 claims in the first half of 2026, compared with 61 in the same period a year earlier.
The claims generally centre on allegations of market conduct, such as misrepresentation, inadequate disclosure of information about ILPs or inappropriate financial advice.
Over the years, the profile of complainants has shifted towards older age groups, said FIDReC chief executive Eunice Chua. Claims from those aged 61 and above made up 35 per cent of the total in the first half of 2026, up from 7 per cent in 2022.
Mediation sessions showed that many consumers lack a good understanding of the product, often assuming it is similar to traditional insurance or that returns and capital are guaranteed.
Some are also unclear about the fees and charges or the premium commitment term.
WHY HAS DEMAND INCREASED?
Two design changes to ILPs account for much of the recent growth, said Alex Lee, president of the Singapore Actuarial Society.
Traditional policies balanced protection and investment, requiring customers to complete lengthy health underwriting questionnaires, he said. Newer ones carry only minimal death cover, so they can be issued with few or no health underwriting questions.
The “welcome bonus” that many newer ILPs offer may also have spurred sales, said Mr Lee, referring to extra units in the fund that are given to the customer when they first purchase the policy, so they are holding more than they paid for.
He noted, however, that the bonus is typically funded through higher charges in the early years and comes with a minimum investment period.
Mr Eddy Cheong, chief executive of insurance advisory Havend, said strong capital markets over the past decade may have made ILPs an easier sell.
“People like the idea of growing their wealth,” he said, adding that fixed deposits and endowment funds may be seen as too safe or too slow.
With hardly any long-term market corrections in recent years, people may also think investing is easy to navigate, he said.
Many customers are not investment-savvy and rely heavily on advisers, leading them to buy ILPs instead of investing directly, he added. Others may view the policies as “safer” because they are insurance products, even though they are not insurance.
WHAT BUYERS NEED TO KNOW
For those considering ILPs, the experts cautioned that returns and capital are not guaranteed – so money put into a policy may not grow and may even shrink.
LIA's Mr Chan said customers may mistake “capital guaranteed” for “death benefit”.
A death benefit is an assured insurance payout triggered upon death. It should not be conflated with a capital guarantee during the policy term, because the investment value fluctuates with market conditions, he said.
FIDReC's Ms Chua said consumers frequently assume the policies are “safe” like traditional insurance products and need no active monitoring. Returns also fluctuate based on what the customer chooses to invest in, she added.
Mr Cheong, whose company does not recommend ILPs to its customers, said consumers should be aware of fees and charges that can eat into returns even when markets do well.
ILP holders have to pay policy fees and fund fees, whereas those buying directly into the same investment fund only pay fund fees, he said. The policy fees are similar to what a consumer would pay for insurance, even though the ILP is more of an investment product, he added.
Red flags and what to look out for when buying an ILP
Given their complexity, consumers may not know what to look out for when assessing ILPs.
Ms Chua from FIDReC said consumers can ask advisers to point out key terms and should look out for phrases such as "not guaranteed", "projected" and "possible loss of the principal amount invested".
SAS' Mr Lee said consumers should first be clear on how much money they can commit regularly, when it might be needed and what it is for.
"Only then consider whether an ILP fits, compared with alternatives such as investing directly in funds or separating protection from investment," he said.
Some warning signs customers should look out for:
- Pressure to sign quickly
- Pushing one product without exploring other options
- An adviser not taking the time to understand the consumer's financial objectives, risk appetite and investment horizon
- Being sold mainly on the headline bonus or projected returns that may not be realistic
- Being advised to surrender existing policies to fund the ILP
- Being encouraged to increase premiums to reach a higher bonus tier
- Not being shown the impact of surrendering the policy in the early years
Mr Cheong also pointed to administration charges payable every year for the stipulated period. In some cases, the charge is a percentage of the account value – meaning the more your account grows, the higher the amount charged.
Mr Lee also pointed to charges for early termination and premium holidays. Premium holidays are periods in which the policy owner can stop paying premiums without surrendering the policy. The insurer usually sells existing units to pay for any charges during this time.
Consumers should make use of the 14-day free-look period, which allows buyers to get a refund, to review documents before deciding, they said.
TRAINING FOR FINANCIAL CONSULTANTS
Income Insurance told CNA that complaints related to ILPs arise for various reasons and are not limited to market misconduct.
It said financial advisers are required to conduct a needs-based assessment and explain relevant information to customers before making a recommendation, and that it supports this through structured training and development programmes.
Manulife’s chief distribution officer Khoo Poh Huat said the company continues to reinforce appropriate advisory and disclosure standards through consultant training and customer communications.
“We are proactively working with customers to address their concerns and improve customer education around ILPs,” he said.

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output.
A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”
Cut once, measure twice
To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.
To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.
In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

Many mainstream Australians would feel as if they’d been dropped in a foreign country at the Conservative Political Action Conference, lost amid oblique references to transgender swimmers, blue hair, women’s bathrooms, jokes about falling off stages and Matt Canavan in hi-vis and speed dealer sunnies.
It’s an interesting spectacle. At this year’s conference in Brisbane, rightwing campaigner Monica Smit was deep in conversation with a Donald Trump impersonator, opera singers belted out the national anthem (the first verse, twice, for unknown reasons), senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price and her folk singer husband sang the anthem again, and Karl Stefanovic jokingly thanking CPAC for “rudely interrupting my unemployment”.
Stickers depicting Albanese with a Pinocchio nose, holding a brown burlap sack and a large blue sex toy emblazoned with “United Nations global citizen award” were found in the conference hall and in the men’s urinals. They carried no authorisation message, and did not appear to be officially endorsed by CPAC. Journalists were asked to wear a large red media accreditation lanyard emblazoned with “FAKE NEWS” – a gag CPAC has been pulling for years.
There was Barnaby Joyce handing out a few notes as props during his free-wheeling lecture about the value of money and the historical silver content of Roman coins, and seemingly every One Nation figure with a public profile (besides Farrer MP David Farley) wandering the halls.
Alongside boilerplate rightwing chaff like lower taxes, fiscal discipline and welfare, CPAC is a hotbed for hyper-engaged conservatives riled up on the red cordial of Sky After Dark. Last year’s event featured speakers criticising Peter Dutton as “Labor-lite”.
For all the twisting rabbit holes which various speeches followed, there was only really one prevailing theme which most boiled down to, and which this year’s conference revolved around.
Preferences.
To put it more accurately, the conference was about how Australia’s conservative right planned to boot Albanese and Labor out of office at the next election. With 94 Labor seats, and a splintered rightwing vote with Angus Taylor’s diminished Coalition opposition being whacked by Pauline Hanson’s surging One Nation, it’s a tall task.
To attend this year’s CPAC was to see Australia’s right recognising in real-time that they needed to figure out a way to cooperate; that for all the mocking of Albanese Labor as allegedly “the worst government in history”, conservatives face a third successive election defeat.
CPAC, in messages to attenders, identified what it saw as the problem: “If you support One Nation but won’t preference the Coalition, or support the Coalition but won’t preference One Nation, you risk reinstalling Labor.”
But identifying the problem is only half the challenge. By the conference’s end, it wasn’t clear how parties of the right would, or could, cooperate. While Hanson signed a pledge to “to work together”, challenging Taylor and Canavan to follow suit, it came hours after she’d told the conference they shouldn’t trust the Coalition, and appeared to call the Liberal leader a “smarmy management consultant” unfit to replace Albanese.
Hanson at CPAC 2025 said she would “no longer be the bridesmaid” to the Coalition. She seems wedded to that, and said the ball was in Taylor’s court as to how their two parties would coexist.
Taylor had earlier dodged questions from Karl Stefanovic – to boos from the audience – about how the Coalition should cooperate with One Nation. He tried burnishing his conservative credentials by apologising for net zero, pandemic spending and immigration increases under Coalition governments, and later claiming “I know how to get Australia out of the hole Labor has put us in”, but it was clear many here had only come to see the Hanson show.
In previous years, the mood at the conference has been a decent weathervane indicating where the wind of the right is blowing.
In 2022, CPAC’s prevailing theme was urging the opposition to oppose the Indigenous voice referendum; a month later, the Nationals did, later followed by the Liberals. In 2025, alarmed Coalition speakers begged attenders for their loyalty in the face of One Nation’s rise, culture warriors railed against Sussan Ley’s leadership, and Canavan said the Liberals were on “the cusp” of dropping net zero. Within months, the Coalition split again, the Liberals dumped net zero and then Ley, and Hanson’s surge continued.
There’s some way to go before the next election, due by May 2028. The conservative side of politics still lays splintered. We’ll look back on this weekend to see if it was the start of the right’s rebuild, or just another forum to bag the prime minister.

Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.
But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.
Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.
Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.
Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.
But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.
On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.
In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.
Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.
Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”
The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.
Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.”
Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.
Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”
“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”
Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.
But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.
Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.
Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.
Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.
Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.
Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.
“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

The SC unday directed authorities to prevent illegal detention of people participating in peaceful gatherings.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Sunday said its purpose was to instill faith of the people in the system and addressed Kapil Sibal's "no faith" remark, saying his "confidence is most vital" for the top court's "fight against injustice".“Our purpose is to instill faith of the people in the system and in that process your (Sibal’s) confidence is most vital for our fight against injustice,” the bench said.The Supreme Court on Sunday directed authorities to prevent illegal detention of people participating in peaceful gatherings amid the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests in Delhi. It also asked the Centre to ensure that metro services operate normally and internet access remains uninterrupted, subject to law and order requirements.Sibal welcomed the court's order in connection with the restrictions imposed in Delhi amid protests, saying it restores faith in the country's justice system.“We are deeply grateful to the Supreme Court for having passed an order that restores faith among professionals in the system of justice in this country,” Sibal said.A bench comprising Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Centre while hearing a petition seeking contempt proceedings over alleged violations of the court's earlier order against a "complete prohibition" on metro and train services in the national capital during the protests.
The CJP and several student organisations had called for demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission.The authorities prevented a planned mass mobilisation at Jantar Mantar on Saturday following a major security clampdown. More than 7,000 protesters were detained, including CJP leader Abhijit Dipke, several opposition leaders and YouTuber Dhruv Rathee.During the special hearing, the bench asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to ensure that Delhi Metro operates according to its regular schedule and that internet services are not disrupted, subject to law and order requirements.The court also directed authorities to ensure that lawyers, journalists and others are not prevented from carrying out their professional duties."Internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, as per law....When we are saying internet facilities shall remain undisturbed, we are not taking away the powers under the Information Technology Act."There shall not be illegal detention, save and except by procedure established by law, particularly with regard to assemblage of people beyond the area within which it's imposed," the bench said.The Supreme Court also directed authorities to remove a notice board outside its premises announcing the imposition of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which empowers authorities to restrict assemblies in certain circumstances."We have been informed that a notice board stating imposition of Section 163 BNSS in and around the vicinity of the Supreme Court has been put up."We direct the authority concerned to take down this board, if not already done, so that citizens as well as lawyers can have access to justice," the bench ordered.
During the hearing, senior advocate Kapil Sibal, appearing for Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD) MP Manoj Jha, alleged that police were detaining people travelling on trains and those found outside the four-kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, where prohibitory orders were in force.Sibal also told the court that 45 metro stations had remained closed to passenger entry and exit despite the Supreme Court's October 9 order.The petition sought contempt proceedings against the authorities over the alleged failure to comply with the court's directions on maintaining access to public transport during the protests.

We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
Get ready for a smart home hub, a refreshed HomePod Mini, a faster Apple TV, and maybe some LG smart locks.
What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month.
“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. Here’s more about what to expect.
A proper smart home hub
Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere.
It will also supposedly use voice or facial recognition to identify who is interacting with it, pulling up the relevant contacts, calendar appointments, and more. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called…
homeOS
The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls.
The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.
HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh
Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. The designs will remain the same, but they’ll get a new processor to help handle the added demand of Siri AI. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink.
This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. In addition to supporting Siri AI, the new processor will also speed up navigation, which can get a bit laggy. Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.
LG and other partner devices
It’s likely that we’ll get a mention of products that integrate with HomeKit and offer new features built on top of homeOS and whatever Apple’s hardware hub ends up being called. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners. We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more. They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “Proximity Control” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “tap to set up without power” pairing feature.

'You're Russian now': Ukrainians raised in Crimea share how Russia trained them to become future soldiers
They say indoctrination began at school with military training, erasure of Ukrainian language, identity
Growing up in Crimea under Russian occupation, Matvii Chos feared he would be drafted into the Russian army as soon as he became an adult.
"If you're a man and you turn 18 years old, they almost immediately draft you," said Chos, 19, who enrolled at a Moscow university to avoid conscription and later escaped Russia with the help of a Ukrainian non-profit.
But he says the brainwashing and militarization started much earlier. Chos says they began having special cadet classes in 2020, when he was a sixth-grade student. They were trained in a range of military techniques — loading and reloading weapons, marching, tactical medicine — a co-ordinated effort, Chos says, to create future soldiers to fight his fellow Ukrainians.
"What Russia is doing is occupying territories, kidnapping children and turning them [into] Russian soldiers," he said.
Fifty countries signed a pledge at the Pathways to Peace international conference held in Toronto on Sept. 29, expressing concern about the militarization of children in occupied territories and calling for the “immediate, safe and unconditional return” of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred into Russia.
The indoctrination and forced military training Chos was subjected to is an experience shared by many Ukrainian youth in territories controlled by Russia — an issue especially urgent, human rights experts say, because of how vulnerable children are.
"Childhood has an expiration date," said Oleksandra Matviichuk, a Ukrainian human rights lawyer who heads the Center for Civil Liberties, which won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022.
"The children from occupied territories, they're losing their childhood. We lose these children."
Speaking Ukrainian forbidden
Other young Ukrainians who spoke to CBC News outlined the various ways Russian culture and values were imposed on them as children.
Daria Fursova, 23, remembers how quickly her elementary school curriculum changed after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 when she was 11.
"The administration said that there will no longer be Ukrainian books in school, in classes," she said, recalling the start of fifth grade.
Not long after, Fursova’s school stopped teaching Ukrainian and instead began instructing them in Russian history and the Russian language.
Speaking Ukrainian and Crimean Tatar — a language considered "highly endangered" by UNESCO — was forbidden, even during breaks, according to 18-year-old Daria Tomashova, who says the indoctrination was "everywhere," from textbooks in school to what was broadcast on TV.
Chos has similar memories of the sudden shift after the occupation.
"We started to learn [the] Russian anthem at school, learn Russian songs, learn Russian poems," he said. "They said to us, 'You're Russian now. You lived all of your life in Russia.' "
Fursova left Crimea to study in Kyiv in 2021 before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but says the situation in Crimea has since become "way worse." Her old school posted lessons on social media defending the war, and she says many of her former classmates have since joined the Russian army.
Daria Fursova, 23, shares her experience growing up in occupied Crimea at the United Nations General Assembly on Sept. 23, during the sixth summit of the Crimea Platform. (UN Web TV)
20,000 children abducted
Beyond the Russification of occupied Crimea, the international community has raised particular concern with how Russia has forcibly separated tens of thousands of Ukrainian children from their families and taken them into Russian territory — an act Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as "mass kidnapping" amounting to genocide.
Many of those children have shared stories of abuse while in Russian custody, including being placed in isolation cells for not being co-operative in Russian re-education camps. Other children are given new identities, naturalized as Russian citizens and forcibly adopted into foster families in Russia.
Ukrainian officials estimate that Russia has unlawfully deported 20,000 children since the invasion began in February 2022. Of those, only about 2,650 have been returned so far.
The co-ordinated campaign has led to charges at the International Criminal Court against Russian President Vladimir Putin and Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand says she holds Putin personally responsible for the policies that have led to Ukrainian children being "stolen" from their families.
"My hope is that we ensure the full return of all Ukrainian children, and every single person who has committed an injustice in stealing these children face the consequences that international law requires," Anand said in an interview with CBC.
Children just want to return to 'normal life'
Anand says Canada has committed nearly $7 million to support organizations that work to bring Ukrainian children home and fund psychological support for the trauma endured as a result of the "indoctrination, militarization and essentially the Russian attempt to convert these Ukrainian children into members of Russia’s war machine."
One of those organizations is Save Ukraine, a charity that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to rescue them.
Its founder, Mykola Kuleba, says he is grateful for Canada’s leadership on the issue, but emphasized how critical the present situation is, with some young Ukrainians now presumably fighting as Russian soldiers and dying on the battlefield.
"We should understand that we're running out of time for these children, and we're losing every day someone who's taken forcibly to the Russian army," said Kuleba, the former commissioner for children’s rights in Ukraine.
Kuleba says the children they bring home tell him they just want to live in peace with their families in their hometowns.
"They want [to] survive. They want to return to a normal life. They want to stay with their loved ones."

Chos was eventually able to escape Russia with the help of Save Ukraine, which gave him food, shelter, mental health support and documentation.
But the process was nerve-racking: Chos had to travel to the Ukrainian consulate in Belarus twice, and said if Russian authorities had searched him and found anything suggesting he was pro-Ukraine, he would be facing over a decade in Russian prison.
Chos, left, and Tomashova speak at the Pathways to Peace international conference in Toronto on Sept. 28. The Ukrainian couple fell in love and married after being rescued by Save Ukraine, a non-profit that identifies kidnapped children and conducts operations to get them to safety. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)
Now a married couple, Chos and Tomashova shared their experiences at the recent international conference in Toronto.
"I managed to escape," Chos told the room of delegates, "but a lot of children are still left there."

Ethiopia tells UN it is acting in self-defense against Eritrea
Ethiopia has told the United Nations Security Council it is taking self-defense measures against Eritrea
NAIROBI, Kenya -- NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Ethiopia told the U.N. Security Council on Friday it is taking measures in self-defense against Eritrea, accusing its neighbor of sending troops across the border and occupying parts of northern Ethiopia.
The declaration adds to fears of a wider conflict as government-allied forces report advances in Tigray, a region devastated by a previous war.
In a letter dated Friday, Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos invoked Ethiopia’s right to self-defense under Article 51 of the U.N. Charter. He did not specify what measures the country was taking.
The letter, obtained by The Associated Press, accused Eritrea of deploying infantry and mechanized units in recent weeks and supporting, financing, arming and directing insurgent groups. It did not identify the occupied areas or provide evidence supporting its allegations.
Ethiopia had repeatedly urged Eritrea to withdraw its forces, Gedion wrote. The AP could not independently verify the allegations.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Friday of pursuing aggression against Eritrea through its demands for sovereign access to the Red Sea. Writing on X, he did not explicitly confirm or deny the reported troop crossings.
Eritrea announced last week it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated Monday that Ethiopia must have access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said it remained committed to dialogue with its neighbors.
The accusations deepen a rift between countries whose armies fought together against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front from 2020 to 2022.
Researchers at Ghent University in Belgium estimated the previous war caused about 500,000 civilian deaths in Tigray from violence, famine and the collapse of health services.
Government and allied forces took Idaga Hamus early Friday and Abiy-Adi, in the Tembien area, on Thursday afternoon, according to Ermiyas Ababu, a commander of the government-allied Tigray Peace Force.
Residents also reported the takeover of Idaga Hamus. Gebremedhin Kihishen, a business owner in Tembien, said government-allied forces controlled Abiy-Adi.
It was unclear from those accounts who held the towns immediately before the reported government advance or whether Eritrean troops were involved in the fighting.
Ermiyas previously reported Eritrean personnel entering Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, citing reports from his personnel.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data monitoring group, known as ACLED, separately said Eritrean troops crossed at Zelambesa on Wednesday and came under drone attack while traveling toward Idaga Hamus. It attributed the strikes to Ethiopia’s military. The AP could not independently verify either account.
The TPLF joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy. Fighting escalated late in September, undermining the 2022 peace agreement, and rebels seized Tigray's capital Mekelle and its airport.
The rebels announced their withdrawal Oct. 3 and government-allied fighters entered the city.
In Mekelle, federal police on Friday called over loudspeakers for residents to help establish a new administration. Government offices remained shut, and no administration had taken office by that morning. The Tigray Peace Force imposed an overnight curfew Wednesday.
The U.S. Embassy said Thursday that telecommunications had resumed in Mekelle and much of Tigray, while mobile banking and electricity had partially resumed. All remained subject to interruption.
During the previous war, the AP documented accounts accusing Eritrean soldiers of killings, rape and looting. Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki dismissed allegations of abuses by his forces as “a fantasy” in 2023.

The Bangiya Christiya Pariseba (BCP), an umbrella forum representing Christians from different denominations in West Bengal, on October 5 formally submitted complaints to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), the West Bengal Human Rights Commission (WBHRC) and the National Commission for Minorities, alleging a pattern of targeted violence against the Christian community, including attacks, vandalism and desecration of small house churches and prayer gatherings across the state.
A public hearing was also held on the same day at Christ the King Hall on Syed Amir Ali Avenue in Park Circus, Kolkata, where pastors, victims and eyewitnesses recounted alleged incidents of attacks and intimidation before representatives of prominent human rights and civil rights organisations, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR) and Banglar Manabadhikar Suraksha Mancha (MASUM). Civil society figures, including retired IAS officer Jawhar Sircar, were also present to hear the testimonies.
The gathering was held amid a series of reported attacks on Christian communities, mostly in the hinterlands of Bengal. Alt News has previously documented at least 35 such incidents of violence and intimidation between July 1 and September 20, 2026.
Based on the testimonies of victims, the BCP, which is the eastern chapter of the All India Christian Council, formally submitted its complaints to the rights bodies alleging recurring patterns of targeted violence and intimidation, as well as institutional and governmental negligence in responding to the incidents.
The BCP identified four key concerns:
1. Systematic attacks on peaceful prayer gatherings – According to the BCP, small house churches and local Christian congregations conducting prayer services have repeatedly been targeted over the past three months. The organisation alleged that the intruders had assaulted worshippers, vandalised places of worship and desecrated religious symbols and objects. The BCP also criticised the efforts to downplay the attacks, saying, “Regrettably, some public figures and local leaders have characterised these lawless disruptions as “public protests” while remaining silent on vigilante groups taking the law into their own hands.”
2. Disinformation and manufactured narratives – The BCP alleged that several incidents followed similar “scripted patterns”, in which aggressors forcibly entered private prayer gatherings to disrupt services, “engineer chaos” and “record selective footage”, which was subsequently circulated on social media in edited form. According to the organisation, the videos were then used to make allegations of “forced conversion through inducement”, allegedly fuelling communal tension. BCP founder Herod Mullick said, “These edited videos are subsequently circulated online after false allegations of forced conversion to mislead local authorities and justify vigilante actions”. The organisation further alleged that such videos were presented to local district magistrates (DMs) and sub-divisional officers (SDOs) as evidence, and used to promote what it described as false narratives. The BCP rejected the allegations of forced conversion as “unfounded”, saying that “peaceful believers gathered for routine prayer are being falsely framed as perpetrators.”
3. Discriminatory police action and non-registration of complaints – The BCP further alleged that police responses to the incidents had been inconsistent. It said alleged aggressors were often allowed to leave the scene without immediate action, while injured believers and pastors who reported being victimised were taken to local police stations, “subjected to late-night questioning” and allegedly intimidated. Of the dozens of reported incidents, the BCP said FIRs have been registered in only 13 cases, and only “after extraordinary effort and legal intervention”. “In all other instances, local police authorities have displayed severe reluctance to accept formal written complaints from the victims,” the BCP added.
4. Institutional apathy and unaddressed concerns –The BCP also alleged that repeated appeals to local administrative authorities had failed, with officials “consistently declined to engage in dialogue with state church leaders or representatives of our organisation”, the organisation said. It further alleged that “no independent or impartial inquiries have been instituted to verify the authenticity of these viral video clips”. According to the BCP, “this persistent administrative apathy creates a climate of impunity for vigilante groups and deprives minority worshippers of equal protection under the law.”
Citing violations of Fundamental Rights guaranteed under Article 14 (Equality before Law), Article 19 (Freedom of Speech and Assembly), Article 21 (Protection of Life and Personal Liberty), and Article 25 (Freedom of Conscience and Free Profession, Practice, and Propagation of Religion) of the Constitution of India— the BCP urged the NHRC, WBHRC and NCM to direct the West Bengal Government and the director general of police (DGP) to conduct a high-level independent investigation of all the recent incidents of violence targeting the churches and prayer gatherings.
The organisation also sought an investigation into alleged cyber disinformation and circulation of edited videos allegedly intended to portray worshippers as perpetrators of violence. Additionally, the council pleaded for clear directions to the police and administration to immediately register FIRs in all pending cases and ensure prompt legal action against those responsible.
The BCP further requested the commissions to direct district administrations to provide police protection to vulnerable house churches and congregations during weekly prayer services, and to ensure that victims are not harassed, intimidated or pressured by law-enforcement authorities under alleged influence from vigilante or extremist groups.
After attending the public hearing, former Union culture secretary Jawhar Sircar shared a post on Facebook describing the recent attacks on Christian churches and communities in West Bengal as “tragic and unprecedented” and condemned the attacks as “dastardly”. Sircar expressed his support for the Christian community and their right to practice their faith peacefully.
