Adhikari launches Durga Puja festivities, cites adherence to religious norms
This is the first Durga Puja since the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in May this year, ousting the Trinamool Congress government
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday launched the festivities centred around this year’s Durga Puja, the biggest festival for people in the eastern state, at a grand ceremony at the Netaji Indoor Stadium in Kolkata.
“Our government decided that the Durga Puja (festivities) cannot be initiated during the Pitru Paksha phase. That’s why it is being launched today, as the Devi Paksha has begun. On one hand, we decided to maintain the cultural tradition of the Durga Puja; on the other hand, we decided to adhere to the religious norms and our scriptures,” he said.
This is the first Durga Puja since the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in May this year, ousting the Trinamool Congress government.
Former CM Mamata Banerjee faced criticism in 2025 from the opposition and some religious and Hindu rights organisations for inaugurating puja pandals before Mahalaya, which marks the transition from Pitru Paksha to Devi Paksha.
“Till last year, around 45,000 community pujas were organised by various clubs and organisations across the state. This year, the number has jumped by around 12,400. Earlier, people had to approach the Calcutta high court to seek permission to organise Durga Puja. This year, there has been no such instance to my knowledge,” Adhikari said while addressing the programme, which was attended by an audience of around 40,000.
West Bengal governor RN Ravi, ministers, senior bureaucrats and leaders from various spiritual organisations attended the programme. Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen also attended the event.
The dignitaries first attended a roadshow led by Adhikari and then attended the grand ceremony. Apart from the cultural programmes, at least 3,000 drones lit up the sky over the stadium, depicting Goddess Durga and scenes including the traditional Dhunuchi Naach.
The state tourism department and the information and cultural affairs department will organise special cultural programmes in various cities and tourist destinations, including one on Digha beach, over the next four days before the main Puja celebrations begin.
The new BJP government in the state had earlier reduced the grant for Durga Puja committees from 110,000 provided last year by the previous Mamata Banerjee-led government to ₹100,000 this year. It also announced a complete ban on DJs during the festivities and the closure of liquor outlets and bars on Maha Ashtami. The Durga Puja carnival, a pet project of Banerjee, has also been cancelled this year.

How to properly clean your solar panels (and why it's important)
Dirt can cut solar output, but cleaning only pays off when the numbers make sense.
Solar panels are outside for the duration of their working life, so it's optimistic to think they will remain spotless. Dust, pollen, bird droppings and sometimes a layer of mystery grime will build up on the glass — and if enough of it accumulates, the amount of sunlight reaching the cells below does get affected.
Not all roofs that are a little dusty require an emergency wash. The amount of cleaning that is necessary is highly dependent on the location, amount of rainfall, angle of the panels and what is on the panels. The bigger concern is cleaning them badly. Scratches on the coating, hard-water deposits and a zealous pressure washer can result in an even more costly issue than the dirt you began with.
Cleaning can help, but don't expect a magic 20 percent boost
The power loss of dirty panels is not a fixed number. According to the IEA Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme, soiling is responsible for approximately four to seven percent of global PV energy losses, and an NREL study revealed that pollen reduced energy production by up to 15 percent at several solar energy sites in North Carolina. Rain wasn't enough to completely fix it either, with wet mechanical cleaning improving performance by five to 11 percent.
Real-world results can be all over the place. In an informal test on YouTube, three progressively soiled 100-watt panels experienced a gain of approximately 2.4%, 10.8% and 13.4% following cleaning. Another Tesla rooftop array owner reported a much bigger improvement, but this one was partly based on projected output rather than a comparable control setup.
And that's the point. If a cleaner guarantees that washing your panels will automatically unlock another 20 percent, your roof may not be willing to comply. Uniform dust primarily means lost production. Localized mess can be more of a problem. Bird droppings may unevenly shade individual cells and contribute to hot spots, and salt-laden air and some pollutants may increase the risk of corrosion in more severe environments.
There's also the money. UC San Diego researchers found that panels that went 145 days without rain or cleaning lost 7.4% of their efficiency, but cleaning a typical 5kW residential system halfway through that period would have produced only about $20 in additional electricity before the drought ended.
If grime is costing you $20 a month in extra grid electricity and the cleaner is $200, then you have a 10-month payback. That only works if the loss persists for 10 months.
How to clean solar panels without making things worse
Always start with the manual for your panels. No, seriously. Manufacturers don't all recommend the same cleaning products. Some allow mild soap while others permit certain glass cleaners or limited isopropyl alcohol for stubborn marks. The safest place to start is still clean water.
Work during cool times of the day, preferably early morning or late evening, since solar panel temperature can affect performance too. Check the glass for cracks or damage first and contact your installer if you spot either. Otherwise, rinse gently with clean, low-mineral water. Use a soft sponge, cloth or non-abrasive extension brush for grime that will not come off. Rinse any approved cleaner off thoroughly.
Hard water can leave another light-blocking layer of mineral deposits behind as it dries, which rather defeats the point. Avoid abrasive pads, metal scrapers and pressure washing. Qcells states that improper cleaning can damage the glass or anti-reflective coating, cause delamination and leave the resulting damage outside its warranty. It also doesn't prescribe one fixed cleaning interval for every installation.
Your production data is a better clue. Cleaning may be worthwhile if output drops following a prolonged dry period or heavy pollen. If production appears normal, a dusty look alone may not justify paying someone to get on your roof. If reaching the panels requires climbing onto the roof and you're not trained for it, hire someone who is. Thumbtack says most people pay around $209 for professional solar-panel cleaning, with a national average range of $142 to $310.
Automatic cleaning systems are another option, from timer-controlled rooftop sprinklers to water-free robots. Smaller sprinkler systems are sold for homes, while fully autonomous robots are largely aimed at utility-scale sites. Ecoppia, for example, targets ground-mounted solar projects of 50MWp and larger.

Schumer truly said this days following the November 2022 midterm elections, specifically during a news conference about protecting Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals legislation. This week, social media users sharing his remark as a quote or video failed to mention that he said it almost four years ago. For example, one popular user misleadingly posted the matter as "BREAKING" and that Schumer "just" said it.
Less than a month away from the midterm elections on Nov. 3, people shared a rumor claiming U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said that "our ultimate goal" is to give citizenship to millions of migrants who already crossed a border into the U.S.
For example, on Tuesday, a popular X user posted (archived), "Sen. Chuck Schumer: 'Our ultimate goal' is to give every illegal alien citizenship."
(@LeadingReport via X)
On the same day, another popular user on Facebook posted (archived) a photo of Schumer with the word "BREAKING!" and police car light emojis, with a text caption reading, "BREAKING: Sen. Chuck Schumer just that 'Our ultimate goal' is to give every illegal alien citizenship. We knew this was their strategy and why they wanted open borders! Remember this when you vote!"
(David J Harris Jr. via Facebook)
Others shared videos of Schumer appearing to make the same comment, including on Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and X (archived).
The videos show Schumer talking behind microphones outside the Capitol in Washington, surrounded by people who at one point cheer him on. He speaks about protecting "Dreamers," a reference to Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — a federal immigration policy allowing some immigrants who came to the U.S. as children to receive temporary protection from deportation and eligibility for a renewable work permit:
Now more than ever, we're short of workers. We have a population that is not reproducing on its own with the same level that it used to. The only way we're going to have a great future in America is if we welcome and embrace immigrants, the "Dreamers" and all of them, because our ultimate goal is to help the "Dreamers" but get a path to citizenship for all 11 million or however many undocumented there are here.
In sum, Schumer truly said this. He made the remark in November 2022 as part of an effort to urge the Senate to pass protections for "Dreamers" during a lame-duck session of Congress, prior to the start of a fresh session in the new year. Users omitted that month and year from their posts.
Snopes emailed Schumer's office to ask if he still believed in what he said in the video, if he meant Democrats or "Dreamers" were the ones who had the "ultimate goal" he described and if he wished to share a statement responding to users reposting his comment. We will update this article if we receive further information.
More of Schumer's remarks
Schumer spoke about "our ultimate goal" and "Dreamers" on Nov. 16, 2022. He began his thoughts as follows (bolded emphasis ours, notes section from users' posts):
I believe in this so much. I believe in it in a personal basis because I know "Dreamers" who have been such great people here in America and who have just struggled every time they get a phone call, every time they walk down the street, they're worried, will someone grab them and take them away. So that's personal about them and what they have done. But I also believe in it as an overall, as an American who wants to see our country be stronger because immigrants make us stronger now more than ever.
Now more than ever, now more than ever, we're short of workers. We have a population that is not reproducing on its own with the same level that it used to. The only way we're gonna have a great future in America is if we welcome and embrace immigrants, the "Dreamers" and all of them because our ultimate goal is to help the "Dreamers" but get a path to citizenship for all 11 million or however many undocumented there are here, and we will be pursuing that in the next Senate, in the next Senate, the comprehensive immigration reform. Right now, our focus is on "Dreamers" and we retain the Senate.
Schumer later closed his comments, saying, "We will not stop fighting till we get a fix for DACA, a pathway to citizenship for Dreamers and a pathway to citizenship for all undocumented." More of the event is available to watch on C-SPAN and YouTube.
Senate Democrats ultimately failed to secure the 60 votes needed to pass the bipartisan immigration deal before the end of that year.
For further reading, we previously reported the untrue claim that Schumer had said in 1996, "The No. 1 reason people come to the U.S. illegally is to defraud systems like Social Security and I want to stop it."

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, fifteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty six startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. Capital, SBI Capital Markets, DAM Capital Startups That Have Taken The IPO Plunge In 2026 AceVector Founded by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, AceVector traces its roots to 2010, when the duo founded ecommerce platform Snapdeal. Over the years, this umbrella company expanded to include listed ecommerce enablement startup Unicommerce and house of brands Stellaro Brands. The three companies unified under the AceVector banner in 2022. Now, three years on, the consolidated entity is gearing up for a public market debut. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, AceVector filed its confidential DRHP with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in July 2025. The regulator greenlit the offering in November 2025. Almost a year later in September 2026, AceVector filed its red herring prospectus with the SEBI, which outlined a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS component of up to 4.16 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr at the upper end of the spectrum. Subsequently, AceVector’s public issue was oversubscribed 4.93X, receiving bids for 36.61 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer. The company eventually made a weak debut on the exchanges on October 5. Shares of AceVector listed at ₹28.30 on the BSE, a discount of 11.6% to its issue price of ₹32 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹28.32, an 11.5% discount to the IPO price. On the financial front, AceVector’s operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr in FY26 from ₹395 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, losses also shrank nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr versus ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Amagi Founded in 2008 by Baskar Subramanian, Srinivasan KA and Srividhya Srinivasan, Amagi offers a comprehensive cloud-based suite that enables broadcasters to create, manage, distribute, and monetise content worldwide. The platform also provides advanced broadcast and targeted advertising tools tailored for both traditional TV and streaming services. The company filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 and secured the markets regulator’s approval in November that year. In January 2026, Amagi filed its red herring prospectus (RHP), detailing a fresh issue of ₹816 Cr and an OFS component of up to 2.69 Cr shares. Subsequently, the public issue closed with an oversubscription of 30.2X. The company had set a price band of ₹343–361 per share for its public issue, valuing it at ₹7,966 Cr (nearly $885 Mn) at the upper end of the spectrum. The SaaS major’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the stock exchanges. The stock listed at ₹317 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 12.2% to the issue price of ₹361. On the NSE, it listed at ₹318 per share, 11.9% below the issue price. Financially, Amagi turned profitable in H1 FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹6.5 Cr as against a net loss of ₹66 Cr in H1 FY25. Operating revenue rose 35% YoY to ₹704.8 Cr. Aye Finance Founded in 2014 by Sanjay Sharma and Vikram Jetley, Aye Finance is an NBFC that leverages its AI-powered credit assessment platform to offer loans to small businesses across India. The company has raised $500 Mn to date from marquee investors such as Google, ABC Impact, and Dutch development bank FMO. In December 2024, Aye Finance filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, and received the markets regulator’s approval for its listing in April 2025. Nearly a year later in February 2026, the NBFC filed its RHP with SEBI for an ₹1,010 Cr IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹710 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹300 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an undersubscription of 97%, with investors cumulatively bidding for 4.42 Cr shares against 4.55 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a flat debut on the bourses, listing at the issue price of ₹129 on the BSE and the NSE. On the financial front, Aye Finance’s net profit declined 40% YoY to ₹64.6 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue rose 21.8% YoY to ₹843.5 Cr during the year-ago period. ESDS Software Solution Founded in 2005 by Piyush Somani, ESDS provides cloud computing, data centre, managed services, and AI-led digital solutions to government and enterprise customers. It operates five data centres in Navi Mumbai, Nashik, Bengaluru, Mohali, and Noida. The data centre company claims to have served 2,501 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with an average revenue per customer of around ₹19 Lakh. Backed by ace investor Ashish Kacholia, ESDS Software Solution has raised nearly $47.3 Mn in funding to date. ESDS first attempted to go public in September 2021 but the plan failed to materialise due to aftershocks of the pandemic. The company then refiled its papers in March 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in December 2025. As per its RHP, ESDS Software Solution’s public issue consisted solely of a fresh issue of shares worth ₹720 Cr. Its public issue, which stretched between August 28 and September 1, closed with an oversubscription of 135.88X. Subsequently, shares of the company made a stellar debut on the bourses, listing at ₹757 on the NSE, a premium of 76.5% over the issue price of ₹429. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹746.30, marking a gain of nearly 74% over the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a consolidated net profit of ₹120.8 Cr in FY26, up 117% from ₹55.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue rose 30.7% to ₹472.2 Cr from ₹361.3 Cr in FY25. Fractal Founded in 2000 by Srikanth Velamakanni, Pranay Agrawal, and Ashwath Bhat, Fractal is a SaaS unicorn that offers AI-powered analytics solutions to enterprises globally. Backed by TPG Capital, Khazanah Nasional, and Apax Partners, the startup has raised $800 Mn to date. It achieved unicorn status in 2022 and was last valued at more than $2 Bn. In August 2025, the SaaS unicorn filed its DRHP with SEBI, and received the markets regulator’s approval in November 2025. The company’s ₹2,833.9 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹1,023.54 Cr and an OFS worth up to ₹1,810.4 Cr. The public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.66X, with investors placing bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 1.86 Cr on offer. Fractal’s shares made a lacklustre debut on the exchanges and listed at ₹876 on the NSE, a discount of 2.7% to the issue price of ₹900. On the BSE, the shares listed flat at ₹900. On the financial front, Fractal’s profit declined about 3% YoY to ₹70.9 Cr in H1 FY26, while operating revenue grew 20% YoY to ₹1,559 Cr. Kissht Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a digital lending platform that offers personal and business loans up to ₹5 Lakh. It uses AI and machine learning to assess creditworthiness. It also offers health insurance products and credit against property. The startup has secured over $140 Mn till date from investors such as Vertex Growth, Brunei Investment Agency, Endiya Partners, and Ventureast. The lending tech startup filed its DRHP in August last year and received SEBI’s nod to proceed with its public listing in January 2026. As per its RHP, its IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹850 Cr and an OFS component of up to 44.4 Lakh shares. It had set a price band of ₹162-₹171 for the public issue, which was oversubscribed 9.5X. Subsequently, Kissht made a stellar debut on the bourses on May 8. The lending tech startup’s shares listed at ₹191 a piece on the BSE, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price of ₹171. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹190, up 11.1% from the issue price. On the financial front, the company reported a net profit of ₹199.3 Cr in 9M FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹1,569.9 Cr during the period under review. Klassroom Founded in 2016 by the mother-sons trio of Alka, Dhruv, and Dhumil Javeri, Klassroom is an edtech startup that operates at the intersection of offline and online coaching. It operates 30 offline partner centres that cater to both academic and skill-development needs. It also collaborates with state governments, private companies and education institutions to deliver academic and skilling programmes. The edtech startup also offers an AI-powered education OTT app that features over 100 courses for classes 8 to 12, and claims to have a footprint of over 4 Lakh registered users across the country. The startup raised over $2 Mn in private rounds from the likes of actor Suniel Shetty, ah! Ventures, LetsVenture, CPT Family Trust, Growth Sense and others. Kicking off its IPO proceedings in February 2026, Klassroom filed its DRHP with the BSE for an SME IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of up to 19.89 Lakh shares and an OFS component of up to 4.66 Lakh shares. The startup subsequently received the in-principle approval from BSE to move ahead with its public offering in May 2026. It had set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for the issue, looking to raise ₹39 Cr at a valuation of ₹148.1 Cr. Subsequently, the startup’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 1.46X. Shares of Klassroom listed on the BSE SME on August 7 at ₹170, a premium of 6.92% to the issue price of ₹159. With this, the company became the second listed edtech startup in the country, after PhysicsWallah. On the financial front, Klassroom posted an operating revenue of ₹23 Cr in FY26, up 128% from around ₹10 Cr in the year prior. Meanwhile, net profit jumped nearly 162% to ₹7.6 Cr from ₹2.9 Cr in FY25. LEAP India A brainchild of Sunu Mathew, LEAP India provides supply chain solutions through asset pooling, enabling companies to share pallets, containers, and other assets. Founded in 2013, the platform also offers inventory management, transportation, returnable packaging and tool repair. It also sells electric and fossil fuel-powered forklifts through its subsidiary TRON. LEAP India has raised over $184 Mn till date from investors like KKR and Sixth Sense Ventures. The startup first attempted to list on the bourses in 2022, eyeing a ₹1,000 Cr listing. But the plan was later shelved amid market volatility. Reigniting its IPO plans, the logistics tech startup then filed its DRHP with SEBI in August 2025, and received SEBI’s nod in December 2025. In August 2026, the company filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹480 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹2,000 Cr. The company then set a price band of ₹151 to ₹159 for its public issue, which eventually closed with an oversubscription of 8.38X as investors bid for 96.32 Cr shares as against 11.49 Cr shares on offer. Shares of LEAP India eventually made their debut on the bourses on August 14, listing at a premium of about 4.4% to the issue price of ₹159. The stock got listed at ₹166 on the BSE and ₹165.90 on the NSE. Financially, LEAP India’s net profits zoomed 65.3% to ₹62.3 Cr in FY26 as against ₹37.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Meanwhile, operating revenue climbed 56.4% to ₹729.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹466.5 Cr in FY25. Moneyview Founded in 2016 by Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, Moneyview started off as a personal finance platform before pivoting to digital lending. Today, it offers services such as UPI payments, gold SIPs, fixed deposits, digital gold, home loans, BNPL and insurance. The company claims to manage over ₹19,800 Cr in AUM and has raised more than $250 Mn in funding. It competes with players like listed fintech MobiKwik, IPO-aspirant Navi, and MoneyTap. It entered the unicorn club in 2024. In March 2026, the fintech startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in late-June 2026. In September 2026, the fintech unicorn filed its RHP. outlining an IPO with a fresh issue of shares worth ₹750 Cr and an OFS component of up to 10.04 Cr equity shares. The startup’s public issue then closed with an oversubscription of 98.46X, led by QIBs and NIIs. The digital lender made a bumper debut on the exchanges on October 1, with its shares listing at ₹55.6 on the BSE, a premium of 64% over the issue price of ₹34. On the NSE, the stock listed at ₹55, marking a premium of nearly 62% over the issue price. Moneyview’s operating revenue grew 43.3% to ₹3,351.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,339.1 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, net profit rose a marginal 1% to ₹242.7 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹240.3 Cr in FY25. Purple Style Labs Founded in 2015 by Abhishek Agarwal, Purple Style Labs is an omnichannel luxury house of brands featuring fashion labels like Pernia's Pop Up Studio & Shop, Wendell Rodricks, and Hemant Trevedi. It operates over 12 Pernia's Pop-Up Studio experience centres across India. Backed by Alchemy Capital Management, Bajaj Holdings and Investment, and Minerva Ventures, the startup has raised more than $78 Mn to date. In September 2025, the D2C brand filed its DRHP with SEBI for its public issue and received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. It then filed its RHP with SEBI in August 2026 for a public issue, which consisted entirely of a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹680 Cr, with no offer for sale component. Subsequently, Purple Style Labs’ public issue opened for subscription in late August 2026 and closed with an oversubscription of 1.29X, receiving bids for 88.54 Lakh shares against 68.49 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on September 7. The stock listed at ₹535 on the NSE, 6.96% lower than the issue price of ₹575. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹539, representing a discount of 6.26%. On the financial front, the startup’s consolidated net loss widened 51.5% to ₹285.4 Cr in FY26 as against ₹188.4 Cr incurred in the previous fiscal year. Operating revenue for the fiscal rose nearly 14% to ₹557.8 Cr from ₹489.9 Cr in FY25. RentoMojo Founded in 2014 by Geetansh Bamania and Ajay Nain, RentoMojo is an omnichannel rental platform to lease appliances, furniture, and furnishings. The startup operates an app, website and physical stores. It operates 20 warehouses and 82 offline stores across 29 cities. Backed by Accel, Chiratae Ventures and Bain Capital, the startup has raised over $45 Mn in funding to date. Hopping on the IPO bandwagon in March 2026, the rental platform filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO and received SEBI’s nod to float its public issue in July 2026. In September 2026, the startup finally filed its RHP with SEBI for an IPO, which comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹150 Cr and an OFS of up to 2.7 Cr shares. It had also set a price band of ₹384-₹404 per share for its IPO. The public issue opened for bidding on September 9 and closed on September 11. The IPO was oversubscribed 72.88X, receiving bids for 158.68 Cr shares against the 2.18 Cr shares on offer. Shares of RentoMojo made a strong stock market debut on September 17. The stock listed at ₹482.45 on the NSE, a premium of 19.42% over its issue price of ₹404. On the BSE, RentoMojo opened at ₹480, up 18.81% from the issue price. The IPO opened despite RentoMojo cofounder and former COO Nain earlier filing a petition before the NCLT’s Bengaluru bench to stall the IPO proceedings. Alleging oppression and mismanagement, the plea claimed that incomplete or inaccurate information was shared with him and sought to declare his 2023 sale of 2,223 shares void ab initio. On the financial front, RentoMojo reported a profit after tax of ₹104.3 Cr in FY26, up 142% from ₹43.1 Cr in the previous fiscal, aided by a tax credit of ₹36.6 Cr. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 45.5% to ₹387 Cr during the year under review from ₹266 Cr in FY25. SEDEMAC Founded in 2007 by IIT-Bombay professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Amit Dixit, and Manish Sharma, SEDMAC designs electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The deeptech company produces motor control units, integrated starter generators, fuel injection systems, genset controllers, and small industrial powertrains. Backed by Xponentia Capital Partners, A91 Partners, and 360 ONE Asset, SEDMAC has raised over $107 Mn to date. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the deeptech company filed its DRHP with SEBI in November 2025 and received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in February 2026. Its public issue comprised solely an OFS component of up to 80.43 Lakh shares. The IPO was oversubscribed 2.68X, with investors cumulatively bidding for 1.51 Cr shares against 56.32 Lakh shares on offer. Shares of the company made a stellar debut on the exchanges on March 11, listing at a premium of 13.5% on the NSE. The stock opened at ₹1,535 as against the issue price of ₹1,352 per share. On the BSE, the stock listed at ₹1,510, a premium of 11.7% to the issue price. SEDEMAC reported a net profit of ₹71.4 Cr in the first nine months of FY26, while operating revenue stood at ₹770.66 Cr during the period under review. Shadowfax Founded in 2015 by Vaibhav Khandelwal and Abhishek Bansal, Shadowfax is a logistics company that offers hyperlocal and on-demand delivery solutions for businesses. Competing with the likes of Delhivery, LoadShare and Pickrr, the logistics major is backed by names such as Flipkart, Mirae Asset Venture Investments (India), IFC, Nokia Growth Partners, Qualcomm and Trifecta Capital. Shadowfax pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI in July 2025 for an IPO, and received markets regulator's nod in October 2025. It filed its updated DRHP with SEBI in November 2025. The company’s IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹1,000 Cr and an OFS of up to ₹907 Cr. The company’s public issue closed with an oversubscription of 2.72X, receiving total bids for 24.23 Cr shares against 8.9 Cr on offer. Subsequently, shares of the company made a muted debut on the bourses on January 28. The stock listed at ₹112.60 apiece on the NSE, a discount of 9.19% to the issue price of ₹124. On the BSE, shares of the logistics unicorn debuted at ₹113, down 8.87% below the issue price. In H1 FY26, the logistics unicorn’s net profit more than doubled to ₹21 Cr from ₹9.8 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue surged 68.4% YoY to ₹1,805.6 Cr during the period. Shiprocket Founded in 2017 by Saahil Goel, Vishesh Khurana, Akshay Gulati, and Gautam Kapoor, Shiprocket aggregates third-party logistics providers. It claims to partner 17 courier firms like Delhivery, FedEx, Aramex, Xpressbees, DTDC, and Shadowfax and serves over 24,000 pin codes across India. The logistics unicorn has raised over $323 Mn to date from investors like Temasek, Bertelsmann, Tribe Capital, Lightrock, and Zomato. Kicking off its IPO proceedings, the Zomato-backed unicorn in May 2025 confidentially pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI and received the regulator’s approval in October 2025. Shiprocket then filed its RHP with the markets regulator in August 2026. The logistics major’s ₹1,617 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS component of up to ₹732 Cr. Subsequently, in mid-August 2026, Shiprocket’s public issue opened to healthy market response and closed with an oversubscription of 99.38X, receiving bidding for 938.53 Cr shares against 9.44 Cr shares on offer. Shares of the company made a strong debut on the D-Street on August 19. The stock listed at ₹131 on the NSE, marking a premium of 35.05% to the issue price of ₹97. On the BSE, it debuted at ₹129.50, a premium of 33.51%. On the financial front, Shiprocket’s operating revenue rose 24% to ₹2,024 Cr in FY26 from ₹1,632 Cr in the previous fiscal year. However, net loss widened over 6% to ₹79.2 Cr during the fiscal from ₹74.5 Cr in FY25. Turtlemint Founded in 2015 by Dhirendra Mahyavanshi and Anand Prabhudesai, Turtlemint operates an insurtech platform that enables financial advisors to distribute car, bike, health, and term life insurance to their customer networks. It claims to serve over 3 Lakh advisors nationwide. The startup has raised more than $197 Mn to date from investors such as Amansa Capital, Jungle Ventures, Peak XV Partners, Vitruvian Partners, and Nexus Venture Partners. In September 2025, Turtlemint pre-filed its DRHP with SEBI, and secured market regulator’s approval three months later in December. Subsequently, the insurtech unicorn filed its RHP in June 2026. The IPO comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹660.7 Cr and an OFS of 1.46 Cr shares. Its public issue opened on June 19 and closed on June 23, with an oversubscription of 1.2X. Despite this, the startup made a muted debut on the bourses on June 29. Shares of the insurtech startup listed at ₹134.90 on the NSE, a discount of 11.25% to the issue price of ₹152. On the BSe, the stock listed at ₹136.2 apiece on the BSE, a discount of 10.4% to the issue price. The insurtech company’s net loss rose 19% to ₹184.7 Cr in the first nine months (9M) of FY26 as against a net loss of ₹154.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed 80% to ₹741.1 Cr from ₹411.1 Cr in 9M FY25. Startups That Have Filed DRHP Atomberg Founded in 2012 by Manoj Meena and Sibabrata Das, Atomberg began as a B2B supplier of energy-efficient BLDC fans before entering the D2C segment in 2016. It has since expanded to manufacture mixer grinders, water purifiers, and small appliances. The startup designs and manufactures its products in India and sells them via offline retailers, online marketplaces and its own website. Backed by names such as Steadview Capital, Jungle Ventures and A91 Partners, Atomberg has raised over $126 Mn in funding to date. Taking the first step towards its public listing, the D2C appliance brand, in July 2026, converted into a public entity and changed the name of its parent entity from Atomberg Technologies Pvt Ltd to Atomberg Technologies Ltd. In August 2026, the startup filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO, which will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. The startup is also considering raising up to ₹90 Cr through a pre-IPO placement. On the financial front, Atomberg’s losses widened 26.5% to ₹149 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹117.8 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Meanwhile, operating revenue grew 34.8% to ₹1,293.8 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹959.5 Cr in FY25. AVPL International (AITMC Ventures) Founded in 2016 by Preet Sandhuu and Deep Sisai, AITMC sits at the intersection of agriculture and drones. It manufactures drones, offers drone-as-a-service, and runs more than 70 drone training centres across 16 states. In July 2025, AITMC kicked off its IPO plans once again as the company’s board approved a proposal to increase the fresh issue size of its IPO to ₹200 Cr from ₹125 Cr previously. AITMC then filed its draft papers with SEBI via the confidential pre-filing route in October 2025. It received the markets regulator’s nod to float its IPO in January 2026. Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

Loneliness among parents whose adult children have migrated abroad is associated with higher psychological distress, difficulties in regulating emotions and problematic series watching, an exploratory study by researchers from NIMHANS has found.
The findings assume relevance on World Mental Health Day, observed on October 10, which draws attention to mental health and the need to address psychological well-being. The study highlights the emotional challenges that parents may experience when their children settle abroad and everyday family interactions become less frequent.
64 ‘empty-nest’ parents
Published in BMC Research Notes, the study examined 64 ‘empty-nest’ parents aged between 45 and 65, whose adult children had emigrated and lived away from home for at least two years. The sample comprised 30 fathers and 34 mothers from different families in Karnataka, Haryana and Punjab. Most belonged to middle socioeconomic backgrounds and nuclear families, and more than half had been in the empty-nest phase for over five years.
Rajesh Kumar, associate professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and the corresponding author of the study, said the findings highlighted the relationship between loneliness and emotional well-being among parents adjusting to life without their children at home.
“We found a significant association between loneliness and psychological distress. Loneliness was also associated with difficulties in emotion regulation and problematic series watching, which refers to excessive or difficult-to-control viewing that interferes with everyday functioning. This also resulted in the risk of developing non-communicable diseases (NCDs),” he said.
Loneliness significantly predicted psychological distress even after accounting for age and gender. Of the 64 participants, 22 (34.3%) were classified as having higher levels of loneliness, while 42 (65.7%) fell into the lower-loneliness group. Those reporting higher loneliness also reported greater psychological distress, more difficulties in regulating emotions and higher levels of problematic series watching, Mr. Kumar said.
Social changes
Manoj Kumar Sharma, professor in the department of clinical psychology at NIMHANS and head of its SHUT Clinic, said the findings needed to be understood in the context of the emotional and social changes that parents may experience when their children settle abroad.
Dr. Sharma, who is one of the authors, cautioned that the study did not establish that loneliness causes psychological distress or excessive series watching. As it was cross-sectional, it could identify associations but not determine the direction of the relationships, he said.
Mothers reported greater loneliness
Women in the study reported significantly higher levels of loneliness and psychological distress than men.
The researchers said that this was consistent with earlier research suggesting that mothers may experience greater emotional difficulties during the empty-nest phase, potentially reflecting their involvement in caregiving and emotional relationships with their children.
Possible coping mechanism
The researchers said digital media and streaming services could provide an easily accessible form of solitary leisure for parents experiencing less day-to-day interaction with their children.
However, the study did not examine why participants watched series or whether they used viewing deliberately to cope with loneliness or negative emotions. The researchers cautioned against assuming that excessive viewing was necessarily a coping response.
Other factors that could influence media use include social support, physical mobility, retirement, living arrangements, marital relationships, the frequency and quality of communication with adult children, and access to technology.
Social and psychological support
The findings underline the need to pay greater attention to the emotional well-being of parents whose children migrate abroad, as changing family structures and international migration can reduce opportunities for regular face-to-face interaction, Dr. Sharma said.
The authors said interventions to strengthen social connectedness, promote adaptive emotion-regulation strategies and encourage healthier technology use could potentially help parents navigate the empty-nest transition.

'Disrespect for wildlife': Multiple grizzly bear poaching incidents under investigation in Alberta
Body of bear found abandoned with paws removed in northern Alberta
WARNING: This story contains graphic images of grizzly bears killed by poachers.
Provincial officials are investigating multiple cases of poachers killing grizzly bears in Alberta.
The province told CBC News that Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement Services is investigating the illegal killings of four grizzly bears at three separate locations.
One grizzly bear was found shot dead Sept. 30, along a road about 20 kilometres north of Swan Hills, northwest of Edmonton.
The next day on Oct. 1, another grizzly was found dead in a remote area between Little Smoky and Fox Creek. All four of the bear's paws had been removed.
It comes after two grizzly bears were found shot dead in June along a road near Sundre, about 95 kilometres northwest of Calgary.
And in March of this year, the province announced it was seeking public assistance in a poaching investigation after a grizzly bear was found dead from a gunshot wound in November 2025.
"The illegal killing of any grizzly bear is taken seriously," the province told CBC News in a statement.
This grizzly bear was found dead off Deep Valley Road between Little Smoky and Fox Creek in northern Alberta on Oct. 1. The bear had been shot and moved off the main trail, and all four of its paws had been removed. (Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement/Facebook)
Hunting grizzlies has been banned in Alberta since 2006, with the exception of harvesting by Indigenous hunters for subsistence or cultural purposes.
The province is asking that anyone with information about these poaching incidents or other suspected wildlife offences contact the Report-A-Poacher line or submit a report online at alberta.ca/report-poacher.
Through the province's Report-A-Poacher program, a tipster who provides information leading to charges being laid could be eligible for a cash reward.
'Disregard and disrespect for wildlife'
Gordon Stenhouse, the biologist behind much of Alberta's grizzly bear population research, said shooting grizzly bears and abandoning their bodies is "disappointing" but doesn't surprise him, as "people have been doing that for a long time."
"To shoot and leave any animal, and especially a grizzly bear, a threatened species, shows a disregard and disrespect for wildlife," he said.
This grizzly bear was found shot dead on Sept. 30, about 20 kilometres north of Swan Hills in northern Alberta. (Alberta Fish and Wildlife Enforcement/Facebook)
Stenhouse said it's likely the number of bears found after being poached is "probably only a fraction of what's actually happening."
"I think there's lots of bears that are never found," he said.
- More grizzly bears killed in 2024 than any other year on record in Alberta
- Grizzly bear killings have spiked through provincial program; government says recovery still priority
The Alberta government keeps track of human-caused grizzly bear mortality. From 2020 to 2025, there were 28 documented cases of grizzly bears killed illegally — about 17 per cent of grizzly bear deaths during that time. Other leading causes of grizzly bear mortality include being killed by the province and struck by vehicles.
Grizzly bears have been a threatened species in Alberta since 2010.
University of Alberta ecology professor Mark Boyce said he doesn't consider poaching "a major issue" when it comes to grizzly bear conservation, but he considers these latest incidents "really unfortunate."
"There's a black market for grizzly bear paws," he said. "It's highly illegal, but poaching the bear was highly illegal in the first place."
A file photo of Mark Boyce, ecology professor and Alberta Conservation Association chair in fisheries and wildlife at the University of Alberta. (BoompaCanada/Flickr)
In addition to financial motivation, Boyce said poaching can happen because people hate or fear grizzly bears.
Better co-existence needed: bear safety expert
Bear Safety and More founder Kim Titchener says she considers poaching a symptom of a larger conflict between humans and bears struggling to share the landscape.
"We do live with grizzly bears in Alberta," Titchener said. "When they come into communities, walk onto a golf course, go onto a rancher's land ... we start to see conflicts with these animals."
"For some people, it creates a lot of fear and they want to get rid of bears. For other people, they want to try to live with these animals."
- Grizzly bear trapped, killed after trying to break into central Alberta chicken coop
- Honey-hunting grizzlies are 'one of the realities' for beekeepers in Bearberry, Alta.
Titchener says communities in and around bear country should prioritize resources such as electric fencing, guard dogs and bear-resistant containers over killing grizzly bears.
"You can go and shoot and kill that bear that is killing your chickens, but another bear is just going to show up and eat your chickens too," she said. "So you really need to address the cause of this."
- Conservation groups call for 'science-based' approach to Alberta grizzly bear hunt proposal
- 'No plans right now' for grizzly hunting season in Alberta, minister says as rural residents call for hunt
The Alberta government announced in 2024 it would invest $700,000 over five years to help keep large carnivores away from rural properties in southwestern Alberta, including setting up electric fencing, upgrading grain bins and removing dead livestock.
The province supports BearSmart programs across Alberta in an effort to minimize the risk of human-wildlife conflict and reduce grizzly bear deaths.
The province estimates there are about 1,000 grizzlies in Alberta today, though there hasn't been a provincial grizzly bear population study since 2018.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Erin Keating, an executive analyst for Cox Automotive. It has been edited for length and clarity.
People should scare themselves. In public.
I tested that theory out in my mid-40s by taking five seasons of improv classes at the DC Improv Comedy Club. My goal was not to become a comedian — I wanted to take on a challenge that I could easily fail at.
And to add to the pressure, I had to perform in front of my family.
I work as an executive analyst in the auto industry at Cox Automotive. I distill data to explain the industry's market dynamics to automakers, dealership groups, lenders, and journalists. The material I cover can quickly get boring if I'm not careful.
Some of those conversations happen in small rooms, others happen in high-pressure settings: on stages in front of hundreds or thousands of people, on live television, at product unveilings, in podcasts, you name it.
I also consider myself an introvert. I didn't always feel so comfortable in front of people — and I certainly haven't always been the funniest person in the room.
Getting on the stage
At my first major corporate presentation, I couldn't stop sweating. My colleagues said I was good, but I was talking too fast. Their feedback was basically, "You did fine. Slow down."
I improved over time and got less sweaty when talking in front of people. There was still more I could learn.
I decided to take the improv classes in 2018 because, honestly, I was a little bit bored. I had just left a marketing communications job and was trying to figure out what to do next.
I knew I liked talking: I was hosting a successful podcast about books, but I wanted to be better at having conversations. Loving to talk is definitely not the same as being a good conversationalist.
The classes with a cast of characters…
So, I joined my first class. I was there with a biology teacher, a German woman who was really funny, an older woman who had done a ton of onstage acting, and a handful of people (like me) who were nervous about participating. The majority of us stuck it out for our five consecutive seasons.
At the beginning, I fought against my preconception that I had to be funny.
I remember playing a game called "Die, not today," where we had to mime throwing a hammer or a spear at each other. If the object was heading your way, you had to come up with how you'd survive the attack on the spot. Most people just tried to shield themselves, but one woman staged a dramatic scene where a spear nearly struck her nose. She grabbed it at the last second, saving her (improv-ed) life. It was amazing.
… And their lessons
Improv is really about paying attention to what another person is giving you. You have to build upon the scenario they set up, a principle called "yes, and." You accept the premise someone introduces, and add something to it.
You also learn about status. In a scene, you might be the character driving the action. In your next, you could be supporting the other person's arc. Scenes are most interesting when you watch people respond to each other and create together through those statuses. Some of the worst scenes are when two people are just trying to compete to be the funniest.
All of that applies to work and your life more than you might realize.
Before I speak at big conferences, I talk to people in the audience to understand the energy in the room and what is on their minds. I don't like working from a script. It can get too prescriptive and keep you from responding to the people in front of you. I'm listening for the thought that is begging for a "yes, and."
The same goes for one-on-one conversations. When someone talks, improv has taught me to follow the unexpected and respond to what was actually said.
Those skills also matter a lot for office politics. Those classes taught me to recognize an awkward moment, assess the reaction, and apologize if I misread it. I am now comfortable saying, "Thank you for receiving that with the intent it was given," when I know I don't express myself well.
The final big lesson was authenticity. Near the end of my third improv season, I jumped into a scene and used the New York Jewish-grandmother voice I'd always been able to pull off (do not ask me to do other accents — even when I think I sound like a señorita, I always revert back to that Eastern European drawl.)
I'd avoided that voice because I thought, "This is not acting, I'm not supposed to do that." But for that scene, it was exactly what my partner needed. My classmate asked me why I had never done it.
That voice was a breakthrough for me. I realized I could bring my whole self to that stage.
Onto the next challenges
Human skills are becoming more important, especially as AI changes how we work.
Sure, technical skills will remain important. But I think people who can listen, relate to others, read a room, and recover gracefully from an uncomfortable moment will have a real advantage.
Those are human skills that you can't fake by memorizing a script.
So, I suggest doing the thing that scares you: get onstage, take a class, give the speech. You may sweat, and you may talk too fast. But you'll get through it — and learn something about how you show up for the people around you.
I plan to keep testing that theory myself. My first stand-up comedy class starts on Tuesday.
And I'm terrified.

Cairo, Oct 11: A Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, less than a day after a missile struck it and killed 12 people.
There were no immediate details about the latest strike, which hit the same complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights.
The sharp escalation in the new front in the Iran war threatens to draw in greater US military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the rebels.
The strike came shortly after the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.
Saturday's missile attack on the Riyadh international airport was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 people were wounded, some of them critically.
The strike on Sunday occurred as King Khalid International Airport remained closed and authorities moved schools in the capital online.
At stake, again, are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz -- along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.
Trump says he is weighing joining strikes against rebels
Trump on Saturday said he was considering whether to join Saudi strikes against the rebels. He later said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf.
Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defence support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the US has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.
Meanwhile, deeper US involvement in an unpopular regional war could further threaten Trump's Republican party in upcoming midterm elections. Both Trump and Iran insist the American election calendar has no effect on their decisions on how to end the seven-month-old conflict.
Houthis have targeted Saudi airports, military and oil facilities
As the Riyadh airport remained closed until at least 9 pm Sunday, according to Flightradar24, fighting continued in Yemen.
Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60 per cent of them women and children.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.
And there remained no claim of responsibility for the Saturday attack on Riyadh airport, though the Houthis at times have kept silent when an attack brought widespread international condemnation.
But the rebels have acknowledged targeting Saudi airports and oil installations in recent days, and on Sunday they again warned: “all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theatre of operations for our forces."
Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the group's military spokesperson, wrote on X that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina were exempt.
The dead in the airport attack included several nationalities
The missile on Saturday struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorised to speak to the media.
A Saudi statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, who worked for Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.
The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, a relative told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida. Her niece, Nisreen Oweida, said she had left during Syria's civil war. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot, and a Sudanese national. The airport has no military facilities.
Iran can use the Houthis to pressure a key US ally
Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key US ally.
The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognised government.
Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July, when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land. That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas.
Now, fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb, a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.
But Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire. “Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign,” he said. (AP)

Conventional wisdom is that cars are bad investments. Drive one off the lot, and it starts losing value the minute its wheels touch the road. That makes what’s happening with the 2026 Toyota Rav4 downright weird.
Some used vehicles are listing for $3,000 to $6,000 above brand-new dealership prices, according to new data from the online automotive marketplace CarGurus. The months-old cars are aging like fine wine.
The crossover SUV—one of the top-selling in the US—went all-hybrid last year, after Toyota announced it would drop the gas-powered model from its lineup. That’s likely why we’re catching a glimpse of an economic Upside Down. Kevin Roberts, director of economic and market intelligence at CarGurus, says the situation reminds him of the pandemic-era chip shortage, when a supply crunch for new cars also drove up used prices, and buyers flipped them months later for a profit.
“Hybrid demand is so strong, the Rav4 is still in that 2021 world,” he says. Toyota can’t make new models fast enough.
The leaves are changing, and America’s hot hybrid summer has become a toasty hybrid autumn, for new cars and for old ones. Toyota reported this month that its hybrid sales are up 29 percent in the third quarter of 2026; Kia said its sales more than doubled. Nearly one in six new US cars sold is a hybrid, according to Cox Automotive data.
“The American market has a reputation for gas guzzlers, but we're starting to shake that reputation because of how much we like hybrids,” Roberts says.
The major driver is gas prices. They’ve skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war and the ensuing conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, a global center of oil and gas production and shipping. Nationally, a gallon costs an average of $4.40, up 40 percent from this time last year, according to AAA; Californians pay an average of $6.36. Car buyers are a simple bunch, Roberts says—when prices start rising, they immediately look for more fuel-efficient cars. Soon, drivers actually start buying them.
For now, struggles in the US electric vehicle market are hybrids’ gain. New EV sales are down by almost half from last year, after the Trump administration cut a federal tax credit that made the often-expensive powertrains more affordable. Unlike electrics, hybrids don’t necessarily force drivers out of their familiar gas station routines. (Even plug-in hybrids sometimes need a gas top-up, though smart owners depend mostly on electricity.) Finally, more hybrids are available now than before. A buyer interested in nearly every major sort of passenger vehicle—three-row SUVs, pickups, minivans, or luxury cars—can find one with the powertrain
Interest has spread to the used market, where hybrid prices are up almost 5 percent over last year, according to the automotive data website iSeeCars.com. At $34,500, the average price of used hybrids is higher than used EVs or gas-powered cars. Used buyers seem to be especially keen on long-term fuel savings.
Hybrid tech has been around for decades, but it still may be just the beginning of its reign in the US. “Certainly from a philosophical, functional, and cost perspective, they make the most sense,” says Karl Brauer, iSeeCars’ executive analyst. Several hybrid models already outsell their gas counterparts, including the Toyota Highlander and the Ford Maverick. Soon, he predicts, most US cars will come with a hybrid drivetrain.
US automakers seem to see the hybrid writing on the wall. At the beginning of the decade, General Motors said that 40 percent of its 2025 lineup would be electric. That didn’t happen, and the subsequent pivot left it well behind its Asian counterparts in the new hybrid race. Now, GM has changed its tune. Hybrids “are part of the plan,” an executive told CNBC this week. “We’re not tone-deaf to our customers. We know what they want, and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can.”

Republicans face midterm backlash from factory workers squeezed out of jobs by Trump's tariffs
President Donald Trump's tariffs are turning factory workers against his Republican Party over fears the import taxes could lead to fewer jobs instead of the manufacturing renaissance he promised
